A new German alloy of aluminium, magnesium, and zinc is called Zimalium. It is slightly heavier than aluminium, has greater tensile strength, and is harder and more suitable for working. It can be made into wire and sheets like Lrass, while the castings can be filed, forged, cut, planed, &c. It resists chemical action less than aluminium, has only two-thirds as great electric conductivity, and costs about 10 per cent. more.

Rumours of Another Royal Marriage.—lt is not only among the younger Royalties that engagements and weddings are on the taps, for there has been talk that the King of Belgium is contemplating a second marriage with an Orleans Princess. Ring Leopold is now seventy and was only eighteen years of age when he married in 1853, a year before the Emperor Francis Joseph wedded the late ill-fated Empress of Austria. Both these reigning soverAgns took to themselves very young brides of not more than sixteen or seventeen, and their after life was also in both cases not altogether free from the unhappiness that so often attends early marriages. This fact was further exemplified in the unhappy relations in the family of King Leopold, whose two daughters were both married before they had reached their eighteenth year. Princess Eon's Ball.—Princess Henry of Battenberg, who, like Queen Alexandra, seems to have discovered a charm against all attacks of Father time, is to give a , dance next week at Kensington Palace. it will be 1 Princess Ena's ball, and the guests will include a great many of the younger members of the Royal Family, amongst whom engagements and weddings are so much in evidence this season. The Duke of Saxe-Coburg and his fiancee, who have been staying with the Duchess of Albany at Claremont, are expected to be present, and , also Princess Beatrice of Saxe-Coburg, and Prince and Princess Alexander of Teck. The two pretty and in-. teresting young Princesses of Connaught and their brother Prince Arthur will be among the dancers, and of course Prince Austarius Adolphus of Sweden will be with his fiancee. He has been staying at Clarence House with the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, and was received the other day, on hisarrival, by the Ring who had not seen the Prince before. Princess Margaret's future husband is not overburdened with wealth, and ,the sllowance voted him by the Norwegian Parliament I Is only £2,800 %year. The Union Jack Club.—The Ring and practically all the members of the Royal Family staying in London, were present at the concert at the Albert Hall in aid of the Union Jack Club. The institution is intended to be a sort of Soldiers'and Sailors'Home in the Metropolis but it is upon a larger and more ambitious scale than usual, and owes its inception and success to Miss Ethel McCaul. Sir George White, and Sir lan Hamilton are amoogst the many leading military men who have given their assistance to the scheme, for which something like £70,000 is required. The greater part of this has already been raised and the sum derived from the Albert Hall concert, will go far to cover the outstsnding balance. An entertainment has only to be fashion.tble to be an astonishing success, and nearly all the great people of the social world were present at the concert, whilst the majority of the Souvenir sellers' were well known women of title.

Princess Henry of Pless.—Princess Henry of Pleas who has returned from the Continent for the season, is in a somewhat similar position to that of the daughter of the late Sir Blundell Maple, who by the condition of her father's will, is required to reside for during the greater part of the year in this country. Princess Henry, who is a sister of the Duchess of Westminster has hitherto spent much of her time over here, but the father of Prince Henry does not like his son and daughter-in-law being so much away, and has stipulated that they must spend at least six months of the year in Germany. To a girl so familiar with fashionable life in London, the society of Furstenburg can hardly have very great attractions, but she will now be less able to follow her inclinations in this matter, than hitherto....

Going to Extremes.—The preachini of the simple life is surely carried to extreme when the moralist tells women that it is wrong to wear pearls because the fisher is liable to be eaten by sharks. On the same principle we should have to give up many of the most beautiful furs, and refrain from eating fish because of the dangerous calling of the fishermen. Similar reasons would also prevent us from using coal, and in fact from enjoying most other advantages derived from the re- sources and progress of the world. Such matters as the taking of the osprey plume, or the use of the tight bearing-rein, which involves wanton cruelty, are in a different category, but good causes are always more or less spoiled by the extremists, and the pearl-fisher, the hunter, miner, and fisherman, would all strongly advise the moralist to mind his or her own business,

The Spring Bogey.—Once more the crinoline bogey is being trotted out, but we have become so used to its appearance when May comes round, that we have ceased to be frightened by it. Fashions in dress can rule us in many ways, and afflict us with many inconveniences, but it may safely be said that it is beyond even the pow-ers of Dame Fashion to revive the horrors of the crinoline period. That fantastic Old Lady is in fact no longer the arch tyrant she was, and despite her decrees, the idea that clothes are made for women, and not woman for her clothes, is steadily, if slowly, making headway, Some women are seriously contemplating the formation of an Anti-Crinoline League, but there is really little occasion for them to bother themselves, as The "unspeakable thing" would prove an impossibility in these advanced days. .

Paper Headgear.-:Paper hats promise to have a tremendous vogue this summer, and very dainty, pretty, and becoming they are. Strands of soft paper are so plaited as to give the appearance of a fine rush straw, and the crowns and brims are carefully wired, so as to avoid all suggestion of floppiness. Som are trimmed with wreaths of roses, others with soft silken scarves, while more dressy specimens, intended for garden parties, water fetes, etc., have ruches of Valenciennes lace about the crown. Provided the weather is kind, such headgear will stand quite a moderate amount of wear, but need- less to say the faintest suggestion of the "little summer shower" is disastrous in the extreme. When on boating or picnic excursions, an emergency cap should always be carried by the wearer of this particular form of head- gear. which by the way, is of little use to the cyclist, golfist, or motorist. These bats are wonderfully light, And cool to wear, and taken altogether. are a marvellous improvement upon the lamp-shade arrangements we had last year. A Healthy Craze.--The craze for ju-jitsu culture is steadily gaining ground and Society could employ its time very much less usefully, than in following the majority of the ninety-seven rules laid down for students of the cult. First and foremost, the student must sleep with his or her window open top and bottom, and take an hours' walk before breakfast. Two quarts of water must be swallowed in every 21 hours, and sugar is for- bidden, while two meals per day only—breakfast and dinner—are deemed necessary. Hurry and excitement must be avoided, daily exercise, such as swimming or gymnastics are compulsory, and a complete rest is advised to be taken every afternoon. If the Society girl and woman would follow these rules as far as possible through the season, there would be fewer haggard faces, and less talk about "rest cures," than is the case usually, when July comes round. Concerning Cures.—The "White Cure" is the one preferred at the moment, and many smart women set aside an apartment in their establishment in which this can he taken. The room has white e-ails and ceiling, furniture, hangings, and carpet, and the patient when in residence" wears white and white only. After a few days of this bleaching treatment, she emerges with her complexion marvellously restored, and her nerves wonderfully refreshed' MADGE.

div.head: PLUTOCRATS AND ARISTOCRATS.
div.p: PLUTOCRATS AND ARISTOCRATS.

Dreadful pictures are drawn for us by indignant ladies living in comfortable villas, or by young gentlemen in Bloomsbury lodgings, of the extrava- gance and frenzied luxury of the upper classes, says Ella Hepworth-Dixon in a ladies' paper. Of gambling, of extravagance in dress, of bridge scandals we have heard enough and to spare, and that there is a cel;tain amount of truth in some of these accusations none can deny; but the charge of over-feasting and intemperance which is so often brought against our aristocracy is so absurd as scarcely to need refutation. There will always, in every society, be a certain number of gourmets and epicures of the wine-cup, but I suppose it may fairly be said that good society in England has never been so sober and even so abstemious as at the beginning of the twentieth century. The ostentation which we shall see displayed during the next two months in London will be in the mansions of the plutocrat, not in the homes of the men and women of ancient lineage. Nothing, indeed, astonishes the intelligent foreigner or the visiting American more than the perfect simplicity of young girls who are making their debut in the best English society. In short, the simple life is more often led in the stately homes of England than is generally supposed. Exercise, early hours, sports in the open air, hygienic clothing, short, well- cooked meals, and a fair amount of work are the usual lot of Britain's aristocracy.

div.head: SMART COAT AND Srlirr.
div.p: SMART COAT AND Srlirr.

The sketch !thews a smart coat and skirt for immediate wear. The material used for its con- struction is a very fine faced cloth, in the palest shade of biscuit. The coat it very well cut, and fits closely to the figure, being finished with a stitched collar and double revers of corded silk exactly matching the cloth in tone, jet buttons being used as a further ornamentation on the coat. The sleeves puff to the elbow, where they, end in a short accordion-pleated frill of the corded silk; the long suede gloves which axe

worn with the costume being also a perfect snatch. The skirt is long and full, and is almost covered by the deep basque attached to the coat. The basque is so arranged that it may be de- tached at will, leaving the tight-fitting coat and long skirt quite complete for wear on warm days. The front may ho of lace, tinted to match the cloth; or may be of some note of colour struck by the small floral toque which accompanies this spring costume.

GOSSIP.
Mrs. Humphry Ward has already finished her new novel, and it will be commenced in the Century Ragazine for September.
Miss Alice Balfour, who has been far from well during the spring, is gaining much benefit from her visit to the Riviera. She will be home in time for the mid-season.

Just now, if one were to speak of the "new woman," one would mean a character very different from that which was so spoken of ten or fifteen years ago. To-day. declares Household Words, the "new woman" is the woman who is turning her back on public affairs, business, agitation, and examinations.

div.head: ABOUT SLUM.
div.p: ABOUT SLUM.

One of the most noticeable features of the pre- sent season's fashions is the great variety in the arrangement of our sleeves. Two features they all possess in common—they must be full at the shoulder and they must fit tightly at tho wrist. Apart from these their variety is endless. The elbow sleeve is very popular just now, and for those who possess beautiful arms it is a pretty fashion._ For those who do not—and I venture

to think they are in the majority—there, is the little close-fitting inner sleeve, buttoning down the outside of the arm. Then we have the sleeve split from the shoulder to the elbow, is puff filling up the opening—an excellent pattern, this, for renovating an old frock. Our old favourite the bishop sleeve is once more popular, though with extra fulness at the shoulder. A modified bishop with a very long cuff is another pretty mode, being both useful and smart for blouses.

MAT Mummy. Tulle is to be much worn in the new millinery. Some of the prettiest hats are of white tulle, with medallions of hand-painted silk or Chantilly lace let into the inside of the brim. One or two large black feathers are the only trimming. The stiff tulle toques of last summer are not likely to reappear. The prettiest new French sailor hats are in brown Panama, with a narrow bind of brown velvet softening the brim, and a lace or shot chiffon scarf. _

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

BKETROOT CREAII.—A delicious and inexpensive soup can be made with the help of a cooked beet- root, if treated as follows: Take one quart of good brown stock, loz. of butter, loz. of dour, one large cooked beetroot, half a stick of celery half-gill of cream, salt, and pepper. Melt the bui...er in a stewpan, stir in the flour, and cook it without browning over the fire for a few minutes. Add the stock, or use milk and water, if you have no stook. Stir this over the fire until it boils. Peel the beetroot, and cut it into shreds; wash, trim, and shred the celery, and add both to the stock. Boil the soup with the lid on for about half- an-hour, not more, or the colour will be spoilt. Strain the sOUD threilA a sieve, and rub enough of orecrooc tnrougn to give it a nice colour an... consistency. Season carefully, add the cream, heat it up thoroughly withoilt letting it bo;.1 again. div.head: HER •MERCENARY SPIRIT,
div.p: HER •MERCENARY SPIRIT,

Looking at these girls of the day, one thinks of their future with some misgiving. Many of them are to become - wives and mothers; and what kind of wives and mothers will they make? Excellent wives, no doubt, in the days of pros- perity, but darker hours are certain to follow, and the virtues then required will be those of patience, endurance, self-sacrifice. The mod- ern girl is far more worldly than her mother was in her maiden days. She scouts the idea of love in a cottage ; she. wants a good house, a good income' and above all, plenty of amuse- ment. It is the love of luxury and amusement that seems to be gaining ground amongst us •, and it is not a development which promises well for the Empire. The wife who looks on her husband as a mere provider of clothes and meals is not likely tti prove a help-meet in the day of trouble. When we note the increase of cases in which husband and wife separate from each other, we wonder whethez that terrible " in- compatibility " of temper Might not have been overcome, if the wife liacl possessed the char- acteristics of an earlier time. Had she shown herself unseltish, tolerant, patient with his faults, capable .of. " putting up " with small vexations, perhapi the qiiarrels would never have been begun, and the rift would not have widened to the destruction of a home. But think of the young wife's training as a girl, and then ask yourself how she could have at- tained the qualities which would have preserved her happiness? What has she learned?
AND SELF-ASSERTIVENESS

Well. first of all, she has learned that her own advancement is the, chief thing that she must strive for ; that her tastes and capacities must, of all things, never go t 3 the Ivan ; that it is her duty not to yield a hair's breadth when it is a matter of individual opinion. She has al- ways understood that one had a duty to oneself, but she expects her husband to sacrifice ,his in- clinations and ideas to hers. She wants Lim to Wait upon her, to work for her, to admire her to the: end of time ; and she cannot in the least understand that a busy mall cannot give all his thought and attention to her as he did in the days of their engagement. Her vanity is offended and she begins to fret and sulk. The husband is impatient witk a wife who cries and grumbles when he comefishome at night; and therefore his temper soon matches her own, and domestic strife becomes the order of the day, Happiness has flown out of the window ; and Whose was the fault

lithe wife is also a mother, matters are worse. The children learn only too early what discord and dissension mean ; and the years of their childhood, which ought to be so beautiful, are filled with memories of dispeace !
KKK LACK OF WOMAN'S GREATEST CHAIM- S Y.

It is well for a man, said the greatest of sages, that he should bear the. yoke in his youth. Well for a woman, also. Not a yoke of tyranny or enforced servitude ; but the yoke of obedience, humility, faith. If a girl rever- ence her parents, she will respect hex husband and train up her children to the same law of subordination. For we cannot . all- be equals ; we must be subordinate one to another ; and there is nothing humiliating to a properly trained mind to feel that we are filling our proper place in the world—some intermediate space, most likely, neither too low nor too high. After all; the old lessons are the best: The young should give all deference to• the aged, and the aged should show consideration for • the aggressive- ness and " cocksureneFs "of the young. These be trite saying ; but there is good reason in them all.

And so I come back to my earlier contention —that the modern girl i•liould cultivate the power of sympathy if she wishes to resemble those great and wise and lovable women who have swayed the men who rule the world. And quite half of sympathy. consists hi imagi- nation—in being able to put oneself into an- other's place. It is only where a girl can do this that Ale, will fill her proper place hi the world, and after she has been a good daughter become—if fate pericit—a perfect wife

RAILWAY BRIDGE ON FIRE.

The St. Helens Fire Brigade had a somewhat novel experience on Wednesday afternoon. They were called to Marshall's Cross, some two miles out of town, where they found a ten foot wide wooden bridge over the London and North Western. main line on fire. They encountered considerable difficulty in reaching the seal of the fire between the thick woodea boards, and while they were at work several trains passed beneath the burning bridge. Railway servants were on special duty to warn drivers of approaching trains.

div.head: SOLIDIFICATION OF 'THE MOON.
div.p: SOLIDIFICATION OF 'THE MOON.

M. Loewy, director of the Paris Observatory, and M. Puiseux, in a communication to the Academie des Sciences, hold that the solidification of the moon extends from the surface to the centre, and not, es the English scientists think, from the centre to the periphery. This view would modify various existing theories. Their conclusion is drawn from tlie examination of photographs executed at the observatory for reproduction in the new Lunar Atlas.

THE SAHARAN SEA. I M. De Lapparent has announced, in a communi- cation to the Acal6naie des Sciences, that he has received fossils discovered by two French officers, Captain Theveniaucl and Lieutenant Desplagnee, a little to the north of Timbuctoo. A calcareous bloek containing fos.ils of the Cretaceouß has also been found .350 kilometres from Timbuctoo. There- fore the sea which bathed the region of Bilma on the east extended more than 300 kilometres to the north of Timbuctoo.

div.head: BREAKING STRAINS OF ALLOYS.
div.p: BREAKING STRAINS OF ALLOYS.

According to M. Leon Guillet, bronze alloys con- taining More than 92 per cent. of copper have their breaking strain and elongation increased by temper- ing at a temperature between 400 deg. and 600 deg. Centigrade. Bronze alloys containing less than 92 per cent, of copper have their breaking strain and elongation increased to a remarkable degree when tempered at more than 500 deg. The maximum breaking strain is got with a temperature of tempering of about 600 deg. The maximum of elongation seems to vary with the composition of the alloy.

div.head: TROLLEY LIMIT.
div.p: TROLLEY LIMIT.

Evidently the trolley problem has not been solved yet; for there are still plenty of applications at the Patent Office for patents on trolley guards, and the like. But an American inventor his apparently given up the idea that trolley wheels can be made to stick to ,the wire, and has endeavoured instead merely to alleviate the trouble by providing an electric light near the end of the pole to assist the 'conductor in replacing the trolley at night. The electric lamp is lighted by a battery located in the body of the car. A switch is interposed in the circuit near the lamp, and to one end of this switch the trolley rope is attached. Normally this switch is held open by a spring; but when the conductor pulls the rope to draw down and replace the trolley the switch is closed, lighting the lamp, and thereby facili:ating the work of placing the wheel in proper contact with the wire. Connected in series with the tiolley lamp are a number of lamps in the car, which serve to illumine the same while the trolley is being replaced.

div.head: MAKES THE WATER PUMP ITSELF.
div.p: MAKES THE WATER PUMP ITSELF.

A current motor conceived with reference to its use in connection with irrigation has been patented by Mr. John Roeh, of Spokane, Washington, and Is now being introduced throughout the Western States, says the Scientific American. The mechanical principles upon which it is constructed are those of deflection and 1 verage, which until now have never been combined for purpose intended. The current pressing agaimit a sheet-iron blade resting in the stream,and placed at an angle to the current, causes the blade to swing bin k and forth. The force generated is communicated through a lever back to pumping mechanism or other machinery. Alter lever has reached the limits of its sweep, the blade is forced automatically to a reverse angle to that formerly occupied, which causes the blade and lever to travel in an opposite direction until limit is again reached, this performance continuing without introduction of any other power than that furnished by the stream and without any attendance or super- vision. The lever or sweep is hinged to supporting timbers, so as to make the motor self-adjustable to any stage of water. All parts are above water, thereby making it an easy task to oil and keep in repair. The expense is confined to first cost of plant and installation, and the absence of any cost incidental to operation and maintenance makes it the cheapest known irrigating device, and by reason of this fact it will doubtleas appeal to those interested.

div.head: [ALL RIORTS RESIP.VED.) DAUGHTERS AND WIVES.
div.p: [ALL RIORTS RESIP.VED.) DAUGHTERS AND WIVES.
ADELINE SERGEANT (Author of Vie Story qr a _Penitent 4.a.)•

Speaking as one who has left girlhood a long way behind, Imo his seen the daughters of her old school friends and contemporaries emerging from babyhood into girlhood turd womanhood, I notice a considerable change of type in the mod- ern maiden. In some respects the change is ad- mirable : in others it requires modification. • lint in all ways the change is extremely marked. lam not going back so far as to the Early or mid-Victorian epoch ; I , speak now of the . girls who flourished in the seventies and eighties, and I think thftt even in .the space of twenty or five and twenty years a great change has come about. The typical girl of the present day glories in her strength. t...qie can play cricket and hockey ; she can ride and drive and swim ; she ,can walk ten miles with ease, row a boat with her brother and enjoy life with the zest of a schoolboy. Very often i•hie is accomplished in some particular line ; she has a taste for carving or music, .or for managing girls' clubs , and she throws her- self into a pursuit of this kind as whole-heart- edly as into her amusements. If she is of the wage-earning or salaried class, • she does he: work in business-like faShion and makes herself valuable to her employers. She is good hum- nred, buoyant, generally brimming over with good spirits, a capital comrade, a trusty friend. Ent she is not sympatbetic. People do not feel inclined to confide their affairs to her; and those who are sick or sorry pass her by.
THE OLD STYLE GILL,

Still, she is a more complete human being, in many respects, than her predecessor of the. seventies, who suffered only too often from in- sufficient exercise and misdirected energies. Public examinations and crowded High Schools were in their infancy ; end the education of girls was almost 'entirely ,in the hands of private teachers, schoolmistresses and governesses. In the better class schoolrooms there was an almost exaggerated conscientiousness about small duties, proceeding from the efforts of teachers to follow Dr. Arnold's method?; an excellent ideal if well carried out, but apt to produce a morbid scrupulosity mid (in some cases that I myself remember) a positive fear of any sort of enjoyment. "It can't be right, because I like it so much," was a sentence uttered by a girl of my acquaintance in all sincerity. There was also a good deal of religious and philanthropic activity amongst the girls of that times in the way of Sunday school teaching, tract distribution, and the carrying of soup and puddings to the poor Political economy (lid not. in those days, affect us. .We believed that we were doins, a great deal of good to others, when, as a matter of fact, we ourselves profited more .by our exertions than the recipients of our gifts. 3liss Charlotte Yonge has some very wellsdrawn specimens of girls of this sort in her books. Take, for instance, Ethel May or Amy Morville. In our day. Ethel's classical attainments would be the chief factor of her life ; she would have had a coach, and gone to Girton ; instead of settling down to keep her father's home and build a church at Cocksmoor. Amy, Widowed at seventeen, would most assuredly have made a second brilliant marriage, instead of enging off her hair, wearing a widow's cap (at seventeen) and "living for " her child: The girls of the present day are not likely to suffer by the sacri- fice of their intellectual gifts or the renuncia- tion of all worldly enjoyment at the age of seventeen. They would laugh the idea to scorn. AND TIM NEW. And yet—is there not something amiss ? Ethel May's self-suppression, Amy Morville's abnega- tion—had they not theirs origin in some real conception of the divine ? These girls had ideate, and did their best, in what we may per- haps think mistaken fashions, to live up to them. I am very much afraid that a large proportion of modern girls have left " the ideal " out of their consideration. They have plenty of ambi- tion ; they want to get on in the world ; and most of all they want enjoyment—pleasure excitement ; anything to give them . a constant change of sensation, and to disguise from themselves the monotony of ordinary life. The modern girl too often leaves out of her life that ever-working leaven which we may call the spiritual sense ; she is frankly materialistic. And where this spirituel sense is left out, the tendency of a human being is always to become self-centred ; to concentrate all its energies on itself, its own advancement, its own happiness, and to fight down any invitation to self-sacrifice; to condemn eelf-denial as morbid, and self-re- strainkas feebleness.

The -results are strikingly apparent, although we may not have guessed their origin. Im- patience of pain, and a great sense of one's own importance, are of course the characteristics of all young people. lam not sure whether the last does not include the first. For most young persons begin life with the firm conviction that they are comulete exceptions to all rules ; that no one ever lied such trials before, or suffered such exceptional agonies ; and moreover that fate or Providence is particularly hard, and has some especial spite against them. That they should be laid low by disease, or overwhelmed with misfortune or bereavement, seems to them an intolerable thing
" But why 8110111 d I lime to bear this ?" they cry ; mid are not satisfied with the only possi- ble reply : " Why not ?"

SHOULD WE as I'UT VPON ? This impatiende of pain used not in old days to be very characteristic of women. It was supposed to be woman's place to endure. Often she endured too much ; she was foolishly sub- missive, and self-sacrificing ; I know of cases where a wile has milled her health out of com- plianee with some unimportant fad of her hus- band's ; but self-sacrilice carried to that ex- , tent has fortunately been condemned by all reasonable persons. The only danger is that the girls of the present day should carry their lawful desire to be well, to be happy, to be corn- fortable, th too great an extreme. They talk of 66 self development" instead of self-denial ; they feel that they are not doing their ditty to them- selves when they are " put upon," and they very much resent any infringement of their pri- vileges. In theory they ore often very right ; in practice, only too often extremely selfish. After all, att I once heard a wise man say— " True Christianity chiefly consists in letting yourself be pug upon." Or, as Frederick Ro- bertson said : " Do not talk ahout your rights, think of your duties." And the modern girl is a trifle too much inclined to fight for her rights, and to neglect some of the . Most obvious duties of a girl's home-life. For this brilliant young creature who playa hockey and the violin, or reads Greek and cul- tivates her intellect, or seeks out and pursues every form of amusement that she call devise, is generally the cherished daughter of two middle-aged people who have spent a good part of their lives in: working for her, in thinking about her, and planning her welfare. Her father is often a busy mini with whom she has little intercourse ; but she can at least meet him with affection, and play a dull game at back- gammon with him after dinner, and listen to his tales without a yawn ! Then her mother—not clever, perhaps, not intellectual—how does the modern girl behave to her F Is it not too true that the daughter constitutes herself , the queen of the household. rides her elders, sets aside their tastes, sometimes even actually snubs her parents and is openly rebellions when they try to exert a little authority i• These •• revolting daughters " have no charms for the sensible man or wolll/111. Better by far the old days of subjugation, when a girl was taught to rever- ence her father and to adore her mother ; when she believed it to be really her duty to honour her parents, and to treat them with the most delicate respect. the most untiring devotion.

Willies" who did not work, but lived upon what they could 'cadge or steal. These " Weary Willies " coin- plicsted the position for the respectable workingman unable to find work, and made the problem more difficult of solution. A saggestion made was that these " Weary Willies " should be swept into the labour colonies to be established. If they would not work they should be locked up. If that course were adopted, the "statesmanlike measure" the Government had introduced would have a chance of solving the problem of the unemployed. 'rhe vagrant question, continued Mr. Thompson, was a national problem and ought to be dealt with nationally. It covered a very wide field. For instance, that Board at the weekly meetings of the relief committees turned men out of the House to go on the road. What had those men to do? They had a right to come into the Union and to be kept there if they could not find employment. They were turned out of the House as ordinary tramps. , Where could they obtain a night's lodging? Ultimately the question would have to be taken up in a thorough manner, and men who were discharged from the House should have tickets entitling them to relief in some way without begging for it. He trusted that something would soon be done to remedy the vagrancy evil which was very great indeed. The CLI,RIC said that probably no subject connected withPoorLaw administration had been so fully considered or was receiving greaterattention than the treatment of vagrants. It appeared to him that the weakness of the present resolution (a similar one to which was adopted ; by the Board at the last meeting) was to introduce the local element—the district of Mr. Jenner Fust—instead ;of the national movement. To have a uniform treat- ment in Mr. Jenner Fust's district and not a correspond- ing arrangement in the surrounding districts, would give a very awkward effect. The resolution the Board had passed was best being carried out by conveying it to the Commission which was now sitting in connection with the vagrancy question. The subject was also constantly before the Poor Law Unions Association in London. In accordance with the instructions of the Board he ' wrote to Mr. Jenner Fust suggesting that Mr. Awber3 I should be called as a witness before the Commission in ' order that the feelings of the Board might be embodied in his evidence. Mr. Fust replied : " I have nothing to do with the Departmental Committee on vagrancy, but I am forwarding your letter to the committee who, I feel sure, will give it every consideration." Later he (Mr. Sutton) received a letter from the secretary to the Departmental Committee stating that in the event I of the committee desiring further evidence from the point of view of a Workhouse Master, he would not fail to bring Mr. Awbery's name before them. Mr. Sutton added that the Board had moved in the matter 1 as far as was practicable, but really the whole thing must become a national question. The minutes of the committee were approved, but as the Board had already passed a resolution on the question it was not considered necessary to adopt another.
A RECORD EGG. . .

—• A buff Orpington hen, belonging to Mr. John Dutton Cleaford, Middlowich, Cheshire, has just laid an egg weighing five and one-tenth ounces. The egg is three and a half inches long, with a circumference at the widest part of 80'7E71 and a quarter inches.—Recently Scotland was credited with an abnormal egg of four ounces, which, however, fulls far. below the record ot the Cheshire hen.

THE PRICE OF TEA. At a meeting of the House Committee, a letter was read from the grocery contractors, Messrs. Milling, intimating their intention to take the 2d. duty off the price of their contract teas on and after July Ist.

div.head: Selection of Candidates.
div.p: Selection of Candidates.

A meeting of the Selection Committee appointed by the General Purposes Committee was held on Monday evening at the Town Hall, when the following gentle- men were selected to appear before the General Purposes Committee at their next meeting, when one of them xvill be appointed Deputy Town Clerk to succeed Mr. Stanley Wilson:—Mr. Allen G. Brown, who has been eight years in the Town Clerk's office at St. Helens; Mr. F. Fernihough, four years in the Town Clerk's office at Southport; Mr. R. C. Graves, seven years in the Town Clerk's office at Devonport ; Mr. A. T. Holloway seven years in the Town Clerk's office at Carlisle; Mr. Roger Pierpoint, and Mr. A. B. Fox, who are in private practice in Warrington; and Mr. Elarola Thorne, in private practice in Wolverhampton.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The Extension Question Again.
MR. HICKMAN'S ALTERNATIVE SCHEME.

A meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, Mr. J. Billinge presiding. There were also present :—Rev. Dr. Mercer, Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson, Dr. Murray, Messrs. A. J. ' Jolley, R. Forshaw, I'. H. Ashcroft, D. Davies, W Houghton, A. Brooks, R. Bolton, G. Thompson, J. 'Pluton, G. Mather. M. W. Seton, W. Flannagan, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master) and A. Wright (superintendent of Padgate Schools.)

div.head: EXTENSION QUESTION.
div.p: THE EXTENSION QUESTION.

At a meeting of the House Committee held on May sth the following resolution submitted by Mr. Hickman was considered :—" That a suitable corrugated iron building be erected to be used for workshop and the storage of all inflammable articles and materials, and that the premises known as the old hospital be removed and rendered habitable for the accommodation of the various indoor classes." To this Mr. Jolley moved an amendment that the words " corrugated iron " be deleted from the resolution.—Rev. Dr. Mercer seconded and the discussion stood adjourned. Upon resuming Mr. Brooks submitted a second amendment that a committee be appointed to consider the resolu- tion in all its bearings and that the committee be instructed to call in to its aid professional advice and if considered advisable to submit their conclusions to the Local Government Board with a view to ascertaining whether that body would approve what might be eventually adopted.—Mr. Ashcroft seconded and the amendment was carried. The following were con- stituted the committee :—Messrs. Forshaw, Thompson, Billinge, Hickman, Brooks, Jolley and Davies, and the meeting, it was stated, would be arranged after the Board had approved the recommendation. Mr. FORSITAW moved the adoption of the minutes. The CLERK pointed out that the Local Government Board approved a plan for the erection of another building but recently that scheme was deferred for twelve months. Did the present resolution interfere with that ? Mr. FORSITAW : Not at all. Continuing, he said Mr. Hickman was of opinion that the Board could put the old hospital to some use and provide further accommo- dation, but after a long discussion the House Committee thought it would be better to have professional advice as to Mr. Hickman's proposals and a committee was appointed to go into the whole question and report to the Board. Mr. M 4THER pointed out that it was not stated in the minutes that the deliberations of the committee would be reported to the Board. Mr. FORSITAW s ad that was understood. The minutes were approve I. THE VAORANCY VROPLEM. SUGGESTED UNIFORM TREATMENT.

At a meeting of the House Committee on Nlay 12th, the Master contributed a paper on the vagrancy probleni and a general discussion ensued. On the proposition of the Rev. Dr. Mercer the following resolution was adopted That the House Colllllllttee suggest to the Board the desirability of the adoption of the uniform treatment of vagrants throughout the area of the North Western Conference." Mr. FOniliAW said the, e was a very long and inter- esting discussion on the subject and it Was felt by the House Committee that it would be wise for the board to adopt a resolution advocating that in the North Western districts all unions should have a uniformity of treatment of vagrants as regarded tasks imposed, the food provided, and the hours of detention. It was not wise that different systems should obtain in the various unions. Mr. Awbery also suggested preventive steps to reduce the number of vagrants, but the committee felt the time had not yet arrived to put into operation the courses he named, although they were very good. One was the formation of Labour colonies under State con- trol to provide work for those who were unable to find other employment. Mr. THONIPSON said be had been reading the report of a speech delivered by a member of Parliament for Liver- pool (Mr. W. Rutherford, M.P.) on this question. With regard to the unemployed, Mr. Rutherford, said one of the essential elements In dealing with that matter was to clear the conntry of the 60,000 tramps or "Weary

div.head: BLACK MOTOR CAR.
div.p: THE BLACK MOTOR CAR.
By J. B. HARRIS BURLAND.
CHAPTER XL
A RUINED MAN.

JORDISON and his servants spent the next three days in converting the spacious stables into a temporary residence in shifting furniture and in endeavouring to adapt themselves to circumstances. The Red House was palpa- bly unsafe. Jordison had no means of gauging the thickness of the rock that lay beneath it, but if, as he feared, that rock was cracked in half from end to end it was proba- ble that the whole building would one day crash through into the cavern beneath it. It was not until the third day after the disaster that Lipp, carrying a washing stand on his brawny shoulder, stumbled in the debris at the hall door, and turned up a 'letter from the pile of glass and plaster on the noon He brought it to Jordison in t,he harness room, which the latter had fitted up as his own particular sanctum. Jordison looked at the postiaark and saw that it was three plays old. But he opened it without any feelings of annoyance at the delay. On the outside the letter was dull and un- interesting—a business envelope, addressed in a clerk's hand-writing. But before he had finished reading it, his face was aslwhite as the paper it was written on, and he rose to his feet with a look of fear and rang the bell. When Jordison had returned to England some months previously, lit had resigned his seat on the board of the Motor Company, but decided to leave all his savings in a business which promised so well, and which he had himself built up to a high position in the motor world. The other directors were men of integrity and ability, and he had every -reason to believe that he had left his money in •saf4 hands.

This letter, however, broke in upon his security like a thunder bolt. It was written by a crabbed and methodical old French lawyer, who had been something of a friend to Jordison in Paris. iThe following is a trans- lation :

"Dear Mr. Jordison,—l write to tell you that Jacquart et Cie are on their last legs. Sell your interest before the news becomes public property. The Jew financier, whom v/esupposed to be wealthy, and who has, as you know, taken your place on the Board, has played ducks and drakes with the whole concern. He enlarged the business to such an alarming extent that the other directors refused to sanction the expenditure without some personal guarantee for the additional capital that would be required. This guaran- tee was given by Jules Lanstein, and the company has shone splendidly on the strength of it. But I happen to have found out that this Lanstein is an adventurer who lives by his wits, and that his guarantee is not worth the paper it is written on. I have ascer- tained this for a fact, and all Paris will know it before the week is out. The Company has committed itself to enormous payments. Pay day will arrive shortly. Sell by telegram .at once. The shares stand high. .
:! With my most profound sa-lutations, I am,. my dear Mr. Jordison,

- " Yours, HENRI DUCHELLE." 1111 Jordison read and re-read the letter again and again, in the hope that he had not trans- lated it correctly, and that he might have missed the true purport of its contents. But they were too clear, and he roused himself for -action. Lipp entered the room in answer to the bell. Jordison wrote out a telegram to some brokers in Paris, instructing them to sell all his holding in the Jacquart Co., but to do it in such a manner as to least disturb the market. Andi then he told Lipp to get the motor car ready. But scarcely had the man left the room, when a boy rode slowly up on a red bicycle and delivered a telegram at the door. It was brought up to Jordison, who tore it open, and took in its contents at a glance. . .

• " Jacquart in liquidation. Shares unsale- able. Hope you have sold already.— DUCHELLE. The thin piece of pink paper fluttered gently • to the floor from Jordison's fingers. He sat as still as though he had beea carved out of .stone. His white face was drawn and . haggard, a mere pale mask of flesh, with two burning eyes that were fixed on the dirty panes of the little window. "Shares unsale- able, shares unsaleable," echoed and re- echoed through his brain. Yet he could not grasp the full meaning of the words, till his eye fell on Bysouth's account, which he had received that morning, and which lay open on the table. £175 I These figures were con- crete facts and easily to be comprehended. Here was a bill that had to be paid at once, and yet perhaps but a m,ere fraction of the bill that might have to be paid to Messrs. Briggs & Warlock before they obtained the informa- tion he desired. The piece of paper 'nought the truth home to him—the hard, incontro- vertible truth. He was a ruined man, a powerless, feeble, helpless man. The ground had been knocked away from under his feet. His brain and limbs were bound by poverty. He would never know if his son were dead or alive. He would never find Marie de la Mothe, or press his hard fingers into her white throat, as he had dreamed of year after year, in his prison cell. He was an inert log on the ocean of life, a piece of driftwood that can neither move where it will, nor sink into oblivion beneath the waves. The truth was gradually driven home into his brain like a piecp of red hot steel. Ruin I Ruin I Ruin! The word sang through his brain until it seemed to rhyme in with the beating of his heart. He could stand the music no longer. For a whole hour he had listened to it in silence, a mere statue, beaten with it as a rock is lashed with waves. He suddenly staggered to the tiny table, sank into a chair, bowed his head, raised it again and looked into the fire. Then his hand stole ,into his pocket, and he felt the cold steel of his revolver. , For a few minutes he fingered it lovingly, as though it were indeed a friend. Then he laughed bitterly, and tried to collect his thoughts. Was this the only way? He placed the weapon on the table before him and looked at it enquiringly, as though it 'could give him an answer from its small round mouth. It was silent, though he could have made it speak one answer in its own decisive - way. He thrust it far from him, .among the papers on the table, and rose to his feet. His brief spell of madness was past. His strong will reasserted itself. Rage and disappointment were thrust into the back- ground. He was the old William Jordison again, cold, hard, calculating, a man with a purpose that no accident nor untoward circum- stance could alter. He paced up and down the room with knitted brows, and a mouth -closed tight with determination. " Money I Money Money I " was the song that now ,echoed through his brain. A hundred schemes for making money flashed through his mind, and one by one he cast them aside. Some were uncertain, some required capital, and all were too slow, far, far too slow. The best of • them would mean seven years' servitude for 'his ' Rachael, the love that he hugged to his heart, the accomplishment et' his revenge. His meditations were interrupted by the :entrance of Susanson, the most despicable a the three precious scoundrels he had chosen for his servants. He was a little Jew, plump and self-satisfied, an excellent cook, for he had -once been chef in a large restaurant, where he lost his situation and liberty by defrauding his employers out of £l,OOO in various ac- counts with tradesmen. He received twelve months' imprisonment and came out with a ,distaste for the culinary art. .11e then turned _his attention to high-class burglary, and found the occupation a remunerative one in which his confederates bore all the risk. An unfor- tunate 'miscalculation, however, on his part, and the treachery of a man who had some old .scoreS to settle, made a blank of five years ia his life. It should properly have been seven, but he interfered with the arrangements of a Prejudiced government, and took his present situation as a place of refuge. He had every intention of leaving it as soon as he had , . d Other arrangements. His life was not exactly a happy one at the Red House. The other Nrc) men looked down on him as an iliferior

type of criminal, and they kicked him into the position of a general drudge. He came in, as he usually did, with some whining complaint about his fellow servants. He had a wholesome fear of Jordison, but he knew that the master of the house .was deter- mined to keep order in his own household. . "If you pleathe, thir," he lisped. Jordison stopped and gave him a glance that sent the miserable fellow's heart into his boots. "If ydu Peathe, thir," he repeated nerv- ously. i" " Well," said Jordison sharply„" what is t ? The man plunged into a long and doleful 'tale to Jermy's discredit. Jordison scarcely listened to [the details, but he gathered that owing' to Jermy's conduct the dinner hour would have to be altered by forty-five minutes. Directly he had arrived at [that fact, he stopped the story. "That'll do," he said roughly. "I'll speak to Jermy, but see that I get dinner at the proper time, or there'll be trouble." " I'll try, thir ; swelp me bob, I'll try, thir." " Get out." The man crawled out of the room, and Jordison was left alone with his thoughts. A very trivial event will sometimes alter the whole course of a man's life, and it so happened that this chance entrance of Jacob, Susaiason was destined to influence the whole career of the master of the Red House. The mere sight of the man suggested an idea to Jordison. The suggestion came at a critical moment. At first he thrust it from his mind as wild and impracticable. But by degrees it forced itself upon him and became a concrete fact. And that night he dreamt of illimitable wealth, and saw a stream of gold and jewels pour down from Heaven like a Jacob's Ladder, glittering with, every hue of the rainb6w.

div.head: CHAPTER XII. THE DOWNWARD STEP.
div.p: CHAPTER XII. THE DOWNWARD STEP.

ON misty night in November, a broad fat, of white light moved swiftly and silently' southwards along the old Roman Road. Behind it lay the long dark body of an, enor- mous motor car. Its speed was terrific, but more noticeable than the speed, from a motorist's point of view, was the almost ghostly silence with which It tore along the straight road. There was no throb nor beat of machinery; no jar, nor rattle, nor vibration in any part. A. low hiss of the wheels as they whizzed over the damp surface of the ground was the only sound that broke the stillness -of the night. It was no more, proportionately, than the noise a bicycle might have made. The ten miles between the Red House and the plantation at the foot of Heatherstone Park, was covered in twelve minutes, and the machine was only run on its second speed. When it reached the place where Arthur Holine had pulled Lord Harry Quy out of the water, it slowed down, and came to a stop under the shadows of the trees which over- hung the road. The three men alighted quickly. One of them turned out all the lights but the little lamp' which hung behind. This he unhooked, and let its rays fall on the motionless mass of metal...

"She's a beauty, Lipp," he said, in a low voice, punching one of the back tyres with his clenched fist. There's not a car like her in England." Lipp grunted doubtfully. He was not a judge of the beautiful and certainly there was little to admire in the car from an aesthetic point of view. It was made entirely of steel, and bore some resemblance to the engine of an armoured train. It had a seven foot wheel base, and was 18 feet in length. As it lay at rest, it looked a huge unwieldy monster, an inert mass of metal, that four horses would have found a good load for them to draw. It weighed no less than three tons. It was painted black—body, bonnet, wheels, all a dead dull black, without any lustre of enamel to relieve the gloom of its surface. It was in truth an ugly thing, a cross between a hearse and a locomotive. Yet it represented the , last 'word in motors. It was William Jordi- son's triumph—the almost perfect car, He looked at it lovingly for a minute or two, touching the bearings here and there to see if they had become hot, and laying his hand tenderly on its long and hideous frame. "Come along," growled Lipp roughly, " this aint no beauty show. If we're out on business—"
"Have you all we want," jordison broke in quietly, turning the light on the man's face. "Aye, aye," the man growled impatiently, " unless I've left my card case on the 'all table."

" Well, keep close to me. I wish it were not so infernally dark, but it will be all in our favour later on. Jermy, you stay by the car and keep your eyes and ears open. If anyone comes along, pretend to be tinkering with the machinery. If you hear a shot 'or cries of pursuit, or anything that sounds as if we had been discovered, start the engines. It's just possible I,ve may be in a hurry to.get off." With these parting instructions he climbed over the wall, and the two men crept through the narrow belt of trees. The wet bracken, breast high in places, swished softly as they moved through its tangled fronds. A small animal , of some kind rushed away from beneath their feet. Just as they emerged into the open ,a brace of pheasants rose with a whir from the branches above.

" Curse the bird's," muttered Jordison, "we'll have a keeper on us before we have done, and there'll be another 'Serious Poach- ing Affray in Essex.'" However, up to a certain point fortune was with them that night..- They crossed the undulating park without attracting the atten- tion of the two under keepers whose duty it was to patrol the estate after sunset, and reached the garden where they breathed in comparative safety. The outline of the house was invisible against the dark sky, but a long line of win- dows on the ground floor glowed with yellow light. The upper part of the great pile of buildings was in total darkness. They paused under the branches of a gigantic tulip tree, and consulted in whispers. Lipp had already obtained a considerable knowledge of the house, by means of a love affair with one of the under housemaids. Jordison had visited it more than once on show days, and a substantial tip to the Major Domo had pro- cured him the information he required. _ .
Jordison looked at his watch ; it was g o'clock, an hour when the bedrooms of a house offer the most inducements to those who wish to enter them unobserved.

From whete they stood they could see the windows* of Lady Heatherstone's private apartments; they were over the White Drawing room, which was now a blaze of light. Lipp knew where to lay hands on a ladder, but it seemed almost madness to place it against that part of the house. On the other hand, if an entrance were effected in another part, the risk of walking along the corridors would be considerable. Lipp was for the latter course, but Jordison preferred to take the bull by the horns and go straight for Lady Heatherstone's bedroom. The whole matter had been threshed out before they started, but the sight of the well-lighted windows re-opened the question. Suddenly a soprano voice began to sing, and the sweet melody of Lassen's U All Souls' Day" came to the watchers on the lawn. The notes brought no message of love or tenderness to their ears. But the same idea struck both of them.
"Now's the time," said Jordison 3 1.1 where's the ladder ? "

In' less than five minutes Lipp fetched it and placed it against the wall. The song had ceased, and a pianoforte solo was filling the drawing room with a loud crash of music. "Nothing could be better," said jordison; "you will stay here, Lipp, and whistle if there is danger. It won't take more than five minutes, if I can get them at all."

Jordison ran swiftly up the ladder, opened the catch of the window with a penknife, and ooftly raised the sash. "then he thrust his head round the corner of the silk blind and listened. The bedroom door was open, and he could see into the well-lighted corridor beyond. The upper part of the house was perfectly .quiet. He could hear neither footsteps not voices. But from the drawing room below there still came the low deep chords of Rach- maninoff's Prelude. He crept quietly into the

room, and closing the room, locirea it. rnea he went to another door, opening into—the next room. It was closed, and he turned the. key in the lock. Then he drew the heavy curtain across the window and taking a small but powerful electric lamp from his pocket, threw its rays on the walls and floor. His eye caught the faint sparkle of jewels on the dressing table. He went eagerly across to it and gatherF.d up everything of value that he could see—a magnificent diamond brooch, 3 or 4 rings set with rubies and emeralds, a jewelled purse of gold net work, with ten pounds in it, the hair brushes, scent bottles, and all the fittings of a lady's dressing case, every one of solid gold, bearing an "H" and an Earl's coronet in diamonds. ,All these he thrust into a small canvas bag he had brought with him, and his eyes glittered with excite- ment.

His task seemed no longer a sordid one. 1 As he had crept into the room he had felt himself on a level with the meanest thief that was ever put in the dock of the Old Bailey. It I was his first essay in burglary, and the humiliation of the act had pierced even his I hardened conscience. But now, with the glitter of these gems before his eyes, he saw the possibilities of it all—the excitement, the risk, and the reward. Surely here was a sport at least equal to the shooting of big game, where a man carries his life in his hands, and where his safety depends on the quickness of his eye and the knowledge of his craft. For the first • time he understood what the fascination of a highwayman's life must have been, and why so many gentlemen of birth and breeding had risked their necks in pur- suit of what had hitherto appeared to be a mean and sordid occupation. Now he realised that in every sense of the word it was a sport where the sportsman pitted his own wits and courage against that of his adversary. And Jordison was hunting for bigger game to-night than the few knick-knacks a lady leaves on her dressing table. The Heather- stone jewels were famous, well-known and much paragraphed in papers which cater for the envious eyes of humble folk. A single .pearl necklace was valued at L 41,000. There wes a diamond and emerald tiara which had once graced the head of an empress. Jordison knew well the insolent carelessness of rich people in these matters, but it was too much to hope that such treasures as these would be left to the mercy of a chance burglar. Lady Heatherstone had not left her room for two years, and during that period the jewels had not been seen in public. Jordison had ascertained, however, that she would not allow them to be placed in a Bank, but kept them in her own apartments, where she could personally inspect them from time to time. He crept softly and quickly round the room breaking open every drawer and box in the hope of finding something. He picked up a few trifles here and there. But it was clear that the most valuable jewels were carefully concealed. He did his work clumsily, for the sole knowledge of his art had been gleaned from a few conversations with Susanson, and half a dozen practical lessons on the locks of his own house. He was, however, perfectly equipped for the task, and he marirelled at the ease with which the slender steel jemmy tore away iron plates and locks. It was not till he started an examination of the walls that he found the probable hiding place of the jewels. Behind the curtains of the great four-poster bed he found the square outline of a small door. It was flush with the surface, covered with the same paper, and so exactly fitted into the wall round it that a casual observer might easily have passed it by. Jordison tapped it gently with his jemmy. It gave back a metallic ring. He passed his hands along the edge and encoun- tered a keyhole a few inches below the frame- work of the bed. Then he placed his jemmy in the narrow crack, and exerted all his strength to burst open the lock. He might as well have tried to move the foundations of St. Paul's Cathedral. The door did not move outwards the hundredth part of an inch. The jemmy, wrought of perfect steel, curved like a spring. Then suddenly he sprang back from the bed and listened. A low whistle canie up from beneath the window. He walked over to it and drawing back the blind and curtain, leant out over the ledge. He could not see Lipp, but a thin shaft of light from one of the draw- ing room windows fell on the slender form of a young man walking across the lawn. He was smoking a large cigar, and, as he came closer, Jordison could see that he was a mere boy. But the light was too feeble to distinguish his face.

As ill luck would • lave it, he came straight towards the ladder. •He did not, however, notice it, until he was four yards from the wall of the house. Then he stopped, and glanced at it with idle curiosity. Apparently it conveyed nothing extraordinary to his mind; the mere carelessness of a gardener who had been training the ivy and creepers on the wall. But just as he turned to re-cross the lawn his eye caught the open bedroom win- dow. Jordison, from behind the curtains, could see the boy's face looking upwards. The light, streaming through a chink between the blinds and the sash, showed, first a look of enquiry, then surprise, and then the triumph- ant expression of one who has made a great discovery. Jordison instinctively felt that he was trapped, and began to wonder how fast the could run. , Somehow he fancied that this stripling could give him about twenty yards. ix every hundred. But another and a more practised eye hail watched the boy's face from the shadow of the wall, where Lipp lay huddled close into the thick ivy. Before the youth could either move or speak, something sprang out of the darkness and gripped him by the throat. Jordison could see the slender figure borne backwards, and .pressed quietly but with brutal strength on to the soft turf. ,There was Co cry nor sound, only: the writhing and. twining of limbs. From the drawing room window came the clear notes of a girl's voice' singing Tosti's "Good-bye." Jordison felt that it was time to interfere. He slipped out of the window and, sliding down the ladder to the ground, went swiftly to the dark mass upon the lawn. By the time he reached it nothing moved. In the dim light he could see Lipp's hand still gripping something on the ground. But nothing moved. "Hands off, Lipp,", he whispered sternly. The man did not move. Jordison whipped out his revolver and placed it to the fellow's ear.

"Hands off, I say, Lipp," he repeated, 1' you will kill the boy. Lipp knew well that no sane person would fire and bring the whole household ont on to the lawn. But he had already come to re- gard his master as on the border line of in- sanity, and he was taking no risks. He loosed his hold and rose to his feet. The boy's body lay limp and still on the lawn. " Don't want another term, do yer," growled the man in a whisper. "I've saved yer that. D'yer think yer wouldn't get caught between 'ere and the wall, if 'e cried out. Lets off. Gimme the swag."

Jordison handed him the canvas bag with- out a word, and Lipp began to run across the lawn, but his master bent down over the prostrate form and for one brief second flashed the electric light into the boy's face. It was a hard dissolute face for one so young, and looked horrible with the diffused blood which Lipp's powerful fingers had crushed into it. A great fear seized Jordison, and he placed his hand over the boy's heart. It had ceased to beat. Again he turned the light on the face, and looked long and keenly at the features. But strange to say, the thought uppermost in his mind was not that the boy was dead, but that he had seen his face before. He rose rapidly to his feet and tore through the darkness, blundering through shrubs and flower beds and trees till he reached the park wall. In less than ten minutes the motor was half way along the road to the Red House. And all that night Jordison lay awake, and the face of the dead boy glowered at him through the darkness, and all that night jordison puzzled his brain to remember where he had seen the face before.

div.head: CELEBRATING THE VICTORY.
div.p: CELEBRATING THE VICTORY.
Warrington Footballers Honoured.
ILLUMINATED CAR PROCESSION.

The victory of the Warrington Football Club in the Northern Union Final was fittingly celebrated on Friday last week when there was a procession of decorated cars, over the entire tramway system. The streets were thickly lined with spectators and from time to time the players wore vigorously cheered, but on the whole the people appeared to regard the procession more as a spectacular display. Prior to setting out on their 'journey round the town, the players were entertained by the Mayor at the Town Hall and heartily congratulated upon their success, the Mayor making a brief but appropriate speech and also shaking hands with each member of the team.—Thanks for the reception were returned by Mr. W. R. Neil, president of the club, and Mr. H. Ashton, hon. secretary of the club. , Mr. HALLAM also thanked the Mayor for his kind I hospitality to the players. His Worship must know what it was to occupya position like his—he was captain of a football team, and the Mayor was captain of a town council. (Laughter.) He trusted the Mayor would go on, and have as prosperous a season as he (the speaker) had had with the Warrington Football Club. (Laughter and cheers.) The MAYOR : You see you can keep your football team in order, but I cannot keep mine. (Laughter.) HALL.VM (continuing) said he thanked the Mayor and Mayoress for their kind hospitality, and he hoped next season they would again have the privilege of bringing the cup back again to Warrington. (Cheers.) After a few humorous remarks by Naylor. one of the forwards, The health of the Mayor of Hull and the Hull Kingston Rovers team was drunk and the following telegram was sent to the Mayor of Hull :—" The Mayor of Warrington and Corporation, together with the mem- bers of the Warrington Football Club, are drinking your very good health, and wish your town every success.— BOLTON." The party then made their way to the illuminated cars which were in waiting near the Post Office, and which were surrounded by a large crowd. The first car presented a gorgeous spectacle,being ablaze of coloured lights, flags, and bunting, while here and there judici- ously arranged greenery added to the generally hand- some effect. At the front of the car, and surmounted by a crown were the letters W.F.C.," while in the rear was "1005," both being in club colours. The cup was placed on a table inside the car in such a position as to , be easily seen by the people in the roadway, while the players and committee ranged themselves on the seats on either side. The Volunteer Band took their seats on top and the car moved off to the strains of a lively march. The Mayor and members of the Corporation were accommodated in an undecorated car on which also were Crosfield's Band which vied with the 'Volunteers in their efforts to add to the liveliness of the proceedings. Some half dozen other cars followed for the use of the general public, and the rear wasbrought up with a second decor- ated car on which were the "A" team players and the Borough band. Some difficulty was experienced en romte owing to the current failing at Sankey Bridges with the result that the cars were unable to run to schedule time it being close upon midnight ere the journey was concluded. Next Tuesday evening the team and officials will be entertained at Walton Hall by Sir Gilbert Greenall.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
From S. Peters THE INNOCENT (?) RUSS burgcomes a very
AND AFG HANISTAN. quaint expression

of surprise at Mr. BALFotra's statement on the subject of Afghani- stan. Political circles in the Russian capital, we are assured, "recall the time when Great Britain viewed sympathetically the possibility Of a railway Irons Ostend to Calcutta, via Afghanistan, believ- ing that both Creat Britain and Russia would gain from the establishment of direct neighbourly rela- tions." This piece of news will surprise the people of this country, who have never heard any such project,and would not dream of treating itperionsly. Political circles in St. Petersburg have a wonder- ful knack of creating some chimera, and then re- proaching us With cur inconstancy because we do not believe in it. "Some surprise" proceeds thi" interesting announcement, "is expressed that this view appears to have been completely abandoned by Great Britain ; but there is an inclina- tion to believe that that country will return in time to its former view." As the whole of our frontier policy in India is based on the cardinal maxim that " direct neigh- bourly relations" with Russia in Asia are most undesirable, and as we have sedulously maintained the entire independence of Afghanistan for that explicit reason,the expectation that we shall return to a view no English statesman has ever held is diplomatic nonsense. It is evidently put forward solely because Russian diplomacy is completely taken aback for the moment by the declaration of the Prime Minister, who, upon some subjects, can speak without the slightest ambiguity. Another touch of comedy from St. Petersburg appears in the information that Russia has " no railway pro- ject in Afghanistan," and that a guarantee of her unwillingness even to think about Afghanistan in any aggressive sense is furnished by the character of the Russian Governor of Turkestan, " who is described as a perfect nonentity. " It was only the other day that a military journal at Sc. Petersburg took a very different view of this official. He was said to have matured all his projects for a forward movement towards the Afghan border. That may have been a little desire to scare the allies of Japan; but the sudden transformation of this militant Gavernor to a "perfect nonentity" is not the kind of Russian guarantee which can be escribed as reassuring. As for the gnu. tion whether the public mind is reassured by Mr. BALFOUR'S argument against the possibility of invasion on this island, it grows clearer every day that this optimism is not generally shared. Even naval authoritxes who hold that the presence of our fleets would be a sufficient safeguard are far from satisfied with the safeguard which is enough for Mr. BALFJUR. "The serious mistake in

Mr. attFoun's speech," says Sir CYPRIAN BRIDGE, " was to attach such importance to a naval defence by torpedo destroyers and boats and submarines in commission or reserve in the event of our battle fleets being drawn away. Such craft could not move with great rapidity to the point threatened by the invaders if it was at any distance from their stations." On the east coast it is probable that the distance would be very considerable. But the greatest concern excited by MC. BALFOUR'S views about in- vasion relates, as we have already pointed out, to their effect on the Auxiliary Forces. They tally ominously with Mr. AnNoLD•FonsrEa's lukewarm zeal for the Militia and the Volunteer's. One of the chief advantages of the Volunteer force is that it encourages a military spirit in the most genuinely patriotic sense; and if that spirit is to be treated as one of no account we shall run the risk in some sudden emergency of having to face a demand for national service or conscription itself.

The work of educating the constituency in the enduring principles of Liberalism is being carried on in Warrington with a thoroughness which is bound to bear good fruit on the day of the elec- tion. For years the necessity for systematic work in this direction has been admitted, but until recently little has been done to awaken in the general body of electors a sense of true citizenship. They have voted Liberal or Conservative just as they have been told, and thought not for them- selves what the casting of a vote involves. It was clearly the duty of the Progressive party to break down the barriers of political ignorance and apathy, and excellent work is now being done uy Mr. Crostield and his enthusiastic adherents. Workingmen are getting every opportunity of learning how little their interests have been con- sidered by the Government of to day, and of appreciating the democratic aims and intentions of the Liberal party. The addresses which have lately been delivered in different parts of the town by Mr. Crosfield, Mr. Henry Vivian, and Mr. Fred Maddison, have all been remarkable for their high educational value, and we cannot entertain the slightest doubt that considerable support has been won for the cause of peace and progress.

Speaking on Monday, Mr. Maddison remarked that " the representation of Labour be- longed naturally to the Liberal party." This is an asseftion which ardent labour men may be disposed to contradict on first thoughts. Bus a little reflection will convince them that the speaker was right. He was not contending that labour men should leave the whole field of democratic representation to the Liberal party, but for the recognition of the idea that the direct representation of labour was a Liberal prin. "No man," he said, was a Liberal who would disregard the honest and just claims of labour, and no labour man knew his business who was not prepared to work with the Liberal who did recognise them." Mr. Crosfield has made it quite clear in Warrington that ho posseses strong sympathies with the workers in their struggle to secure the national rights and privileges to which they are justly entitled. He is a capitalist by name but not my nature. Few men have made a closer study of social and industrial problems, and labour men need only put their case before him to receive the most intelligent and sympathetic consideration. Their interests will be safer in his charge than in the hands of many of the men who are affiliated to the L.R.C. We hope there will be no hesitation shown in accepting Mr. Crosfield for what he professes to be. The workers of Warrington have forgotten what it is like to be genuinely repro. sented, but the luxuty is one they can enjoy to the full by returning Mr. Crosfield at the next election.

Almost unanimously the magistrates have decided that the George Hotel licence shall lapse. It therefore ceases to be a bone of contention between rival brewers, and the offers that have been made for it fall to the ground. Our readers will remember that Messrs Peter Walker and Sons Ltd., made the most generous offer for the licence, the sum they were prepared to give being £2,500 a clear thousand pounds more than the next highest.bid. The compensation authority—i.e. the whole of the magistrates—have now to decide what compensation they will grant to the owners of the licence—the Corporation—and to the lex-tenant of the hotel, Mr. T. Halton. They have no funds as yet to draw upon, but the money has to be provided by the licencees of the town,who will be taxed pro rata according to their assessment. They will then be entitled to deduct the amount of the charge from the rent of the house they hold, so that thelcompensation, in the long run, comes from the brewers. This is as it ought to be, so far as it goes. The brewing industry is far from con- tributing an equitable sum to the national exchequer zonsidering the profits that are made. The value of the " George" licence is therefore still an open question, and it is interesting to note that the Town Clerk put in a claim of £3,000 on behalf of the Corporation, while Mr. Halton also intimated his intention to claim compensation for his loss. The compensation authority can only award one sum, which will have to be apportioned among the people who make good their claim.

A mild sensation was caused in educational circles on Monday by the announcement in a London daily paper that proposals are under con- sideration by the Board of Education for with- drawing all over the country the grants paid for children between the ages of three and five years in attendance at elementary schools. "E Inca- tionists and medical men " it was stated, " are almost unanimously of opinion that such children should not he at school, and the Board of EJuca- Lion has, in the case of several counties, already intimated to the authorities that they need not now provide new places for such children. If these grants were withdrawn it would place at the dis- posal of the authorities throughout the country a sum of at least £BOO,OOO a year. By the extinction in this way of the gran t-in•aid given under section 10 of the Education Act of 1902 it would be possible to relieve some districts to the extent of almost is. in the pound. In addition to the relief which the local authorities would get directly from those liberated grants, there would be a saving or at least 10s. per head in local charges for the education of these children. What, however, is considered most important in the case of growing districts is that a considerable amount of school accommodation would be set free; so that children in the first standard might be retained in the infant school buildings."

Tha Warrington authorities have not yet received any intimation of such an important change. It is known that the subject has been under the consideration of the Board of Education but the opinion of those In a position to judge, is that any alteration would only he to the extent of i empowering authorities n rural areas to refuse admission to schools of children under five ye.,rs of age. It is interesting to consider what the effect of a general withdrawal of the grant would be in Warrington. There are on the books of the local elementary schools 1,0,50 children under the age of five years, and in respect of every child in avetago attendance at the infants'l Echool the committee receive a grant of 16s. or 17s. On the whole, we are informed, the with- drawal of tl4e grant would tend rather to increase than to reduce the working expenses. It is true that a czatain amount of accommodation would be released, but it should be borne in mind that chil- dren oven of the upper standards if taught in infants school would earn only the lower grant. The expenses of the staff would, if anything, be larger, and the desks in the infant departments would have to be replaced by others more suitable for older scholars. It is questionable whether, financially or educationally, the advantage of such a change would not be more apparent than real.
