"The aggregate of those objects that supply thew wants and contribute to the comforts of man,. wee/Ih."—Robert Dale Owen. * * Warrington." mounted" police were in evidence at , Friday evening's football celebrations. Their mounts, however, were no of the "fiery untamed" variety. Instead of cutting an imposing figure on prancing steeds—as would be the case in some towns—the officers who preceded the procession slow* the whole of the route, rode on bicycles. Nervous females had, therefore, little cause for alarm.

* * Further congratulations to the Football Club! The annual report is as satisfactory as the record in the Cup tournament, and the judicious handling of affairs is a credit to the committee and their able treasurer and secretary, Messrs. T. Pemberton and Harry Ashton. Few clubs in the Northern Union are so soundly established and solidly supported as War- rington and none better deserve the patronage they get. Warrington Football Club has always been a worthy organization. * * * _

" We are not downhear-ted "was the exclamation of an enthusiastic progressive in the audience at the Liberal meeting on Monday. No there is no reason to be down-hearted this time. On the contrary, with such great causes to champion and with such an excel- lent standard-bearer to lead them, the Liberals of Warrington have every reason to view with confidence the issue of the coming fight:

* Tiring of the monotony of their native pastures, two cows sought diversion by taking a stroll on the railway between Sankey and Farnworth on Monday evening. The experiment mtght have ended disas- trously in more respects than one, for the cows were quite indifferent to the approach of an express front Liverpool to Manchester, and, in spite of the repeated warnings of the driver, resolutely refused to budge. The train was brought to a standstill in time to avert a collision, and , the intruders were forced to beat a hurried retreat.

* * Penketh Parish Councillors are evidently lazier than their progenitors. They do not view with favour the idea of " walking the boundary "and are content to rely on the ordnance map. Still, the people of the district would have a much clearer notion of the parish- boundary if they had walked it, and we doubt not that genial Dr. Murray would have had a goodly following had he led the way as chairman of the Council. Parliament might very reasonably have made it a condition for all Parish (councillors to walk , the boundary on taking office each year. * * * The Electricity and Tramways Departments did not entirely cover themselves with glory during the Foot- ball Club celebration last Friday evening. No fault could be found with the.illuminated cars—they were gorgeous—but matters might have been managed better than to have so many cars at once on the Sankey route that the current would not drive them. There was an unconscionable delay on the Liverpool-road which, while it delighted the residents of the district, quite upset the schedule for the running of the illumi- nated cars. Next time the Cup comes to Warrington we shall do these things better!

* * * A "church trust" is the latest idea from America, and it is attributed to the fertile brain of Mr. J. I). Rockefeller. The project is, we are told, to consoli- date all the competitive religious sections in the United States, and work the organisation on the model of the well-known Standard Oil trust. Just imagine religious effort being modelled on Standard Oil! The churches might just as well be handed over to the DeVil forth- with. The notion is rather too Yankee, this time, for British credulity. We can swallow a lot in the wav of tall stories, but, as Kipling's baby elephant said through his nose, "this is too buch ! '

* * No less than five States in America are engaged in an anti-cigarette crusade. One of the laws already passed renders any dealer in cigarettes or cigarette papers liable to fine or imprisonment. The move- ment is, of course, designed to protect the youth of the nation, but so much interference with personal liberty is very unwise. It ought to be sufficient to prohibit cigarette smoking under a certain age, without stopping the whole source of supply to either adults or juveniles. They do things very queerly in America, but straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel seems to have been reduced to quite a simple sort of process.

Patience is a virtue which the Warrington Educa- tion Committee are evidently desirous should be cultivated by the scribes and members of the public: who attend their meetings. Monday evening was not the first occasion on which a meeting has been called for six o'clock and the committee have debated in private as a General Purposes Committee until 6.30, or even later. Perhaps it would not be a difficult matter to so arrange the meetings of the sub-com- mittee that the business of the Education Committee could be commenced promptly at the time named in the summons. The Committee ought certainly to set a better , example- if they expect punctuality front the scholars. - .
F 1

* * It is hardly a matter foi .surprise that the prejudice against motors and motorists shows no signs of dying down in rural districts. The accidents which are con timially - reported and those which narrowly . ni hppe „ being have their effect on the mind 4 of the country people, who are disposed Go ; look upon the motor as a modern Juggernaut. , Fanners in particular resent the presence of the dust-raising, malodorous automobile on the high roads - and their opinions were feelingly voiced at the Run- corn Rural Council meeting on Tuesday with the r, result that a sub-committee was appointed to consider , the advisability of reducing the speed limit. * * * Our sympathy is not altogether with the motorists. They are generally a nuisance to other people, but they can be tolerated if they behave .reasonably. Unfortunately recklessness is a characteristic of good many, and until this bad fault is guarded against more generally the motoring coin- munity must expect to suffer considerable restriction , on their pleasure. We were talking to a well-known Warrington motorist only the other day when a big car came swinging along Sankey-street from Liverpool at a pace farmn excess of the town limit. He pointed to it at once with the remark "that is the soi-t of thing that gets us into bad repute, and it is quite unneces- sary." We heartily add "hoar, hear !" * * * Trade Unionist organizations will have nothing to do with Mr. Chamberlain's fiscal proposals. -11° Parliamentary Committee of the Trade Unions Con- gress at a meeting on Thursday passed a resolution declaring that they were ignorant of any organization whatever, consisting of Trade Unions' leaders appointed to represent the Trade Unionists of the country, who were in favour of Mr. Chamberlain's fiscal proposals. The only organization of the Trade Unionists of the country was declared to , be the Trade Unions Congress, which at Leeds last year, passed a resolution condemning Protection and declaring that any departure from the principles of Free Trade woutd be detrimental to the interests of the working classes. It would be well if all workingmen would bear this in mind.

The heavy cost of Education as administered bY , municipal and County authorities, is the subject of art interesting comment in the "Spectator." Opinion in favour of the nationalisation of Education has made • great headway since the present Act mune into force, and as rates increase the need for some radical change in our educational system is forcibly impressed upot!, every responsible citizen. The " Spectator remarks: "Though passive 'resistance and the unhapPi reawakening of hostility to the Established Charon in places where such hostility had become dormant for the last fifteen years, are most serious evils in them- selves, they are nothing from the party point of view' compared with the wave of dissatisfaction that is nolo •.:.; passing over the country in regard to the great ext i ra financial burden which s being imposed by the new , Education Act," ," • * * Mr. Marshall Hall, K.C., M.P., is apparently no more inclined to fulfil his promise of "Three acree , and a cow" than Mr. chamberlain. At the Con' servative meeting at :Reigate on May sth, 21v. certainly offered to give three acres and a cow conditionally. Ile offer, however meant, was taken seriously by a fledhill gardener, who has since claimea the fulfilment of the promise. Mr. Hall refuses point blank and denies that such an offer was ever made or •: accepted. For a lawyer, the member for Southport :T has been singularly indiscreet. His remarks certainlY took the form of an offer, and the wonder is that he has not had more claimants for the bounty. We fear the Redhill gardener has small chance of realising 00_ his claim, but he has once more emphasized the fact that however lightly made, the Promise of. "three acres and a cow" is not readily forgotten.

The " See-saw ," was made to go round and when a good speed had been obtained one of the lads jumped • off with the result that the other lad, Samuel Johnson 11, Milner-street, Warrington, had his back injured. He was conveyed to the Infirmary, , Asir for CUNNINGHAM'S lIIGH-CLASb MIIINERAL WATERS.—AdVt. Shopbreakers' Singular Haul. On Monday night some person or persons succeeded in entering the lock-up shop of Mr. Groom, Ilewsey- street, by means of the skylight in the roof, and made eff with a number of watches, a gold chain, and several rings. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55,BrIdge st., Warrington.—Advt. Unhappy at Eighty-Five. At Lymm Sessions, on Wednesday, Mr. Brown, Solicitor, Warrington, applied for a separation order en behalf of Ellis Leigh, of Sandiway, Northwich, against his wife, Mary Jane Leigh. It was stated that the complainant was eighty-six years of age, and his wife sixty-five. In consequence of his wife's drunken habits he was neglected. Mr. Brown now Stated that complainant was unable to appear, being in feeble 'health, and he would withdraw the case. Defendant was at present in Knutsford Workhouse. The complainant was contributing Os. per week towards her maintenance. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS.—Advt. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Is Christianity True? PhotograPhin Society's Exhibition. The annual exhibition in connection with the War- rington Photographie Sxiety was brought to a close on Saturday. As stated last week the exhibition has been unusually successful and a great advance upon similar exhibitions in connection with the Society, and during the week attracted a large number of visitors to the Museum Art Gallery. The concluding stages witnessed the distribution of prizes to the successful exhibitors, Mr. E. J. Hall, performing that office before a large attendance in the lecture room at the Museum. Mr. Mathias presided.—ln presenting the prizes, Mr. Hall referred in high terms to the work of the society, and hoped the exhibition would prove a stimulus to local photographers, especially in assist- ing them to make themselves useful in collecting mementoes of disappearing land-marks in Warrington. Wooleas,a fine representa- tion of an old harbour scene, to Mr. Mathias, in celebration of his approaching marriage. div.head: INDEPENDENT METHODISM.
div.p: INDEPENDENT METHODISM.
A SHORT HISTORY BY MR. ARTHUR
MOUNFIELD.

We have this week received a copy of "A short history of Independent Methodism," which has been compiled by our townsman, Mr. Arthur Mounfield, as "likely to be read with interest on the occasion of the celebration of the hundredth annual meeting." In a preface Mr. Mounfteld says: "From the year 1797 the early Churches of our denomination held much useful intercourse, but it was not until 1806 that they formally joined themselves into an organisation. Since the annual meeting of that year was described as the first, it follows that the meeting of the present year-1905 becomes the hundredth. To mark the occasion the General Committee decided upon the issue of the present volume and entrusted its preparation to George Hunter, James Vickers, and Arthur Mounfield—the latter to fulfil the duties of Editor." The demaeds of space have compelled much of the historical narrative to be abridged, but the hope is held out of a more extended and complete work in the future. Nevertheless the two hundred and odd Imes of Mr. Mounfleld's book comprise a Valuable and interesting record of the begin- nings and growth of Independent Methodism. There are many local references, extracts from some of which we take the liberty of quoting. THE FIRST SOCIETY AT WARRINGTON. The origin of the first society at Warrington,says Mr. Mounfield, is a matter of deepest interest, for though not the oldest in point of years it became the for na- tive agency of the denomination. It was the privilege of the Society to have within its fellowship men of fine intellectual power From Warrington went forth the men who first expounded the principle and whose own society could always be pointed to as an object-lesson of the ideal they proclaimed. The Quaker-Methodists have been often described as a society that separated from Methodism as a protest against existing usage. Such a statement is far from describing the facts and would not be fair either to the old or the new body. Indeed, the story of the formation of the Society has not hitherto been fully told. It was not as a protest against current usage so much as an unwillingness to accept a new order that the Warrington Society began a separare existence. Among the preachers who formed the first Society—the names of others have not been handed down—were Richard Harrison, Richard Mills, Peter Reid, Saul Rigby, William MoGuiness, and John Meredith. The separation took place in 1796. The meeting at which they formally organised a society is stated to have taken place" in a room behind the premises, then a grocer's establishment, next door to the Rose and Crown in Bridge-street," but the date has not been pre- served. This room served as a meeting place for some little time. Approached from Rose and Crown-street by a staircase, it would prove a central and convenient meeting-place. The premises—now part of an electric lighting store—still exist, and though devoid of beauty and interest are worthy of remembrance as the scene of an historic meeting. PETER PHILLIPS. Though one of the youngest members of the first society in Warrington, Peter Phillips has by general consent been described as its founder. From this has followed the wider desoription—"Founder of Independ- ent Methodism." We cannot suppose that Peter was regarded as the leading spirit in the formation of the new society, for though gifted beyond his years he had not yet reached his nineteenth birthday when the crisis came in 1796. It was at the end and not at the beginning of his career that he was hailed as founder of the denomination.. A title whichhe himself would have been swift to repudiate was placed iipon his grave-stone loving hands, and from thence has passed intcr current speech. His father, John Phillips, was one of the picturesque figures of old Warrington. As town crier she displayed every day the glories of a scarlet coat and velvet breeches with the added peculiarity of a pig-tail of plaited hair. Peter was a chairruaker by trade and followed his calling through life. In 1802 he was married to Hannah Peacock, with whom he had been a fellow teacher in the Wesleyan school, and a fellow labourer in the Quaker-Methodist Society. Every account of Peter Phillips describes him as a teacher of rare insight. Only once as far awe know did he announce a sermon beforehand, and the circum- stance is too interesting to be left unmentioned. It was during the days following the massacre of Peterloo. The Quaker Methodists, from their democratic tend- encies, were under some suspicion The suspicion seemed to be confirmed when Peter Phillips surprised the congregation at Friars' Green by announcing that on the next Sunday evening he would preach from the text, "He that bath no sword let him sell his cloak and buy one." People gatherod in crowds to hear the prophet of revolt, and the officers of the law took prominent places in the audience. The neighboues took the pre- caution to barricade their windows in anticipation of riot. But it was a needless precaation. The preacher calmly proceeded to show the spiritual significance of the text and to describe the mission of the true disciple in every age. The law officers left before the sermon ended. Peter Phillips passed away May 11th 1853. THE FIRST MEETING HOUSE. An interesting chapter is that relating to the first meeting-house, "Old Friar's Green," of which a picture is given. The building was hallowed by its association with the names of Dorothy Ripley, the American Quakeress, and Lorenzo Dow, In 1859 it gave place to the present building. I Mr. Monalleld adds :—" The old gateway is left to us, and imagination may conjure up the long lineage of good men who have passed ' and repassed in their advocacy of great causes : tly. Quaker-Methodists standing firmly by an unpopular cause, but living to find themselves an honoured community ; Dorothy Ripley and Lorenzo Dow bringing from across the Atlantic great and strange gifts of ministry ; James Crawfoot, for the offence of preaching here suspended by the Wesleyan Methodists, and becoming thenceforward a force in the shaping of Primitive Methodism • Hugh Bourne and William Clowes bringing the zeal which afterwards built the denomination ; George Harrison Birkett, the pioneer of total abstinence, and Joseph Livesey, its most ardent apostle; henry Auderton, Dr. Grinrod, James Teare, Edward Grubb, presenting the pathos as well as the science and logic of the temper- ance cause. We may well be proud of the associations of the old meeting-house, for these names are cherished to-day as representing the best influences that have shaped modern thought and habit." WAREtINGTON DISTRICT. Warrington district, with its 13 churches and two mission stations, 700 members, 2,330 Sunday school scholars, and property valued at £22,700, has no lass than 16 pages devoted to it, though even here much more might be recorded. There are numerous pictures of the churches and missions. Other ehapters,many illustrated, deal with the various districts in the denomination from Great Yarmouth to Glasgow. Mr. James Vickers contributes an article on "Independent Methodism: Its Constitution and Polity."

People would do what they conceived to be to their own interests, and he thought Alderman Bennett would give the mannfacturers credit for being alive to the question of water navigation. In the course of further discussion Mr. P. Monks said it was not to the interests of Manchester to let War- rington go too far ahead in the development of canal traffic. He had done his best to send traffic by the canal but could not do so because the necessary facilities were not provided. The following resolution was unanimously adopted : —" In view of the heavy disability imposed upon the industries and commerce of the United Kingdom by the excessive cost of inland transport and the neglect into which the waterways of the country have fallen, this Association earnestly calls upon his Majesty's Govern- ment to take steps for the purpose of the full utilization, the co-ordination and the extension of British and Irish canals, either by the establishment of public Canal Trusts, or by some other method to create a national system of cheap inland water transporatitni." div.head: SHOULD CANALS BE NATIONALIZED?
div.p: SHOULD CANALS BE NATIONALIZED?
CHAMBER OF COMMERCE DISCUSS THE QUESTION.
Warrington and the Ship Canal.

The Warrington Cumber of Commerce held a special meeting at the Town Hall on Thursday afternoon, for the purpose of considering the best method of improv- ing and more fully utilizing the inland waterways of the United Kingdom. The result was the adoption of a resolutiop in favour of the creation of a public canal trust or the adoption of some other means of creating a national system of cheap inland water transportation. The president (Councillor J. Fulton Smith) occupied the chair and there were also present:—Colonel Ridg- way, Messrs. F. Monks, F. W. Monks, C. E. Parker, 1-1„ Kingdon, John Fairclough, T. A. Mosso, J. W. Hayward, T. E. Gibson, J. H. Smethurst, and Alderman Bennett (secretary of the Chamber). Mr. [done! Wells, an authority on matters pertaining to inland navigationott- Vended for the purpose of placing useful information at the disposal of the Chamber to assist them in arriving at a decision. . _ .

a The CHAIRMAN said that in the past most people appeared to have been swayed by the idea that when railways were introduced there would be no further need for the old-fashioned canals, and the railway system had certainly developed in a way which was unequalled all over the world. lie had no doubt the quick and efficient transit which they inaugurated had militated very much against the progress of the canals. alderman BENNETT announced the receipt of letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr. .T. Charlton Pare, Mr. Andrew Rathbone, and Perrins Limited. The discussion was introduced by Mr. F. W. MONKS, who referred to the variety of views expressed on the subject by responsible bodies. He thought everyone would agree that if by re-organization a cheaper and I more efficient service for the trading community could be arranged, it was in the interests of the community that such a state of things should be brought about. (Hear, hear.) How it was to be done was the knotty point. One view was that the canals should be national- ized—that was, taken over by the Government and managed by it. That, in theory, seemed very nice and simple, and perhaps the easiest way for the trading community to settle the matter. Still, one hesitated about creating another Government department when there were so many which they could not say were really well managed. He doubted if the placing of a responsibility of that kind on the Government's shoulders would give them the most satisfactory work- ing scheme. A second plan was that a sort of National Trust should be legalised by Act of Parliament. A national Trust would mean that there would probably have to be representatives of all the various interests concernel, but the Trust would certainly be simple in one respect —that it would deal with the canals as a whole and therefore any alterations, extensions or improvements that weee effected would certainly be in the direction of co-ordinating the general scheme and bringing it all up to one standard. Two sevenths of the canals of the country, pointed out Mr. Monks, were owned by the railway companies. The Trust would be extremely large and unwieldy, and it could only make progress, by deputing portions of the work to smaller sub-cora- mittees representing certain areas.lf that idea was to be carried out, it wolild be better to form a Public Trust to work in connection with the local and district authorities. The people would then be more personally interested and give more time and attention to the work. The Trust would be able to exercise a better and closer supervision and probably control the expense more effectively, than if the scheme were all worked , from one Central office in London. Mr. Monks dealt I with the schemes in force in continental nations, and I pointed out that, with the exception of the Manchester Ship Canal, we in England were practically where we were fifty years ago. By means of the canals in Germany goods could be transported from one end of the country to the other at a very small cost, and he believed steel billets a ere received in Warrington which bad come from the South-Eastern corner of Germany. He believed there would have to be a great deal of educational work on the subject before English traders would be willing to take advantage of an improved canal system. Probably that was because the railway companies offered such remarkably rapid means of transit which enabled firms to keep much smaller stocks than would be the case if goods were forwarded by canal. Neither this nor any other Government would, he thought, take up the subject until strong pressure was brought to bear upon it by bodies which represented public opinion through the trading community. Mr. LIONEL WELLS, who was for ten years engineer for the River Weaver Navigation, delivered an interest- ing address. The question, he said, should be stated as one of the cheapening of the carriage of goods and minerals in the country. Up to fifty or sixty years ago the cost of carriage of products in England was the cheapest in the world. We had a good system of canal navigation which, combined with the rivers, served the districts where trade was the most important, and we had supplemented that with the beginning of the rail- way system, making us ahead of all the world. Since then other nations had gone on improving their method and now the cost of carriage in this country was dearer than in any other. There was a danger of the question being loft like the education question, until it became extremely pressing, instead of grappling with it early in the day. Given a good waterway, they could carry goods a great deal cheaper by canal than by rail. He thought the one feasible way of dealing with the question was for the Government to take it up. He hoped he would bear something as to what the Ship Canal had done for Warrington. Before that waterway was opened it:always appeared to him that Warrington and Ellesmere Port were the two places which would benefit most largely from it. There was no doubt as to the benefit which had accrued ta Ellesm we Port. but Warrington seemed, as far as he knew, to make little or no use of the canal. Was it because the traders were satisfied ? If so, of course there was nothing to be done. Trte difficulty in moving the country seemed to him to be that directly tbey stepped out, someone inter- fered to prevent progress. There were so many vested Interests that they were at once acting directly anyone wanted to start a new thing. Mr. C. E. Parker expressed thehope that the Chamber would give Mr. Monks a strenuous backing in the matter. He thought the railway companies had pro- bably been short-sighted in allowing their canals to be practically idle. If they had allowed the canals to be used for the carriage of the lower grade traffic at cheap rates, it would probably have had the effect of increas- ing the higher grade traffic on the railways. Instead of that, they had discouraged the use of the canals. The system of horse haulage was a great deal out of date, and it would facilitate the traffic considerably if a system of electric haulage by means of overhead wires could be introduced. Mr. E. L. FLEMING said it seemed a strange thing that Warrington should interest itself in waterways, because they had the Ship Canal brought to their doors, and yet very little use was made of it. He believed the secret lay in the fact that at the Walton lay-bye no ware- house had been put down in order to accommodate the traffic. During the last few weeks representations had been made by the Chamber of Commerce to the Canal Company, and they had set men to work clearing the land In the neighbourhood of the lay-bye with a view, he hoped, to erecting a warehouse. Mr. Fleming pointed out that 200 vessels passei Warrington every week, but they would not stop to take in small consign- ments. Why had not the arm of the river at Walton been utilized for the formation of a dry-dock? There had been gentlemen connected with the Corporation for years, and surely they might have done that in the interests of the traders generally. Even the gentlemen present might form a syndicate for the purpose of undertaking the work. He also hoped Warrington would, before it was too late, acquire the land opposite Wilderspool Brewery which was now being used for the deposit of mud dredged from the river. When they had taken advantage of the water way that lay at their door they might go in for nationalization of all canals. Mr. T. A. Mosse said the question was a national one. When we considered the cost of carriage both by rail and water he did not think we were inn fair position to compete with foreign nations. He did not think they ought to blame the railway companies so much, because the canal companies forced them to buy the canals and they had to pay a high price. Mr. KINGDON desired information as to the saving to be derived from the use of canals. Speaking for his firm (Messrs. Crosfleld) if any considerable reduction were effected in the cost of carriage, they would be ' willing to give the retailers the whole of the benefit of it, because they would expect to recoup themselves by the saving on Imported raw material^. Colonel BLDG WAY said that if they put down the cost of carriage by rail at 100 they might say it would be only 20 by canal. His family had had something like 150 years experience of water carriage on the canals and on the river, and he believed there was not the slightest doubt that it was much more advantageous for heavy goods and goods in large quantities to be sent by water. Representations should be made to Parliament with the object of getting the Board of Trade to see that the railway companies kept the canals in proper repair and did not close them. He thought that many years would pass before the canals could be nationalized. Alderman BENNY:Tr agreed with Mr. Fleming that it was an amazing thing that a huge waterway like the Ship Canal should he comparatively unused by the people of Warrington. In some respects Warrington people were enterprising and , active enough. What seemed to be wanting was the spirit of collective enter- prise among the manufacturers for the general advance- ment of the commerce of the town. With regard to the general question he believed that either by nation- alization or the formation of a Trust something would ultimately be done. Mr. F. MONKS said that So long as the railway com- pany's offered such advan ta aes and the Manchester Ship Canal CompanY made no attempt to MONT and provide facilities for the carriage of goods to Liverpool and

div.head: MR, FRED MADDISON.
div.p: MR, FRED MADDISON.
One of the Knights of Labour.
BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCH.

Mr. Fred Maddison, whose exceptionally powerful addresses have been the featute of this week's meet- ings arranged by the Progressive Labour League, his rendered yeoman service in the cause of Labour and progress. He is a Yorkshireman, and served an apprenticeship as a compositor in Hull. There he joined the local branch of the Typographical Association, and held the office of President for a number of years. In 1880, Mr. Maddison had the honour of acting as Presi- dent of the Trades Union Congress when it met at Hull ; having been the delegate to two previous Con- gresses. Mr. Maddison achieved a further'distinction in 1887, when he was elected the first workingman member of the Hull Corporation. Durifig his term of office he succeeded in obtaining the adoption of Fair Wages Clauses in Corporation contracts, in face of a strong Tory opposition. Mr. Maddison always quotes this as an instance of what Labour can do in associa- tion with the Liberal party, because without the sup- port of the Liberal leaders in the Council he would have been unable to carry the clauses. In 1889 Mr. Maddison left Hull 'to :take charge of the " Railway Review"—the official organ of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Ser- vants. He resigned that work immediately after being elected to Parliament in 1807, owing to a difference he had with the executive as to a proposed I general strike. His interest in the excellent organiza- tion of the railway men, however, remains unimpaired and one of his best friends in political work is the present able f,General Secretary. (Mr. R. Bell; M.P.) , Taking a keen interest in- education, Mr. Maddison was for six years a member of the Tottenham School Board and' in that capacity he proved an active worker on the Progressive side. Mr. Maddison first became a Parliamentary candidate in 1892 when he was asked by the Liberals of Central Hull to oppose the present member, Mr. Seymour King. The, seat had never been held by a Liberal and its capture had always been regarded as a "forlorn hope" ;from the Liberal point of view. The Trades Council and the Libeilisl Association joined hands, and after a short fight, they succeeded in reducing the Tory majority from over 1,100 to a little over 400. Mr. Middison was again the candidate for Central Hull in 1895, but in the interval a ruinous dockers' strike had taken place. This adversely affected Mr. Maddison's candida- ture, and he was beaten by a considerable majority. In 1897, on the death of the late Mr. Mundella, he was selected as candidate for the Brightside division of Sheffield and was returned triumphant after a contested election. Mr. Maddison's position as the Brightside. representative remained a I strong one until the outbreak of the Boer war. Seventy I five per cent, of the electors of that constituency are ' engaged in the production of war materials, and the determined attitude Mr. Maddison took against the campaign was fatal to his re-election. At present he I is the Liberal and Labour:candidate for Burnley where the Chances of success appear good. Mr. Maddison , leads a busy life, and he is now acting:as organizing secretary to the Cobden Club. Though not a socialist in economics, he has long taken considerable interest in what is known as the Copartnership of Labour, believing that the best way to secure real progress is to endow workmen with a greater share of the property lof the country. Pitductive co-operation is already flourishing, and Mr. Maddison and his co-workers are hopeful that in time it will become as popular as dis- tributive co-operation. On the inauguration of Mr. Charles Booth's scheme for the. provision of old ago pensions, Mr. Maddison threw in his lot with the movement and was elected a member of the Committee of Organized Labour for the promotion of pensions. In 1892 he was offered the lucrative post of labour correspondent of the Board of Trade, but declined it, as the duties would have necessitated his retirement from the " fighting line." We wish Mr. Maddison well in his gallant fight at Burnley, for he is one of those level-headed Progressives who has abundantly proved his worth as a champion of Labour.

div.head: NEW SCHOOL FOR STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: NEW SCHOOL FOR STOCKTON HEATH.
-- County Council take Action.

The Cheshire County Council have decided to build a new school in Stockton Heath, and to-day they publish the necessary advertisement calling upon objectors to the proposal to give notice of their opposi- tion within three months. The new school is to accommodate 800 scholars and will'be available for children from Stockton Heath, Latchford without and Walton Interior, and will cost between :e7,000 and .c.:8,000. Of this sum the County Council have the power of apportioning two thirds as a special charw upon the three districts,the balance to be provided out of the general County fund. It does not follow, however, that the maximum levy will be made, but it is almost certain that whatever the amend charged the erection of the sell° A will mean an advance in the rates of the three parishes. The decision of the County Council will come as a surprise to many though it has long been realized in the district that additional school accommodation is urgently , necessary. Under the new Act, air space to the extent ! of ten cubic feet per scholar has to be Provided, and the existing school is deficient in this respect. It accommodates 600 scholars, but on the books, how- ever, there are some 870 children. Some two years., ago this serious overcrowding attracted the attention of several residents, and mainly at the instigation of Hr. E. England, a meeting of parishioners was held to , consider the question. A long debate o-curred, I but while it was recognized that the accommo- dation was insufficient, it was decided not to ! move in the matter on account of the expense which would be involved. The 'school managers fully realized the seriousness of the position and two plans were formulated as a remedy. The first was a 'proposal to enlarge the National school but this (lid not meet with the approval of the authorities. The second, the utilization of the Clmrch Institute,(a large corrogated iron building in Grappenhall-road) for educational purposes, was granted as a temporary expedient, and for twelve months the use of that build- ing has staved off the greater question of the erection of a new school, The authorities saw that things could not continue as they were and as above stated have aken the matter in their own hands. The probable ito of the new school adjoins Rornan-road—within a thort distance of the existing institution.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Warrington ought to have been victorious in their League match with Prescot on Saturday. They were in fine batting form and piled on large scores with ease, but an unfortunate error of judgment was com- mitted in not applying the closure earlier. It was not until 220 had been scored for the loss of eight wickets that it was thought It to declare, and the result was that only eight of the Preseot wickets were down when 7.30 arrived. It is more than probable that had War- rington contented themselves with a smaller score they would have been able to place two points to their credit, for the eight wickets of their opponents yielded only 90 runs. As it was, time did not suffice to dis- miss the Prescot eleven, the first pair of batsmen making a stubborn stand, so the Warringtonians had to be content with a draw.

League cricket is already proving a good attraction at Warrington, and quite a. large gate assembled on Saturday. In the past the interest of the townspeople in the doings of the club has been allowed to sink to zero, but it makes all the difference when there are league points and cups in view! The spectators must have felt more than pleased with the abilities which the Warrington eleven displayed on Saturday, and the pity of it is that the victory which was so well merited was not actually achieved. The visitors were allowed to indulge in the pleasant occupation of " leather hunting " to their hearts! content. Alf. Thewlisi the ex-professional, gave them a particularly warm time. His innings was a splendid display and resulted inthe addition of 55 to the Warrington score. Not a single faulty stroke was noticed, and his chief hits included five fours. J. W. Bibby ran up 34 with that free and vigorous style of cricket which delights the spectator, and he was responsible for one six and five fours.

W. Richardson is proving himself a consistent bat and his 33 was the outcome of steady rather than brilliant play. Throughout he had the bowling well in hand, and he promises to be a tower of strength to the team this season. W. H. Podinore and J. Thompson were in capital form and each knocked up 27.

The Prescot innings was characterised by a deter- mined stand by W. Stephen and G. Prescott who indeed saved the situation and scored 30 and 28 respectively. Mason, the Warrington professional, continues to acquit himself well, especially with the ball, and he accounted for five wickets at a cost of 35 runs.

Warrington second fared badly at Prescot. The home team had matters nearly all their own way and triumphed by 147 runs to 84. J. T. Oliffe made the best displhy at the wicket for the visitors,and was not out with 17 to his credit. We are expecting better things from Warrington second !
To-day Warrington first visit St. Helens, and the second eleven will be at home to St. Helens second.

Encouraged by their splendid start, Sankey Wire Mills followed up their victory over Knotty Ash with an easy win at Hough Green, the majority being just 80. F. ald B. Taylor were the top scorers their in- nings realizing 29 and 23 (not out) respectively. Gleave and Burton bowled most effectively, the ifrst named capturing six wickets for 2-1 runs, while Burton was responsible for two wizkets for 6.

There was an exciting match between Latchford Baptists and Moore and Daresbury, the villagers being fortunate to win by 6. They had a remarkably good bowler in S. Taylor, who took eight wickets at the ridiculously spun cost of 10 runs,

The Secondary School eleven, or the " secOndarians " as an enthusiastic scribe terms them, accounted for Widnes P. T. C., Donaghy, Mee, and Houghton being the most successful batsmen. Minards' excellent bowl- ing contributed largely responsible to the victory, his capture being seven wickets for 12 runs. I

Cheshire Lines Engineers opened their season in promising style, with a victory over Earlestown. Deeley batted in capital style, I,nd complied 22. A. Warhurst and J. McKay bowled brilliadtly their res- pective analyses being : —A. Warhurst 8-1 overs ; 4 mds, 4 wcks, 4 runs ;.J. McKay 8 overs ; 1 Inds ; 6 wcks, 19 runs.

Each of 3lessrs. Walker's Brewery teams was triiimphant, their opponents being Altrincliam St. George's. The first team administered a particularly severe drubbing, for while the Altrincliain representa- tives were all out for 23, the Brewery men compiled 108 for 7 wickets. J. Smith and P. Messiter bowled splendidly, the former taking five wickets at the almost incredibly low cost of 2 runs, and Messiter four wickets for 18 runs. The second team bowlers : were almost equally successful. Dargan taking five Iwickets for 5 runs, and Norman five wickets for 9.

O rappenhall had a surprisingly easy task in dispos- ing of kVinnington 2nd. J. Warburton proved a prolific scorer, and was not out for the grand total of 76. J. rallain, the popular Warrington football captain, was in good form and knocked up 20—a promising start for the season.

It was little wonder that Orford Barracks defeated Grappenhall 2nd by a large margin, f w the military men had two V.C.'s doing ditty. One at least—Sergeant Knight—showed that he is mpable of great deeds, on the field of spwt, for he compiled 52 and also did good work with the ball.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The weather continues to favour tnincllers and on Saturday they again had the pleasure of playing, in a brilliant sunshine. The day, however, was not pro- ductivo of any surprises, the matches which were decided having the anticipated results. Further pro- gress was made in connection with the works tourna- ment, and as I expected, the Liberal Club players came a cropper on the Saracen's Head Green.

The Works Competition matches attracted a large crowd to the King and Queen Hotel Hotel green, interest being chiefly centred in the game between the London and North-Western and Houghton's team, Old rivals, both combinations were equally determined on victory. Houghton were, however, unequal to the task and with four men off the green they were four- teen points in arrears. Matters went from bad to worse and in the end the railway ;men ran out winners by 33 points—an average of almost three points for every game. The closest game lay between A. Cooper and J. Hutchinson, the latter win- ning 15-14. Cooper started well and ran to seven while hi's opponent recorded a single chalk. He then went to 9-2, but fell off. Hutchinson on the other hand improved splendidly and scored six points while Cooper added one to his total. A double to Cooper left the London and North Western man further in arrears, but he pulled up splendidly and peeled four ends later. A single gave him the lead which he kept for two ends when Cooper drew level, only to be beaten by the last throw. -- Joseph Harrison had equally as hard luck as his colleague. Against T. Pickering he obtained a usefill lead which he kept until the 16th end when the score stood 13-9. Pickering then surprised the spectators by running home with four singles and two doubles, Harrison not being allowed to record another point. Houghton's men seemed to have a failing for taking the lead and then being defeated, no less than seven suffering this fate. Only three of their players kept their lead until the end. H. Houghton at the outset ran away from J. Horrabin carrying the score to 11-3. Horrabin then monopolized the scoring and peeled at 12, a double and a single to Houghton however proving his undoing.

In contrast to the majority of his colleagues S. Fletcher started poorly and ended well. Until the thirteenth end his opponent E. Taylor held the lead when he got into the running of the green and by a series of singles ran out winner by 15-11. At one time the score in the game between J. Goulden and J. T. Whittle stood at 10-1 in favour of the former, and yet Goulden only won by 15-13.

The match between the Corporation and Greenings teams was interesting because of the fact that the capabilities of both were an unknown quantity: The result of thelencounter was that the hcnour of the Cor- poration was maintained by a margin of 20 points though it is doubtful whether the representatives of that august body v.ill prove triumphant in the second I round. By practise they can make their presence felt as they are a team of promise. The match was

also interesting from the fact that of the defeated players on either side only two reached double figures, substantial margins in every other case separating the victors and the vanquished. Hunt for the Corporation started very badly his game with Appleton giving Greenings a lead of 13 points. The next three games however saw the, lead reversed. Green- ings were not fated to be long in a disadvantageous position as the defeat of Pdwis and Massey once more gave them strong hopes of victory. The Corporation's tail end however commenced to wag and Greenings had the mortification of seeing their lead reduced and an adverse balance slowly but surely recorded against them, a balance which they were not strong enough to reduce.

Ths first round will be continued to-day when the the following matches will be decided ; Walkers' Brewery v. Thewlis ; Cheshire Lines Committee v. Orford Tannery, and Pearson and Knowles No. 3 v. Richmond. The first match should produce a fine struggle though Walkers' should qualify for the second round Orford Tannery are hardly a match for Cheshire Lines Committee but will probably give them a good game. In the remaining match Rich- mond's are intent upon carrying off the palm, and will probably succeed.

, The main in connection with the Warrington and District League had a singular result father and son dividing the first prize. Evidently age and experi- ence as well as youth and enthusiasm tell in bowling, because between the two' finalists there is little to chose. The fact that the main had been unduly pro- longed, however, prevented the two trying conclusions and had the game been played G.Ball jun. would prob- ably have surprised his father by defeating him. The main attracted some 120 competitors, whose ranks were considerably thinned by a full day's play on Saturday. It was found necessary to continue the , matches on Monday evening when the prize winners were placed as follows :—Messrs. Gearge Ball, sea., George Ball, jun., John Holbrook. A, Gleave, T. Davies, W. J. Woods, W. Eyes, T: Ellison, T. Davies, T. Rigby, T. Cooper, T. Bridge, E. Shaw, J. Bird, and J. Barton. *

The League tournament will be continued to-day four matches being ddwn‘ for settlement. They are : ' Cemetery v. Bulls Head, Penketh v. Horse and jockey, Penketh v. Fanner's Arms, and Sankey v. Horse and Jockey. The principal fixture is that between the Cemetery and Bulls Head as should the Church-street men Win, the championship is practically assured. There is however, little fear of this result and the Cemetery players should prove by a good 20 points the better team. Penketh will win one at least of their fixtures. The one with the Horse and Jockey is however very doubtful and in all probability the Longford men will win their first match. Chapel House are pretty safe and should capture another two points in the League table.

I Some twenty Liberals turned up smiling at the I Saracen's Head. on Saturday, and returned bewailiag their fate, being thoroughly beaten in their match with the Wilderspool club. In the singles they dropped 40 points, while in the doubles they were worse to the extent of 3 points, only winning two of the games. Li the singles the sub-captains were most unevenly matched Hewitt the deputy commander of the Liberal contingent being nilled. Of the twenty games the visitors lost twelve, not a single one of the defeated players reachingdouble figures. The Liberals do not relish so severe a defeat, and intend to clear the slate when the return match is played. In this they will probably succeed.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

The perfect weather of Saturday brought out cyclists in full force. The country-side at present wears its most charming aspect, and there is that delightful spring freshness in the air which is so refreshing to the worker escaping from the town for a short interval. The far-famed resort of Delemere was the destination of the Warrington Cycling Club and twenty-seven members enjoyed the ride through the picturesque old forest. Tea was partaken of at the Abbey Arms, and after a stroll in the woods the return journey was com- menced. A halt vbas made at the Leigh Arms, near Acton Bridge, where an impromptu " smoker " was ' held. Messrs. G. Finch, G. H. Smith, Fred Fieldhouse and P. Redfern obliged' the company with well- rendered items. Altogether the outing ranked was one , of the most enjoyable experienced for some time.

On Tuesday evening the weather and roads were again all that could be desired and over a se )re of members indulged in a spin to Bucklow Hill. To-day's run is to Chester and on Tuesday the fixture is the favourite one of "Budworth via Arley.
The Sankey Bridges Weileyan C.C. is going strong and there was a large muster for Saturday's run to Liverpool. The usual " sights " of the city were viewed, and the outing was a complete success.

The Illy meeting of the Council of the Liverpool Centre of the National Cyclists' Union was held at the Bee Hotel, Liverpool, last week, when forty-four delegates attended, including Mr. E. Pickavnnce (Warrington C.C.) The corresp)ndence included a letter from Mr. Noble, London, calling attention to the eligibility of motor cyclists for membership of the N.C.U. Mr. Waldron (hon. sec.) announced that , private members of the Liverpool Centre had been !granted permision by Lord Derby to cycle through Knowsley Park on the following dates!:—May 13, Tune 22, August 17, and September 16. The Chair- man raised the question of the appeal for voluntary subscriptions to the Defence Puud. The following additional contributions were then promised :—Liver- pool 215.; Warrington C.C., 215.; Chester, C.C., 10s. 6d.; Cambridge C.C., lOs. 6d. ; Liverpool Clarion 0.0„ 10a. 6d. ; which brings the total to date 16 J6s. Gd.

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. There was a fair attendance at this meeting on Sunday. Mr. J. Allitt presided, and spoke upon " Inci- dents." The Rev. R. J. Campbell, he pointed out, once said the incidents of daily life and observation often suggested to him matter for sermons. Mr. S. Hicks, of Salford, was the speaker, and took for his subject" The Kingdom of God or Christ's great sermon on the Mount. The Kingdom. said the speaker, was not around us, but within us. God would put His Kingdom within us if we would allow him. If Christ had possession of our hearts, and he was King over them, then our kingdom of life should be God's. Our bodies should be in Subjection to Him as King of our lives. Love, peace 1 and joy in the Holy Ghost, good living, good working, . good acts, were the fruits of the spirit.—'lr. J. Owen and the hon. secretary (Mr. B. Farrar) also took part in the meeting. Mr. R. Woods sang "Our Father" and "The minister" in an effective manner. Mr. W. H Payton Mus. Bac. presided at the organ.

A SCIIOLNR'S RECORD. The St. Helens School Attendance Committee on Wednesday passed a resolution asking the chairman(Mr. A. J. Foote), the deputy-chairman (Mr. Collins), end the director (Mr. Broomhead), to arrange for the pre- sentation of a special medal and two books which the members had subscribed for, to Margaret Mather, who 1 for eight years was always punctual and regular in her attendance at "Lowe House Catholic Schools.

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL ,CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL ,CLUB.
THE ANNUAL REPORTS.-A SUCCESSFUL YEAR.

The annual report of the Warrington Football Club has just been issued to the members and comprises 1G pages of reports and balances which will afford much food for reflection. One of the most striking facts disclosed is tho largo number of members, there being a net increase on the year of 157, making the total now 80G. Gate-money has slightly decreased, but there are good explanations of this and everything tends to show that the club was in a very healthy condition.
cow,— SECRETARY'S REPORT. The HON. SECIrETARY (Mr. Harry Ashton), reports as follows :
Once more I have the gratification of being in a posi tion to submit for your approval a very satisfactory report. The first team have played 41 matches, 26 being won 12 lost, and 3 drawn.

Tbe form Of the premier team, generally, has not been so consistent as your Committee could have wished. At one period, at the early part. of the season, varied and at times grand form was displayed, our players beating Leigh away, and Bradford at home by large scores. The goal kick at Oldham just robbed us of our points, after we had had most of the play. Victories over Swinton and Hunslet, on their grounds were excellent performances, while at Salford and Broughton we had the greater share of the play and were unfortunate to lose in each case. Our losing two points to Leigh and one to St. Helens proved, later in the season, a very great misfortune I practically shattering our prospects for the League Championship, and making all the difference between winning and losing the South West Lancashire Cup. The return match with Oldham was another instance of "hard lines." Then Wigan trounced us right merrily by 16 points to 8 points, though at one period of the game 3of our men were off the field of play at ODA time. Hereabouts arose misgivings as to the form of several players and some very drastic changes were made. They had a remedial effect and proved that the rest to some of the players was very beneficial. Subse- quently a high standard of play was splendidly main- tained right to the end of the season. Fortune was kind to us in the earlier Cup-ties, the draws being generally favourable. The display against Wigan in the third round was very meritorious as was the semi-final at .Rochdale versus Bradford. The final showed our lads in good form. Considering the doubt about the soundness of several players and the state of the ground, the team's display proved without doubt that the men were training on. They were unquestion- ably a much smarter combination all round than the Rovers and might have won by a much larger score had it been demanded of them.

Records.—For the third time we had the honour of participating in the final for the Northern Union Cup and 9 this occasion the Club achieved the object of its ambition by securing that coveted trophy. The previous gate record at Wilderspool of £315 was also beaten during the Cup ties and, singular to relate, with the same Club—Wigan in the third round of the ties. The gate receipts on this occasion were £406. More points were also scored in the League than ever before viz., -12, and we finished up in the creditable position of fifth. Warrington also enjoyed the proud satisfaction of being the first Lancashire Club to win the Nothern Union Cup on Yorkshire soil. New Players.—Altogether 14 new players have been secured during the season. Two very heavy and clever forwards were secured to strengthen the pack, viz., J. Preston, of Swinton, and F. Shugars from Penygraig, besides the Cheshire County player Joseph Beltoi, and they materially brought about that improvempt in the front rank so greatly desired. T. Hockenhall was selected to play for the County and against Yorkshire sustained a very nasty accident which mitigated greatly against Lancashire's success. international caps were gained by G. Thomas, A. S. Boardman, and J. Preston. Shugars also attending at Bradford as reserve,

IThe " A " team have this season achieved a very honourable distinction by winning the Lancashire Com- bination for the first time ; 27 matches were played, 24 being wosand 3 lost. Several very serviceable members were during the latter portion of the season called upon to assist the premier team, and right ably they justified our Com- mittee's confidence.—Yours respectfully, H. ASHTON. Particulars, which we have already published, are given of each match, the individual scorers, and the records in the different competitions. Mr. ASHTON also adds "Your committee have per- formed their duties punctually, and attentively, and I must express my deep obligation for their help and advice throughout the past year of their office." TREASURER'S REPORT. Mr. T. PEMBERTON, the hon. treasurers, reports as follows :—"I have the pleasure to place before you the accounts for the past year. The membership is now 806, 187 having joined less 30 resigned, or struck off, leaving an increase of 157. The increase in subscriptions is £6O 12s. Gd. The gate money at first team matches shews a slight decrease. This is accounted for by the increased Membership Roll and the fact of our haying replayed two cup-tie matches last year against one this season. Owing to the passing of the rule by the Northern Union whereby members were compelled to pay at cup ties, and which motion was opposed by your representatives, your committee decided to admit members free to the matches. The actual receipts for the three cup tie matches amounted to £553 2s. Bd., hut £624 4s. 2d. had to be accounted for, the balance of £7l Is. 6d. representing the amount pa,yablelby the club on behalf of the members. The A team have had a splendid folio% ing, the in- crease of gate money over last year amountirg to £lOO 10s. 3d. Another increasing source of profit is the bar. The sports though not bringing so much gain to the Club as before, proved very satisfactory,the profit being £B6 us. 3d. The Works Competition was played during very cold weather and in consequence the attendance was rather poor. The Committee this year provided jerseys and pants to encourage more teams to enter, and after payment of other expenses, their remained a disposable balance of £29 which has been distributed as follows :—lnfirmary, £lO ; Nurses Institution .£8 ; Ambulance Society,£2 ; Injured players and attendants, £9. Notice was given to the Warrington Corporation to repay the Bond of £lOO bearing 3 per cent, per annum, and a sum of £3OO bearing 3; per cent. per annum was invested with the Corporation. Provision has been made in the accounts for extra Medals ; also for expenses likely to be incurred in cele- brating the winning of the Northern Union Cup and the Lancashire Combination. Assistance has again beets given to furthering Junior Football. The wages and bonuses to players have been increased; the Insurance premium, fees to Doctor and payments to injured players are much heavier. A large sum of money has been spent in making more accommodation, enlarging the Committee Room and erecting another small office. lam sure that you will agree with me that the past season has been a notable and satisfactory one." The abstract of accounts shows the assets of the Club to be £1,425 16s. 2d., and the liabilities £79 ss. During the season just closed payments for players' wages, transfers and bonuses, have absorbed £1,539 ; repairs and alterations to ground, £127 ; railway fares, £124; dinners and hotel expenses £l4 4s. 9d. ; amount paid to injured players and insurance premium, £232 ; referees and touch judges, £49. Among the receipts are, gate- money £2,362 (Ist team) and £294 ("A" team); entrance fees and subscriptions, £297 ; bar receipts, £224 ; com- mission on cup-tie excursions £36. The accounts for the August sports disclose a profit of £B6. The gate-money was £l6l and other sources of revenue raised the total to £214. On the expendi- ture side prizes cost £72. The Works Competition was al No a source of profit, though the receipts were only £7B 15s. 7d. Economical working resulted in a .£2D balance, the bulk of which goes to charity. The annual meeting of the Club will be held on Thursday next in the Co-operative Hall, Cairo-street. The following have been nominated for office : President, W. R. Neil; hon. treasurer, Thos. Pemberton; hon. secretary,fffarry Ashton; hon. auditors, T. Walling- ton, W. Webster; committee, T. Davies, T. Bowers, T. Locker, W. Hewitt, W. Nevins, T. Barnes, nen. ; retiring committee, A. Jones, J. W. Plinston.

div.head: WARRINGTON HORSE PARADE.
div.p: WARRINGTON HORSE PARADE.

To-Day's Programme. To-day (Saturday) will witness the holding of the fifth annual horse parade which, provided the weather is flue, should prove unusually successful. As compared with last year the number of entries is about the same despite the fact that two new classes have been intro- duced—classes for cabs and hansoms, which in total have only attracted six competitors, throe in each section. The classes for brewers and light horses will again be the strongest and most representative. Competition for the silver cup, presented for the best light lurry or van horse will rest between five animals, while for the silver cups for the best light and heavy horses fourteen animals will compete. In regard to the cup for heavy horses Messrs. P. Walker and Son have intimated that they will not compete. The judging will take place in Arpley Fields in the morning and at two o'clock Lady Greenall will present the prizes to the successful exhibitors. ' Non-competitors will assemble in Slutcher's-lane and join the procession, which will commence shortly after two o'clock, in Parker-street. The route selected 'is Parker-street, Sankey-street, Buttermarket-street, Church-street, round the Lamp, Church-street, Mersey- street, Bridge-street, Horsemarket-street, Winwick- street, Tanner's-lane, Froghall-lane, Priestley-street, Powys-street, Bank Quay, Sankey-street, Bold-street, and Wilson Patten-street. The procession will be headed by the Corporation fire brigade and Messrs. Walker's Band. Five classes for heavy horses will follow, when will come Crosfield's band and fire brigade, followed by the remaining heavy horses and a section of the light horses. The other com- petitors and non-competitors will follckv the Borough Band, and Messrs, Greenall, Whitley and Company's fire engine and drays. Mr. T. H. Pretty will act as chief marshall with Mr. Herbert Burrows as his assistant, and as they are backed ,up by a body of able assistants the procession should ' pass off without a single hitch.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

AN' AMIABLE WIFE.—HLTSI3 AND NEARLY KILLED. At the Borough Police Court, on Saturday, Mary Harris, 15 Pierpoint-street, was charged with assaulting her husband, James Harris, on May Bth.—Superin- tendent Monaghan said the case was before Ale Court on Tuesday morning, and remanded until that day to enable Harris to appear. Inquiries had been made, but it was found that his injuries were not so serious as was thought to be the case. On Monday morning, the prisoner took some clothing to a pawnshop in pledge, and with the money she got drunk. She then went from house to house drinking with her neighbours, and came home at one o'clock. Her husband was in the kitchen, but was just going upstairs, when she asked him for more money for drink. He refused to give her any, and she threw an empty beer bottle at him, just missing his head. She followed him upstairs, and got hold of a piece of broken chair and struck him on the left temple It caused him to bleed very freely, and she was alleged to have struck him several times. He was left on the bed until live o'clock in the evening, "lying in blood." Inspector GOK called at the house, and saw the prisoner bleeding, and he was very weak. He reported the matter to the police, and Sergt. Barnett, and P.C. Hesp went to the house they saw prisoner's husband lying on the bed, blood being all over the bedroom. A cab was at once obtained and he was removed to the Infirmary. Inspector Cox described the house as being "like a slaughter-house."—Prisoner, who made her ninth appear- ance said she was sorry. She was sent to gaol for two months. e_

CHILD HAWKERS DEFY THE LAW. William Humphreys (13) and Joseph Humphreys (7) 12, Phillip-street, were charged at the Warrington Police Court on Monday with hawking without licences , on the 11th May. The boy William was also charged with a similar offence committed on another date.—Thel Chief Constable said that although that was the first ease of its kind which had been brought before the magistrates it was by no means the first offence under the Act. He had from time to time had cases brought before his notice and spoken to the parents of the lads who had met him in every possible way. The present case was however,one of flagrant defiance of the law. One of the defendants had had a license which, however, he gave up months ago, saying he was not going to hawk again. When caught hawking both lads were out later than the law allowed them to be. William Humphries when first caught gave a wrong address. When it was found where he resided the detective asked where he was, and was informed he was at school. The officer at once went to the school, where he was informed that the lad had not been in attendance for some time. The lad William defied the law, as the second offence was com- mitted after he had received the summons for the first. —The Chief Constable explained that he prosecuted the defendants to show the people that the law was not to be regarded as a joke.—Dsfendants were fined in the costa on one summons (3s. 6d.), the other two cases being withdrawn. RCNCORN LICENSEE FINED. At Runcorn, on Tuesday, John Eth.aird Jones. licensee of the Volunteer Inn, Granville-street, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk on the 6th inst. He was convic- ted of a similar offence a month ago.—The defendant alleged that he was nervous and excited, and he handed up a doctor's certificate to that effect.—The magistrates said the defendant could not do better than follow the advice of the certificate—that he should refrain from any alcoholic indulgence. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE. At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, Samuel Joynson, 30, Lythgoes-lane, was charged with attempt- ing to commit suicide by hanging himself in his own dwelling-house at four o'clock on Monday afternoon.— Superintendent Monaghan said the prisoner was a Cor- poration nightsoil man and had been drinking during the week end. He returned home at one o'clock on Monday and lay on the sofa. Later his wife saw him go upstairs and shortly afterwards hearing a noise she went upstairs and found him hanging by a rope i attached to the banister. She called n a neighbour, who was anable to cut him down. A postman named Alfred Woods was also called in, and cut him down. Dr. Adams was sent for and the prisoner was removed to the Police Station, and attended to by Dr. Smith. Joynson, who was a Volunteer, went out to South Africa four years ago, and was there for sixteen or eighteen months. Since his return he had frequently quarrelled with his wife. He (the superintendent) did not wish to offer any evidence against the prisoner as he had promised to be a teetotaller. The doctor certified the man was quite sane. The Chairman said prisoner ought to have been sent for trial to the Sessions, but as he had promised to behave himself the magistrates would dismiss the case. They hoped it would be a warning 0
