div.head: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
THE CLOSING OF SCHOOLS FOR CHURCH SERVICES.

Alderman Smethurst's Indignation. The principal business down for discussion at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Com- mittee, which was held on Monday, was the question of the attendance of children at church during school hours.

_ At a meeting on the 4th May the School Attendance Committee proceeded to consider the replies which had been received to the enquiry made as to the schools from which children attended Church during school hours on Ash Wednesday. It was noted that children had attended Church from the following schools : Fairfield, Hamilton-street National, Ladies School of Industry, St. James', Latchford, St. Barnabas', St. Ann's National, Warrington Parochial, and St. Peter's. No reply having been received from the Managers of the Trinity National School, it was resolved that the managers of the Trinity National school be notified that, unless more prompt attention is given by them to com- munications sent by direction of the Committee, they will be compelled to take into consideration the advirability of taking action under Section 7 of the Education Act, 1902. It was also Resolved that a notification be sent to the managers of all schools that, in future, the school mast open and close at the usual hour unless the previous sanction of Committee has been obtained to a later opening or an earlier closing. An application having been received from the I Managers of the St. Alban's, St. Benedict's, and St. Mary's (R.C.) schools for p,,rmission to close those schools on the following holidays of Religious Obser- vance :—The Ist and 22nd June,it was resolved that the desired permission be granted. Alderman BENNETT presided over a meeting of the Education Committee at which there was also present:l Aldermen Smethurst, and Tinnion, Councillors Burton, Barton, Ellison, Evans, Hulse, Maginn, Roberts, Sankey, Fulton Smith, Wright, and Wilkinson, Messrs. W. Bibby, J. D. Buckton, Et. T. Fairclough, A. J. Jolley, T. May, C. E. Parker, E. Plinston, J. Upson, G. Walker, and the Revs. Morley Stevenson and N. Wilson, Mr. J. Moore Murray (director of education) and Mr. John Fairhurst (treasurer.) The confirmation of the minutes of the School Attend- ance Committee was moved by Councillor ELLIsoN who read the following letter which he had received from the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton:—" Holy Trinity Vicarage, 9th May, 1903. Dear sir,—ln reply to your letter of yesterday, I wish to point out that the information about Ash Wednesday can easily be obtained from the head teachers. I have no doubt that you applied to me for this information out of courtesy; but in all cases of this kind, where information is sought that can be obtained without troubling the managers, I should be much obliged if that method were adopted in order. to lessen correspondence already too voluminous (Laughter.) And apart from this, I have my doubts as to the propriety of making returns to your committee with regard to services in church or those attending them. The point, however, need not be raised if the course I have indicated be adopted. I have deferred writing upon this in the hope that some other manager might make a similar representation, and so obviate the necessity of any communication from me." Continuing Councillor Ellison said that much had been said up and down the country about taking children tol church for religious instruction. It was a practice which ~.ould not be continued without the consent of the local authority. The Board of Education had stated that the practice never was legal if the local authority objected. He should be sorry to see any dispute arise' between the school managers and the committee. Speaking personally, he had always tried to cultivate a friendly feeling towards every section of the churches, but he could not favour one denomination more than another. He believed in equality without fear or favour. Councillor BARTON seconded. _ _

Councillor ROBERTS said he was a manager of St. Peter's School, and he was astonished to find that school mentioned in the agenda. He could not under- stand what the managers had done amiss. Were they to understand that children were forbidden by law to , attend service during school hours? I The CHAIRMAN : I say No " ; Mr. Murray says " Yes." I suppose he knows. Mr. NTURRAY said that the children, if they went to church during school hours, were liable to prosecution by the school attendance officer for not attending school unless the day upon which they went to church was a day of religious observance. Councillor Roeutrs did not care what school it was, but the principal was wrong, although he could not alter it. (Laughter.) If he were a clergyman of a Church school if he could not take his children to service during school hours he would take them after. (Hear, hear). He would take jolly good care he would have them in somewhere—(Langhter)—and so far as he was concerned he would advise the Vicar of St. Peters Ito take that step. Aldermad SMETHURST : Any school can obtain per- mission to take the scholars to church if notice is sent to the Education Committee. Certain schools have taken that course, and St. Paul's is in that category. The CHAIRMAN : It is simply a question of asking for permission. Permission has been granted whenever it has been asked. Mr. PLINSTON said Alderman Smethurst was hardly correct. The Heathside managers had not acted in a proper manner and asked for permission. They inti- mated that it was their intention to take the children to church without asking permission and word was sent back that they must not do so. He did not think the Alderman would make the statement he did knowing it to be untrue._

1 —The Rev. M. STEVENSON said he felt it to be his duty I to move that the resolution relating to the notification sent to the managers of schools be referred back for furtherlconsideration. He did so without the slightest spirit of antagonism to the action of the committee, which from every point of view' was perfectly reasonable and right, and he appreciated very warmly indeed the sympathetic and kindly words which had fallen from Councillor Ellison. He should,therefore,endeavour to couch the few remarks he intended to make in the same spirit. This was, of course, an extremely difficult question, and which might be said to be more or less sub judice, and he thought it must be referred to a higher court before it Was finally settled. To shoe its complexity a striking instance had occurred. The pre- sent Parliamentary Secretary to the Board of Education was a man of calm judgment, legal training, and unbiased mind, and he read the Act as forbid- ding children to be taken to church during school hours except with the consent of the local Education Authority. His predecessor, Sir John Gorst, who was really the framer of the Act, and under whose regime it was passed, was also a man of considerable learning, good judgment, legal training and even more experience than Sir William Anson, and his conclusion was diametrically the opposite. He had heard Sir John Gorst say in the most emphatic terms that he thought the judgment of Sir Wm. Anson was •clearly wrong. Here -they had two gentlemen, to whom they should look with confidence for a right answer on the question who differed considerably. The question would remain in its present unsatisfactory condition until a high legal authority had been obtained As soon as the committee knew what the law was they would loyally obey it at once whether they likel it or not. (Hear, hear.) There was a way out of the diffi- cult°, and he ventured to ask thecommittee to consider the matter once more. Other education authorities, in- cluding the Cheshire Council and Liverpool, had solved the problem by giving managers of schools a certain number of days or half days in the year, in which they were at liberty to close their schools for religions observances and other purposes for which schools were occasionally used. That was a way out of the difficulty they might consider, because they would understand that it was not unnatural that the managers who had been accustomed to give occasional holidays—and other managers were glad of the use of the buildings for various purposes, such as bazaars—liked to take the children to church for service on some special day. They would be very sorry to be robbed of these priqileges. The Board of Education had a right to interpret the Act, and though it was doubtful whether Sir Wm. Anson had interpreted it correctly they must bow to his decision until it was reverssid by some higher authority. Mr. R. T. PAIRCLOUGH seconded the amendment. He considered that if the resolution was carried the managers would simply be so many dummies and nothing more. ' Mr. PARKER supported the confirmation of the minutes. He did not see that the suggestion made by 1 Mr. Stevenson necessitated the minute being referred ' back. It was desirable that if the children were to be I of the authority. (Hear, hear.) If the whole of the children belonged to the church to which they were taken, he did not see there would be any difficulty, but necessarily there were a number of children who were not associated with the particular denomination of the school. These would remain and be taught by some of the young teachers while others had gone to church. It was undesirable that this cleavage should be made as it was putting the parents to some disadvantage. Mr. MAY supported the minutes. .In a great majority of the schools, the holidays were being so arranged as not to raise the objections of the Dissenters. The real authority was the School Management Committee and power should not be given to any subsidiary authority, however powerful, to interfere with the management of the school. It would be a gross interference with the authority of the committee to allow persons not belong- ing to it to decide the matters. He hoped the matter would be allowed to pass over as quietly as possible ,so that they should not raise the religious question on such a trifling matter as the present.l Councillor WILKINSON hoped the minutes would be passed in their entirety, as he could not see what objec- tion anyone could take to them. They were the local education authority, and the people who had .to find the wherewithal. Surely no clergyman or minister of religion could think he was doing anything out of place if he climbed down a step or two to ask for permission for a holiday. (Hear, hear.) He did not think anyone had ever been refused yet. Continuing, he said he did not wish to relinquish their old authority as school managers. He did not think it was taking any hack seat.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday May 20, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday May 20, 1905.

The managers of the schools must remember that the• local authority had taken from their shoulders a tremen- dous responsibility. (Hear, hear.) Mr. WALKER said he was sorry the discussion had taken the tone which it had. They were the authority for the opening and closing of the schools and desired to be recognized as such. 1 The Rev. Father WILSON said he did not understand why Mr. Stevenson suggested a whole or a half- holiday. It seemed to him that if half holidays were granted to certain schools it would have a serious effect upon the attendance at other schools in town. The case would be met if the Education Com- mittee would consent to allow the managers to open the school at ten minutes to ten. That would give time to secure the minimum of secular education which was necessary to constitute attendance. He would suggest a certain number of days in the year. say ten or half a dozen, or even more. Then the children could go from their homes to the church before the school opened. Councillor EVANS agreed with the suggestion made by the last speaker. If it was adopted the committee would suffer no monetary loss. Councillor ELLISON did not think there was any need to refer the matter back at all. He felt certain that if the matter was left with the committee the objections which had been raised by the Revs. Morley Stevenson and Father Wilson would be given every consideration. The sub-committee wished to settle the matter with out difficulty; and they hoped, therefore, that the minutes would be allowed to pass. Colonel BUCKTON thought the question was one for the School Management Committee. Alderman SMETHURST was surprised at the tone the discussion had taken. As Churchmen they had a right to do what they had done for hundreds of years, and simply because a law had been passed within a year or two no obstacle should be put in their way. He con- tended that Churchmen were not so bigoted as some of their !Dissenting friends, who did not obey the law. Churchmen were willing to obey the law and to abide by it, and not pose as martyrs and go to prison because their rates were not paid. The Church had built mos. of the schools, and its members had a right to certain privileges and they should see that they were carried out. Why should they give up schools they had bought with their own money, and in which the greater portion of the children of the country were educated ? As Churchmen they wanted two or three half-days a year in which to carry out their religious principles. All the Dissenters had certain days, feist or fast days, or what- ever they were called,and the Cuurch had also a right to a certain number He (the speaker) had paid School Board rates for many years, and he had never grumbled. Ho fought against the introduction of School Boards, but when the law became law he was loyal to it. He was not the same as some people who tried to stand forth as martyrs for liberty of conscience. Councillor BURTON: I think the alderman is out of order.

The CHAIRMAN: He is certainly wandering from the subject. Alderman SMETHURST: We don't want half a dozen holidays. We want a holiday, and we applied for it. We applied for Ascension Day, and the committee granted it. Mr. PLYNSTON: No, no. Alderman SMETHURST: We gave you notice. I hope all the members of the committee will vote for the amendment. . .

Mr. PLINSTON said he would not have taken part in the discussion had it not been for the statement made by Alderman Smethurst. He was absolutely opposed to scholars being taken to church—he did not care which it was—during school hours on any week-day. Let the religious instruction be given on the Sunday in the Sunday school, and in church. He said fearlessly that ha should oppose any applic tion that came before the sub-committee as strongly as possible. The votinr, was then proceeded with and the minutes carried in their entirity, the Rev. Morley Stevenson's amendment bein,, defeated by a large majority. THE HEAESSIESTRESS OP HOLY TRINITY

div.head: SCHOOLS. INCIDENT SATISFACTORILY SETTLED.
div.p: SCHOOLS. INCIDENT SATISFACTORILY SETTLED.

The School Management Committee reported that they had resolved that free admission to the Secondary School (including the provision of the necessary books) be granted on the recommendation of the heidmaster of the school to eight children at present in their second year at the school whose parents are in poor Circumstances.

The committee had also resolved that the year ended the 31st March, 1905, be counted. as a year of service to Miss Eliza Davies, headmistress of the mired depart- ment of the Trinity National School ; and that her salary be increased in accordance with the committee's scale from £ll5 to £l2O per annum, as from the Ist April, 1905. THE NURSING ASSOCIATION AND CHILDREN'S AILMENTS. __

A letter having been submitted from the Hon. Secre- tary of the Warrington District Nursing Association, drawing attention to the desirability of advantage being taken of the facilities afforded by that association for the provision of nurses to visit the various public elementary schools with a view to the various children's ailments receiving professional attention, and asking if the Committee are prepared to make a grant to that Association in respect of any assistance that they may be ableito render, it was resolved that the same be referred to the special sub-committee appointed by the Education Committee to inquire as to the extent to which children are debarred from obtaining full benefit from the instruc- tion given in the schools by reason of mental or physical defects, with a strong recommendation for their favour- able consideration of the suggestion.

div.head: STAFF CHANGES.
div.p: STAFF CHANGES.

On the recommendation of the sub-committee appointed to consider the applications received for the vacancies for two assistant masters at the Scondary School and Technical Institute. it was resolved that Mr John Boocock Baxter and Mr. Harry Lenton be appoint- ed assistant masters at the Secondary School and Technical Institute at a commencing salary in each case at the rate of £l2O per annum. Subsequently Mr. Harry Lenton withdrew from his appointment, and it was, on the recommendation of the sub-committee appointed to consider the matter, resolved. That Mr. Arthur E. Hoyle, 8.A., be appointed. Au application was submitted from Mr. R. H. Albery, !qr. Paul Fisher and Mr. William Donaghy, science masters at the Secondary School and Technical Insti- tute, for re-consideration of the terms of their appoint- ments, and it was decided to refer the matter to a sub- committee consisting of Mr. A. J. Jolley, Mr. J. Upson, the Rev. Neville Wilson, and the Chairman of the corn- mittee (the Rev. Morley Stevenson), and to request the headmaster of the school to submit a report to that sub-committee upon the matter.

EVENING CONTINUATION SCHOOLS. The committee considered the arrangements for the Evening Continuation School to be held during the next session, and it was resolved that the classes be hold at the following schools, viz. :—Fairfleld (for females), Hamilton-street National (for males), Heath- side National (for males). Warrington British (for males and females), and Wycliffe British (for females); tbat the schools be opened on two evenings each week; that the fees be fixed at fld. a week, or 3s. for the session if paid in weekly instalments before the Ist December. It was further decided to invite applications from the assistant teachers in the public elementary day schools in the borough for the posts of superintendents and assistant teachers in these evening continuation schools The Rey. MORLEY* STEVENSON, In moving the con- firmation of the minutes, alluded to the re,solution with reference to poor scholars. The committee were adopt- ing the principle of trying to help to a limited extent children who were worthy of help, the circumstances of the parents being such as to render it difficult for them to maintain their children at school. (Hear, hear.) With reference to Miss Davies and Trinity School, he was glad to know that incident was closed. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Eirsox seconded.

Councillor WRIGHT said he would like to say some- thing about the fees paid in the secondary and elemen- tary schools. He found from Mr. Robson's book that there were absolutely no fees charged in America. He should be glad if they could be abolished altogether. It was very hard that working class parents, who had children they desired to be well educated, should have to appeal as it were for charity. The school fees had a de.errent effect on many children belonging to the working classes. They would be placing themselves on a footing with other nations if the fees of the secondary and elementary schools could be entirely abolished, because the parents alreldy paid the fees through the rates and taxes, and that was sufficient. The minutes were carried.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICERS' SALARY. Councillor Ef.trsom, in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the School Attendance Committee, said a resolution had been passed to the effect that the salary of yklilliam Bamber, senior school attendance inspector be increased from £llO to £ll5 per annum, as from Ist May, 1905. and thereafter by a further £5 per annum to a.maximum of £l2O. The late Mr. Jones had £145, but ha duties were more arduous. Therefore, the committee thought £l2O a fair maximum for Mr. Bamber. The minute was approved. NEW SCHOOLS. At the monthly meeting of the above committee, held on May sth. It was resolved that the tracings of the plans for the new "Bolton " Council School be adopted and forwarded to the Board of Education for approval. Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH moved, and Alderman SMETHURST jseconded the passing of the minutes, the latter remarking that he had just seen from an evening newspaper that it was the intention of the Government not to allow any child who was under five years of age to go to school. (Ilear,hear.) It was pointed out by the Director that there was a probability that the age mentioned would only apply to rural schools. It would therefore, be well to wait until the official declaration had been received. The plans of the "Beamont" school had been approved by the Board of Education. The minutes were then carried.

div.head: CROSFIELDS' BAND CONTEST.
div.p: CROSFIELDS' BAND CONTEST.
Fourteen Lancashire and Yorkshire

Bands in Competition. Warrington was invaded by brass bands on Saturday. From quite early in the day the typizal sons of toil who comprised most of the bands could be seen making their way from the iailway station. They had come to War- rington to take part in the contest promoted by Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited, and all were determined to make a bold bid for the handsome prizes offered. To the townspeople they speedily announced their arrival by playing lively airs with a vigour which showed they were in first rate trim for the event of the day. The contest, too, had a peculiar interest for Warringtonians, as it is many years since an open competition of this kind was held. The enthusiasm withy with which the project was entered into. augured well for succces, and nothing was Jacking to ensure the compl3teness of the arrangements. It was indeed a happy idea to hold the contest on the Wilderspool Football Ground for the ideal weather con- ditions made it exceedingly pleasant to be out of doors. There was a good attendance of the public, and con- sidering that fourteen bands were heard, the competition was got through very expeditiously. The following is ' a list of the bands and conductors :—Coppull Subscrip- tion (conductor, Mr.ffalliwell); Lindley Brass Band(Mr. B. Lodge); Upper Slaithwaite (Mr. A. Holden); Crooke Prize Band ('it. W. Rimmer),Warrington Borough (Mr. Smith), Trwell Springs (Mr. W. Ritumer) ; Wingates Temperanee(Mr.lW. Rimmer); Goodsha w (Mr. Halli well); Damen Borough (Mr. Halliwell) ; Lea Mills (Mr. A. Owen); Rochdale (Mr. W. Rimrner) ; Hebden Bridge (Mr. Heap) ; Earlestown Viaduct (Mr. W. Riramer) ; Westhoughton (Mr. A. Holden). At two o'clock the adjudicator (Mr. S. Radcliffe, of Ferndale, South Wales) mounted the platform erected in the the centre of the field and using a, walking stick as a baton, conducted the massed bands in a flue rendering of the spirited " Veteran's March." The piece for the compe' ition—Rossinis' " La Ceneren- tola "—was an admirable one, for while it embodied tests of the capacity of the bands in all the various sections, it was not unduly long, and the many bright and tuneful passages commended it to the listener. To the most enthusiastic, however, it became somewhat monotonous to hear fourteen bands play the same selection, and even the adjudicator had to confess to a head-ache as the result of his arduous task. Before the decision was announced, Mr. Henry RonEnTs expressed the firm's gratification at the splendid response to their invitation. They had had some of the finest bands in Lancashire,—which meant some of the finest bands in the world—playing there that day. There had not been a single poor band amongst them, and so gratified were the firm with the result that the directors had determined, as there could only be six prize winners out of the fourteen entries, to return the entrance fees to the eight unsuccessful hands. (Applause). Mr. RADCMFFE, in the course of a few brief com- ments, said the playing had been very good indeed, and the contest had been exceedingly close between many bands. Ha had had considerable difficulty to select four or five bands, but with regard to the first prize, a great difficulty had been lifted from his mind because the award without a doubt must go to the Crooke Prize Band. (Applause). The following is the complete list of p rise winners: —.l, Crooke Prize Band, 435 ; 2, G oodshaw, £25 ; Wingates Temperance, £2O; 4, I rwell Springs, £lO •, 5, Earlestown Viaduct, a ; 6, Hebden Bridge, £4. The seventh position (no prize) was obtained by Rochdale Public Band, and the eighth by Lea Mills. The prizes having been presented to the secretaries 'of the successful bands, the proceedings concluded. For the excellent arrangements praise is due to Mr. T. A. Mosso (secretary), Mr. Lord (treasurer), Dr. Markel, Mr. H. Roberts, and Mr. J. Taylor (committee).

div.head: KING AND THE HOSPITALS.
div.p: THE KING AND THE HOSPITALS.
How a Curvature of the Spine and Abscesses in Back were Treated.
(By a. Frimi of the King's Hospital Fund.)

The interest of His Majesty King Edward VII. in the Fund for the Hospitals is explained by His Majesty's sense of the noble service rendered to his humbler subjects. Once within the wards of a Hospital all are equal. There, without fee, the poorest sufferer receives the services of the very greatest surgeons and physicians in the world. The King, when he was operated upon for Appendicitis in Coronation Year, had no greater skill and no different treatment than what is bestowed on any patient in our Hospitals. This fact lends absorbing interest to the history of a poor Scottish boy who was recently treated in the Glasgow Children's Hospital. He had had scarlet fever, and, as often happens, this terrible fever left after- effects. His spine began to be deformed: it had curva- ture, and there were abscesses, for whichhe was operated upon by the very %blest surgeons—the same men who would have been called in if one of the Royal ,Family had suddenly needed operation while in Scotland. But despite all their care little John Fraser (for that is his name, and his parents live at 1, Maxwell- place. Southside, Glasgow) did not get better. He was painfully weak and thin, and the doctors frankly

div.head: John Fraser in the Children's HospitaL
div.p: John Fraser in the Children's HospitaL

said that little could be done to dry up the fearful abscesses or reduce the lump on his spine. He could hardly eat, and only walked with great difficulty. "If you only !mew what he suffered from the pain in his back," said his father,"and how the abscesses seemed to be sapping the life of him, you would not wonder I am thankful to see him so well to-day. It is all due to Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. He began to take them last June. From the time he cot through the contents of the first box, I observed a distinct change for the better. Very soon his back began to heal. I first heard of this wonderful medicine through reading an account of one who had suffered like ray son,and had been speedily cured of spinal disease by these pills." "There's my daugkter Jeanie, too," added the mother Mrs. Fraser. "After having her tonsils removed she lost a quantity of blood, and became so weak and thin that I grew alarmed. But I gave her Dr. Williams' pink pills and she soon began to make new blood. Before long she was as healthy and bright a lassie as you would see anywhere." Where the best medical skill the world can give has been used in vain, Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people have, in the above and many other cases, cured. The reason is that they make new blood. Thus they are the greatest of all tonics, the readiess and safqst medicine in the commoner, as well as the severest ail- ments. div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair). Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Wilkinson, Messrs. Hayward, Wright, Thornton, W. Roberts and Pilling. DRUNKEN WOMAN'S STRANGE CONDUCT.—Margaret Mellott, last from Newton, was charged with being drunk and incapable on Saturday night, with refusing to quit the licensed premises of the Alexandra Vaults, and also with breaking a glass pannel in the door at the vaults.—P.C. Sankey proved the charge of drunkenness. Richard Thompson, landlord of the Alexandra Vaults, said that on Saturday night the prisoner in company with a man entered his house and called for two glasses of beer, Both were drunk and witness refused to serve them. Prisoner then said she would smash every window in the house and smashed the pannel in the door. She then assaulted Mrs. Thompson.—Prisoner who had nothing to say was sent to gaol for one month with hard labour. ASSAULT. ON TITS POLlCE.—Frederick Davies, 18, Victoria-street, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly and with assaulting P.C. Sweeney, and Mr. John Betley.—P.C. Sweeney spoke to arresting the prisoner for his disorderly conduct When arrested prisoner commenced to struggle and knocked witness's helmet and lamp off. Witness called Mr. Batley to assist him, and prisoner also assaulted Mr. Betley by kicking him in the face and back.—Prisoner who had a good record vvas fined 20s. and costs, or in default one month's imprisonment with bard labour. A DANGEROUS PRACTICE.—Leonard Smith, 14, Earl- street, was charged with bottling wrated waters without wearing a mask or veil as required by the Act.—Mr. A. Lewis, ELM. Inspector of factories, explained that for : the protection of workmen such as the defendant the act provided that they should wear masks when bottling xrated waters. On the 25th April Mr. Platt visited Mr. Cunningham's factory and found the defendant at work. He was not wearing a mask although that article had been provided by his employer, and was placed close to where he was warking.—Defendant said he never worked without a mask. On the date in question he had been repairing the machine and was testing it when the Inspector entere 1 the factory.—Defendant was fined sa. and costs.

div.head: STRANGEST ANIMAL IN THE WORLD.
div.p: THE STRANGEST ANIMAL IN THE WORLD.

The strangest known animal and the most useful vegetable product were both discovered in Australia. The strangest animal is the duck-billed platypus, which has the body of an otter, the head of a duCk, four legs E like a quadruped, feet lie a swan, and claws like a cat. The most useful vegetable product is the particular substance discovered by Mr. Charles Porde, which forms the chief ingredient in the now world-famed medicine— bile beans. After exhaustive research, Mr. Charles Forde discovered this substance and found that it acted so beneficially upon the liver and digestive system as to be a specific for all liver and stomach ailments. When it is borne in mind that such everyday ailments as headache, constipation, piles, indigestion, wind, bilious- ness, and a host of others may all be well traced prim- arily to liver disorder, and that the liver is the largest and most important organ in the body, it will easily be seen how valuable was this great discovery, and how innumerable the persons who may benefit from it. As is the case with the out-of-date so-called " remedies" of forty or fifty years ago, which contain probably aloes, ' mercury, and other harmful drugs, bile beans do not merely purge and give temporary relief. On the con- trary, bile beans, by acting directly upon the liver and digestive organs, strengthen and stimulate them to per- form their natural duties, which is the only way to effect a permanent cure. Do not be misled by claims of half-a-hundred pills in the box, where probably four to six constitute one dose, and which once commenced will necessitate continuance. After the cure is effected bile beans can be discontinued: they are purely veget- able; they contain no harmful drugs, and they are the safest family medicine. Their price brings them within reach of all.

Last week I showed how various right- Ingle screws may be made quite easily, by simply playing half-ball on to the object ball, and striking the cue ball low down and with plenty of strength. This method only holds good, how- ever, when the cue ball is within easy range of the first object ball, say, from lft. to 3ft. away from it. As the distanee between the cue ball and the object ball is increased, the strength of the stroke must likewise be in- creased, but in a nauch greater ratio, so that a point soon arrives (this will vary according to tho player) when it becomes impossible to screw at a right angle with not more than a half-ball contact.
For example, with no red on the spot and the object white as shown on Diagram 100, if

The screw in•off from the D.—The thick infer sected line shows how, by getting well on to thE ball, the baulk pocket and its angles may be avoided. The thin intersected line shows the direo tion the red ball would take as the result of • half-ball stroke.

Even fhe ordinary screw in-off from the red on the spot, which most players have often made, is never played as a. half-ball stroke, though the cue ball has not to screw at any- thing like a right angle. It is true the in-off is just possible by a half-ball screw, though played in this way it would be an infinitely more difficult stroke than when played by a fullef than half-ball screw. Many players are under the impression that the six shot (red ball coubled into the baulk pocket) which is often made, is the result of catching the red ball half- ball or thereabouts but Waxing from the end of the D, a true half-ball stroxe would cause the red to strike the side cushion actually above the centre pocket, as shown by the thin inter- sected line on Diagram 102. This can easily be , proved bi placing a ball quite near the red (el the line that the cue ball travels from the Di and playing a half-ball stroke. By playing, Ea.'', ; only a foot away from the red, accurate half-ball striking may be ensured. Most players when playing the in-off from the red on. the spot, play for the six shot, or at least do not try to avoid doubling the red into the baulk pocket. This, however, is not good bil- liards, for should the six shot come off the Pesi" tion is as difficult as before, and should the red instead of finding the pocket catch the angles (es it so often does) it will in all probability remain in baulk. In playing this screw in-off the player should always endeavour to make the red hall avoid the baulk pocket altogether, and this /0 If best done 'by playing full enough on to the red to cause it to strike the baulk cushion a foot oil s' more away from the pocket as shown by the ". thick intersected line on Diagram 102. Playing the in-off this way does not make the stroke anY, more difficult. Professionals and good amateurs seldom pia,' to screw in-off from the ;red on the spot, for . though the stroke is not a difficult one for a twill good player, it is always an uncertain one. It iS 60 easy to either overscrew or underscrew it- • (Stevenson broke down at this very stroke through overscrewing it, When he made his record break of 602, on February 17th, 1905.) Even if a player could get this screw in-off quite ae often as not, he would in the long run lose far more than he would gain by constantly playing it, . for it successful stroke oftener than not leaves no position to continue with, even if the red rennal out of baulk (and on a very fast table the Ted often remains in baulk after having travelled three lengths of the table). On the other hand, , when the stroke is missed, should the other pla be in hand he will far oftener than not have eeer good position left him. When orte's opponent 10 not in hand the screw in-off is naturally not se dangerous a stroke to play, but even then it is a 6 a rule hardly worth going for. Sometimes, hoe" ever,.-.when a game is in a desperate condition, and the striker is compelled to try and force ell - opening, the stroke (or a similar one from a Inis9 in baulk) may be quite worth going for. Sere; times also a player may be in hand with the rea,,,. on the spot and the white touching the hew: cushion right away from either of the pockets. cannon would be more uncertain than the and the screw can safely be played, for if 11116 Sela the probability is that the other player will nee have anything at all easy to play for with his ball tight on the cushion. One great advantage of the present systems of , control of the cycle is that there is practically no limit as to where riders can stop. In the days before Bowden brakes and back-pedalling brakes it was almost ini2ossible to stop me eyele an Ldescending any hill of more than ordinary steep- . ness. When one reached the bottom of a steep descent there was no going back to gather a grand Bnray of honeysuckle or branches of autumn foliage , that might have been noticed during the descent; but now with a Bowden or a Vim brake one can , pull up almost instantaneously on the steepest hill, and in addition to the sense of security which this gives the rider, it is often of real utility to be able to stop in the middle of a long run down hilL , Every cyclist finds it so when blackberries, sloes, , and wayside flowers are the objects of search, and this is one of the phases of the utility of our improved control of the cycle for which those who remember the pre-Bowden (Lys are duly grateful.

div.head: Pursuit Races on the Road.
div.p: Pursuit Races on the Road.

/The pursuit race Is a comparatively new and rather exciting variation on the ordinary forms of track-racing. The riders start from opposite sides of thetrack, and endeavour to catch one another. The result is generally a most interesting struggle. . Another 'variation of the pursuit race can be ludulged in on club runs and among parties of , friends riding together. The leader is given a :start of two or three minutes. and the main body 'then starts in pursuit. The main body of the ;Pursuers, however, must keep together, and must 'catch the pursued as a body, the overtaking of the 114rsued by one or two fast pursuers not counting. ;As there are always sure to be some weaklings among the main body, this kind of race is less ,Productive of scorching than of fun and good. 'fellowship.

div.head: Impending Rise in Prices.
div.p: Impending Rise in Prices.

Cycle manufacturers are not happy this season. rrices have been cut down to very low figures, and ._%Yery maker is putting forth great efforts to main- rill quality at a very high standpoint. Un- fortunately tyres have gone up in price 7-1 per ‘=ent., steel balls have risen 100 per cent., weldleas i4eel tube has gone up 15 to 20 per cent., and so on all round. In these circumstances there is a natural tendency on tho part of the cycle manu- facturers to look for higher prices; and one conapany at least—the Swift—has given notice of a rise in price, and others will probably be obliged bo follow suit. The advance, however, will probably tot be general for some little time yet. The New Ruclson Cycle Company have issued a notice that, although a rise in price cannot be long delayed, they hope to maintain the present rates till the end (4 the season, and this will probably be the view taken all round.

div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Disfranchisement and Out-Relief.

Eyes, G.Egerton-Warbur- ton, A. Broom, H. M. Davies, C. E. Linaker, C. E. Linaker, jun., .1. H. Davies, J. Smith, T. Wright, H. Meadsley, S. Woodward, G. Pilling, J. L. Jones, E. Bretherton' C. lINDER-FED SCHOOL CHILDREN. The Believing Officers presented reports with regard to the under-fed school children. Mr. Cook, Runcorn, did not think there was any need for provision to be made at the present time for feeding any of the children attending the public elementary schools in his district. Should he, however, receive an application from either managers or teachers under the. terms of the new order it would be immediately considered. The distress in his district had not been exceptional during the past winter. His out-relief during the winter months had been less than usual and was so at the present time. The amount paid in the last week in December 1904 was £37 13s. 9d. ; 1903, £4O 195. 4d. ; 1902, £42 14s. 4d.; 1901, £42 Os. 9d.; 1900, £43 is. Id. The relief for the first week in May 1905 was £37 ; 1904, £3B 13s. lid.; 1903, 1:40 19s. 5d.; 1902, £4l 2s. 7d. ; 1901, £42 17s. 4d.; 1900, £43 13s. 3d. Mr. Pearson said the head teachers in his district had gone carefully over theit schools and had no cases to bring before the Board. Mr. W. It. de Pre; reported that as the result of his own observations and inquiries of the teachers of the schools in the Budworth district he is satisfied that under the present conditions it was quite necessary to undertake any provision for the feeling of any school children,

div.head: MR. RILEY'S THANKS.
div.p: MR. RILEY'S THANKS.

Mr. Riley, late relieving officer, wrote expressing his sincere thanks to the Board for the very liberal addition to his years of service for the purpose of superannua- tion. He thanked the present and past occupants of the chair and the members of the Board for their invariable kindness.

div.head: TIIE GRANTING OF TEMPORARY RELIEF.
div.p: TIIE GRANTING OF TEMPORARY RELIEF.

A letter was rend from the Ipswich Board of Guar- dians in which the writer said " In consequence of the exceptional lack of employment in this town during the winter months, the Guardians have had to grant relief to a number of unemployed workmen and their families. These men have been set to work RS required by the out relief order and the Guardians feel that it is an injustice to them that they should suffer disfranchisement. They have passed a resolution on the subject and have instructed me to forward a copy of the same to other unions in England' and Wales, feeling that a united action on the part of Boards of Guardians might he the means of inducing His Majesty's Government to bring in a Bill for re- moving the disability. They therefore, resolved that this Board regret the fact that the unemployed relieved by them have to suffer disfranchisement, and is of opinion that persons who receive relief for a temporary period consequent upon the general want of work in the neigh- bourhood in which they reside, sickness or other excep- tional cause, should not lose their votes. The Board is also of opinion that efforts should be made to induce His Majesty Government to promote such measure as will remove the existing disabilities." The Chairman said that he personally sympathised greatly with persons who had to seek temporary relief and did not think they should be disfranchised. It was decided to support the action of the Ipswich Guardians.

div.head: PENKETH PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: PENKETH PARISH COUNCIL.
Members Decide not to walk the Boundary.

A meeting of the above Parish Council was held at the Wesleyan Schools on Monday night. Dr. Murray presided, and there were also present, Messrs. J. G. Withinshaw, D. Houghton, W. Hodgkinson, P. Rout- ledge, Ditchfield, Ashcroft and E. Forster (clerk). THE WANT OF A MAGISTRATE. The Clerk said he had written to the Home Office in accordance with the resolution passed at the last meeting, calling attention to the great want of additional magis- trates in the district. This letter had been acknow- ledged, and on May 11th he had received a letter from the Duchy of Lancaster stating that the Secretary of State had forwarded the letter to them and that it should have attention. THE PAVING OF THE FOOTPATH. At the annual parish meeting, a resolution had been passed asking that the footpath on each side of the road from the Red Lion Inn to the Co-operative Stores be paved. The length was 350 yards and the cost was anticipated to be about £36. On the motion of Mr. Withinshnw, the matter was directed to be brought before the District Council. WALKING THE notrxnArty. The question of -galking the boundary of the town- ship was discussed, a resolution to the effect that this custom should be revived having been passed at the parish meeting. Mr. Withinshaw: Who will stand the supper after- wards ? (Laughter). The Chairman : I will perhaps be there at the start, but as to the finish, well (shaking his head). Mr. Routledge : I think everybody would now be satisfied with the ordnance map which .is now in our possession. When they used to walk the boundary, I don't suppose there was an ordnance survey in the town- ship, and such custom was then necessary. Mr. Withinshaw: I suppose in those days, it would be neeessary to settle disputes. The Chairman : I suggest that this matter he left to the residents to arrange. (Applause). Mr. Routledge : Seeing that we have an ordnance map, it is quite an unnecessary proceeding. The Chairman : Then I will move that seeing we have an ordnance map of the township which is kept at the Wesleyan schools and can be inspected by any resident on application to the Clerk to the Parish Council, it is unnecessary to walk the boundary. Any dispute can be settled by the map. Mr. Withinshaw seconded and the resolution was passed unanimously. THE RECREATION GROUND. PROTEST BY MR. ASHCROFT. The Chairman said they had authority from the parish meeting to indulge in a little extravagance. They had authority to expend a sum out of the rates, not exceed- ing £IO, to erect gymnastic apparatus for the amuse- ment of the children. They were also requested to take steps to abate the nuisance near the pavilion. While oni this subject, he would like to call attention to the danger caused by the see-saw which was whirled round with such force. In another part of the village that very day a youth had been injured with a similar apparatus. That on the recreation ground was a danger when the older children used them, though young children could not get up the speed necessary. Mr. Hodgkinson remarked that he had been frightened many times when he saw the apparatus going round at a tremendous speed. It was an amazing thing to him that no serious accident occured. The Chairman moved that the whole Council resolve itself into a committee to meet on Thursday, May 25th, at 7.30 to consider the matter. Mr. Ashcroft protested against the proposed expendi- ture but on a vote being taken the chairman's proposi- tionwas carried.

i" Official reports of'statistical committees from twenty- nine prorinces " stated the extract" describe the con- dition of the peasants as unbearable. Domestic animals have generally a more enviable lot. Work without the fruits of work, and hardship without the hope of relief, make up the destiny to which they are born. Their live stock is dwindling away; their food is growing less in quantity and worse in quality. Disease happily thins their ranks and shortens the lives of their sur- vivors, but it also ruins their health and brings on a tendency to degeneration. In many parts of the Empire cabbage and milk have had to be given up as articles of diet, because the husbandman could not afford them. According to the Czar's government, 330 kilograms of rye is the allowance necessary and sufficient to keep the peasant alive in famine years, and 330 kilograms a head are accordingly distributed by the imperial relief fund. But when there is no famine the peasant is forced to export his corn, and can keep for himself only 240 kilo- grams The dwellings of the people in the rural dis- tricts are not fit for brutes. The huts, when the fire is lighted, are filled with smoke, which escapes through chinks in the walls or the open door, while the inmates lie fiat on the floor like travellers in the desert during the simoom in order to avoid breathing the air. In winter-time the water freezes inside the hovel. Some- times two or three families live like this together in one room. Here they eat; here they sleep on straw ; here the women bring their children into the world; here they spin and weave; here the boys do their school tasks ; here, too, are a calf, lambs, sometimes sucking pigs, poultry; hero a mephitic odour prevails. The outlines of the picture differ little from those of the story of the Russian peasant's life everywhere. Misery, sameness, hopelessness. It Is a description of families cooped up in one filthy room ; fed on food which is bad and insufficient ; working hard early and late ; giving away the fruits of their labour in taxes, and then in their leisure hoots watching their children pine away and die. A curious and disgusting detail is added. The very vermin die out in tho poorer huts. Dr. Shingaroff writes that the familiar animal known to scientists as eimex lectularius was wholly absent in the poorest of the dwellings he examined, and was found only in places where a certain relative comfort prevailed. Blackbeetles and cockroaches being less squeamish, were found more evenly distributed. But even here there are limits. "The blackbeetle does not flourish in all conditions ; certainly extreme poverty is a considerable obstacle to its existence." There are ten per cent, of the huts so poor that even blackbeetles cannot live there. 'lt is not like that throughout the Czardom,'bankers and investors in Russian scrip may object' It certainly is not. Cimex Ilectularins as well as blackbeetles and cockroaches are !found in abundance in most villages and hamlets, even though there be no cabbage, no eggs and no milk for the inhabitants. But poverty, squalor, hunger are the rule everywhere. A first-class authority on the subject, N. Annensky, who is at this momenta prisoner in the fortress of Peter and PauLhaving put this very question whether the conditions of Novo-jivotinnoye and Mokhovatka are exceptional phenomena wrote: There are unhappily no grounds for the assumption. Very numerous sections of peasants, who possess either no land or very little, live in precisely the same general conditions as the villagers under consideration.' " It was those peasants, continued Mr. Crosfield,who were being squeezed to-day, as one might try to squeeze blood from a stone, for the taxes to pay for the war which a few magnates of Russia had embarked the country upon ! What struck him as so significant was that in the countries under Turkish rule they had people who knew perfectly well what Russian autocratic Government meant, and yet so bad were the conditions of things in Macedonia and Armenia that, in face of an account like that which he had read, the people would be thankful to exchange Turkish for Russian rule. He thought that would make them seriously consider whether, after all, the Berlin" peace with honour" treaty which flung back Armenia into the hand of the Turks was a wise treaty.
