Brewery Football Club Dinner. The annual dinner in connection with Messrs. P. Walker Son's Rugby Football Club was held at the Lion Hotel on Saturday. when a most enjoyable evening was spent. During the season the team have done very well, having won the Cheshire Junior League and figured though unsuccessfully in the final for the Warrington Works Competition. An excellent dinner was served after which the evening was spent in conviviality, Mr. J. Monro presiding. The usual loyal and other toasts were honoured, and during the proceedings the Chairman distributed the medals won by the players in connection with ale League. An excellent programme of music was submitted, to which the following contributed ! Messrs. Dowling, Jackson, A. Grounds, J. Taylor, T. Taylor, B. Bate, L. Aukland, R. Grounds, J. Monro, and the Latchford Quartette Party, consisting of Messrs. Grounds, Aukland, Atkinson and Knight.

div.head: Election.
div.p: Election.
The Examiner, Saturday, May 20, 1905.

described at the time, as being like a man in the middle ages in the fortified castle, who went half way across a moat to meet his enemy. (Laughter.) Then we had the Thibet business —and he did not think anyone attempted to defend that—and another little affair in Somaliland which he was bound to confess, he had not attempted to follow. It seemed a very mad enterprise and he really did not know what we gained by it. He believed we m waged to capture the :llthdi's mother-in-law—(laughter)—aud to spend about three ! millions of money on the expedition. He was not going to say anything disparaging about mothers-in-law. I (Laughter.) No doubt4in the economy of nature, they I fulfilled a very useful part of the State.(Hear,hear.) But he did not know whether anyone in that meeting would think it good enough to spend three millions on pur- chasing a mother-in-law—(laughter)—and, he was told, a black one at that. (Renewed laughter.) They had often heard him discuss the South African war, and he was not going to discuss it that nizht, but it was part 1 and parcel of the same business. It had been re-actionary ; work, and he must say that when one considered how I the pretence and misleading statements about South Africa had been exploded, one began to think that many people who were naturally misled i at the time by correspondents from South Africa who were bought bya Press that was controlled entirely by the randlords, rtight now well re-consider whether even from their point of view. and to put it on the lowest footing, the game was worth the candle. He was not quite sure whether that explosion of the South African fallacies and the exposure of what it all meant, did not make it THE PROTECTIONIST CAMPAIGN very suspicious. (Hear, hear). He held that the cir- cumstances under which that campaign was started were , "mighty suspicious." (hear, hear). He would venture I to warn all those present not to allow any red herrings that might have drawn across the trial to divert their minds from the main question which they had to face and deal with. He was reported as having said that Mr. Chamberlain counted on a reaction taking glace inpoonlar feeling and a wave that would bring him into power at the next Election, but he (Mr. Crosfleld) did not say that. What he said MIS that Mr. Chamberlain counted on that reactionary wave after the next election. Mr. Chamberlain knew perfectly well that the Government would get a knock- down blow at the next election. (Applause). What he thought .vas that if the Liberals did not get A sufficiently strong majority, he would be able to work against the Liberal party on some side issue and crawl back to power. Eherefore they had not done by any means with the Protectionist agitation. Mr. Morley was perfectly tight when he said that though Mr. Chamberlain's ship would sink in the end, he would be on the bridge and stick to his colours when it went down. (Hear, hear.) , They could admire Mr. Chamberlain's tenacity of purpose and courage, but it put them the more on their guard, and they must not imagine because Protection was at a discount and was almost laughed at in the country now, that the main question oefore them was settled and that they were out of danger. Whether Mr. Chamberlain would bring the issue before the country next month or whether it would be postponed a little longer was a question none of them could answer. It might be that they would have to fight next month, and then, he was told, it was not quite certain whom they would have to fight in War- rington—whether it would be his friend Mr. Pierpoint or, whether possibly, someone else would step into the field. He had heard it suggested that if Sir Gilbert areenall came out, they would have a terrible under- taking, and, in conclusion, be would like to say a word on that matter. It had been his duty to attack Mr. Pierpoint politically because he utterly differed from him politically—(hear, hear)—both on foreign and home questions, and it would be his duty to attack him again. But he had never said anything which he intended to be personally offensive, either about Mr. Pierpoint or his cery old friend Sir Gilbert. (Hear, hear.) He believed Mr.Pierpoint would be their opponent at the next election, but whether it were him or his old friend Sir Gilbert they would fight their battle in good temper and good humour as they did at the last election. (Applause.) He would like to add that so long as they had on their side such a magnificent posi- tive cause besides what he called the negative on the all important and great cause of Free Trade, it certainly would not make any difference to him whether they brought out Mr. Pierpoint or Sir Gilbert or whether they went to Birmingham and brought down the great Panjandrum himself. (Applause.) He knew his own limitations, but as far as he could, he would fight this battle (A Voice "You will win next time " and ap- plause) in what they called thoroughly good fettle, because they had not one cause but half-a-dozen of the finest causes that anyone could possibly wish to fight for. (Applause.) He hoped that the Progressive Labour League, under whose auspices that meeting was hold, would absolutely put their backs into the work, and that they would remember how much in the history of Warrington politics depended upon every true Progressive putting his shoulder energetically and with thorough determination to the wheel. (Applause). MR. MADDISON ON LABOUR QUESTIONS.

Mr. MAIM tsoN,who was warmly received,said the repre- sentation of Labour belonged naturally to the Liberal party. Mr. Gladstone, who was not what they called a Badical.al ways affirmed in the plainest of language not merely the right but the necessity of the genuine working classes being represented by a large contingent of men in the House of Commons. (Hear, hear). Therefore when Warrington workingmen formed a Labour League and that League supported Mr. Crostield, there was nothing unnatural about it, either on the side of Labour or Liberalism. Continuing, Mr. Maddison said he was "sick unto death" of the talk about the general election If this had been a Government of Mr. Gladstone's, they would have had no trouble a year or eighteen months ago in talking about the general election. They would have said" Mr. Gladstone has lost the confidence of the country and of course he will go to the poll." They could not say that of course " about Mr. Balfour. He had lost the confidence of the country and no one knew it better than himself. His party was riven asunder and his own ministers talked with discordant voices about I the same thing. One bond, however, united them—and thatiwas!officeland pay.(Laughter.)Liberalism and Labour, said Mr.Maddison,were one and the same thing. No man was a Liberal who would disregard the honest and just claims of Labour and no Labour man knew his business who was not prepared to work with the Liberal who recognized those claims. Dealing with the" shams " of the Government, Mr. Maddison devoted consider- able time to a criticism of the Government's attitude on the Trades Disputes Bill. The second reading of that Bill was carried by a huge majority, and the Government did not declare themselves to be opposed to it. Having regard to that fact and to the force of opinion behind the Bill, the officers of the Crown ought to have given some reasonable help to the Bill in Committee. But from the first, had they been Capitalist representatives they could not have acted more diometrically opposite to the measure. Some of his friends said that only Labour men could advocate Labour measures, and that in the House of Commons Liberals and Tories were alike. He would, however,point outthat INIr. Whittaker, a Liberal member, moved the second reading of the Trades Dis- putes Bill, and after his speech men came to him (Mr. Maddison) in the lobby and declared that there was no man in the Labour move- ment who could have moved the Bill better. ' As a result of the proceedings in Grand Committee, it was proposed that it should be an illegal act of picketing if strikers annoyed anyone. That, he con- tended, would be an absurdity for all strikes and lock- outs were annoyances. Strong trade unionist as he was, he was there to say that all the best unions were work- ing towards the elimination of strikes and lock-outs by bringing in arbitration and conciliation, but they were not going to give up their right to strike, because' it would be giving up a liberty. To think I that the great trade union movement was I going to be insulted by the incorporation of such absurd words in the Bill was only to trifle with a great question. The trade unionists and working- men of Warrington were not worth their salt if they I did not take their revenge on the Government for their ' dastardly behaviour in connection with that Bill. (Applause.) The funds of the great institutions whieh had done so much for the working classes were in danger because the Tory Government had no principles behind it, because it was allied to the worst side of the capitalist party. There was only one remedy, and that was to return a Liberal Government to power and the only local application was to return Mr. Crostleld as member for Warrington. (Applause.) Dealing with the Aliens' Bill, Mr. Maddison said Liberals had no objec- tion to the exclusion of lunatics and diseased aliens,. and as a matter of fact they could be deported now He (Mr. Maddison) was also prepared to exclude every alien criminal whose offence came within the four corners of the Extradition Act, but he was not prepared to go one step further. He was strongly opposed to the exclusion of political refugees fleeing from economic and political tyranny. It was

UNTRUE THAT THEY ROBBED THE BRITISH WORKMAN of his bread. A Royal Commission had sat and although they ransacked London for witnesses to prove thatalien immigration had robbed Britishers of their work they were unable to find any. He was not saying that the competition of some of these men in the earlier stages was not not very inconvenient to the British workman, —so was the competition of a lot of Englishmen incon- venient to trade unionists—but in the main they had started new industries. If our proportion of paupers was the same as the proportion among the , aliens it would go down 50 per cent. Even the propor- tion of alien criminals was so small as not to he a really serious thing, and the aliens could already be deported fon serious crimes. The very men who supported the ! Aliens Bill gave their approval to the Chinese labour , ordinance. They were told that the introduction of I Chinese had meant an increase in white labour. Of course there was more white labour than when the mines were not working, but that was not the point. Mr. Lyttieton gave figures showing that in January 1904(before the Chinese were employed) , there were 12,800 white men and 75,000 coloured men at ! work, the proportion of white men being one in six. In February DM there were 97,800 Kaffirs, 31,090 Chinese, and 15,800 white men, making the proportion of white men only one in eight. Had the proportion been at the same rate as before there would have been 21,000 white men. (Applause.) The Aliens Bill would do nothing for British Labour, , and South Africa, which should be a splendid field for

British Labour, was being strewn with the manure of the human race. Chinese Labour was not merely an economic wrong but he feared it most because of its effect upon British thinking and British statesmanship. ! A nation that could stand Chinese serfs could stand anything. Dealing with the

FISCAL QUESTION. ' Mr. Maddison alluded to the description of the state of I affairs in Russia which Mr. Crosged had quoted, and I pointed out that Russis headed the list of protected nations. The only way to keep the Russians out of I England was to turn Protectionist. England would not be worth corning to then. The Russians came 1 here because it was better than their own country, and one reason why England was better was that we had the right to buy what we wanted where we wanted and when we wanted. Mr. Maddison gave quota- tions from statements on the trade of the country made , within two years by Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Balfour, and I Mr. Gerald Balfour, and pointed out that while in effect the first speech of Mr. Chamberlain's (at Greenwich) I which he quoted,stated that our trade was dying,the last (delivered to Birmingham Jewellers' Association) said its prosperity was unparalled, and that he saw no signs ,of decay. In conclusion, Mr. Maddison laid that when at the next election they had made Free Trade safe, they would say to the Liberal leaders : "We have secured the ramparts and strongholds of Protection. You must lead us faithfully and well into the promised land of our longing." (Applause), IRON-WORKERS AND PROTECTION.

Mr. J. ELWELL, jun., moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Maddison for his address. The fiscal agitation, he believed, was introduced to bide the blunders of the Government. Workingmen and all trade unionists ought to do their level best te defeat a Government which had attempted to place their

TRADE UNION FUNDS in danger. They only asked for the rights that employers had. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Pierpoint was prepared to go all the way with Mr. Chamberlain in a policy which would have the effect of crushing the workers down and making it possible to form rings in order to get the trade into the hands of greet trusts. Under Free Trade the con- dition of the ironworkers had improved. Not only were they getting more wages, but the cost of com- modities was reduced. If by Protection they stopped certain materials from corning into the country the iron manufacturers would not be able to export the finished article in such large quantities. (Applause.) Alderman TINNION seconded and said he believed that Mr. Chamberlain sought to cover up the mismanagement in South Africa by embarking upon the fiscal campaign. Mr. Chamberlain was losin,, his grasp on the Conservative party, so far as infruencing its immediate policy was concerned. In none of the resolutions to be submitted at the great Conservative meeting at the Albert Hall was reference made to the fiscal question. The Liberal party were wise in thrashing out the ques- tion and killing the agitation, and he did not hesitate to say that the party by facing the question fearlessly had killed any chance or its being brought seriously before the country again. (Applause.) MR. PARKER AND THE ALIENS QUESTION. Mr. C. E. PARKER supported. He said he happened to be a descendant of one of the foreign aliens, one of his ancestors having come over from France in conse- quence of the persecution of the French Protestants known as flugenots. If the name had descended by the female line instead of by the male line he would have been in possession of a French name. Speaking on behalf of those Ilngenots, he would point out that they did a very great deal for the trade of this country by bringing here the trades in which they excelled—silk, linen, &c. (Applause.) He did not want to pronounce too strong a judgment on the Aliens Bill until he saw how it went through the committee In so far as the Bill was merely a police or sanitary measure it might possibly be made, by the he(i) of the Liberals, into a pretty decent Bill. But in so far as it was intended to keep out men who, while having no money, had brains and intelligence and were willing to work, the Liberals ought to give it their determined opposition. (Applause). The motion was heartily carried. In reply Mr. NTADDISON moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman for presiding. The Rev. H. Dussico seconded, and it was carried with enthusiasm.

In response, the CHAIRMAN said that if it was their favour to support him in the fight that was ahead of them, and if he should be called upon to undertake a public duty he would discharge it to the best of his ability. If returned there was nothing he would look forward to more than the advantage of being on friendly and intimate terms with Mr. Maddison and other able and experienced Labour men in Parliament. (Applause). He would not seek instruction from them alone, but he would seek it from all quarters. There was, however, no section in the House of Commons where they got finer work, where men better knew their own minds and the needs of our great democracy, than from the enlightened Labour members. (Applause).
aid at the meeting held on the previous evening with espect to

VIE ALIENS BILL, He (the Chairman) thought it was just as well for them I to defer coming to any final judgment until the Bill had been thrashed out in committee. When he read the Bill two things struck him as calculated to throw a great deal of responsibilify on the officials who would have to administer the Act,if it were passed. One clause , they would agree with as far as it went ; it was a very small matter. If they went into the figures they would find it affected us in England in a very fractional and infinitesimal way. If a man was a lunatic or idiot, or owing to any infirmity appeared likely to become charge- able upon the rates or otherwise a detriment to the public he should be excluded. We did not want to see criminals and lunatics coming into this country. There was already machinery provided that would largely answer the purpose Thei ther clause was a very different one ; because if a man could not show that he had in his possession or was in a position to obtain the means of decently sup- porting himself and his dependents he was to be exclu- ded. He (the Chairman) should like to know how the official who visited the emigrant ship was going to justly determine a point of thatkind. (Hear, hear.) Then the Bill spoke of an immigrant who proved that he was seeking admission to the country solely to avoid prose- cution for an offence of a political character. He (the speaker) wanted to know how the poor immigrant refugee, from it might be Russian tyranny and oppres- sion, coming in here was going to prove to the official of the port that he had been subjected to prosecution for a political offence ? It was not a prosecution the man was fleeing from. It was persecution. (Applause.) When they saw the circumstances and the time in which the Bill was introduced they would say "What a sham, and a fraud the thing really is, and what an example it is of the efforts that are being made and will be made by the

PLAYED-OUT GOVERNMENT of the Tory party in power to draw red herrings across the path and endeavour to divert our attention from the great issue which we have decide." While they all considered Free Trade in itself would be quite good enough to fight for, they recognized that there was an. enormous positive policy beside that, and there were distinguished leaders on the Liberal side who had said it was very advisable to keep that fact in mind. He fully agreed. He would therefore read to them what appeared to him as good a summary of the main work that lay before them as he had come across A long period of 'muddling through' in domestic affairs, coin- ciding with one of costly extravagance in Imperial policy, has encouraged a growth of social evils, to check which there has been no corresponding growth of social statesmanship. The chief of these are associated with the overgrowth of our cities. When problems of housing and transit, of hygiene, morality, and msthetics, of poverty, rent, rates and 'unearned increment' are crying aloud for a solution, the obverse of that picture is the depleted countryside, the decay of rustic popula- tion, the abandonment of the soil to less and less profit- able uses. Then come problems of capital and labour, the Poor Law and the unemployed, the CRIPPLING OE' TRADE UNION ACTIVITY, by judge-made law, the unparalleled influence exerted upon politics by great financial interests, the growing perception by the public that such things concern the whole community, and that the Government cannot stand aside, as an indifferent spectator, while employer and employed, trust and consumer, land- lord and tenant fight out their battles." (Applause.) Mr. Maddison said on Monday that they must not strive for the impossible, and it was a wise remark. He heard one of the ablest men in business in all Liverpool, with whom he had been associated in trade for 110 years, say " Let us work for the best possible." (Applause). When he read a programme like that, he remembered John Bright's old illustration when he used to advise people not to attempt too much at the same time. He said" You cannot run a dozen 'buses abreast through Temple bar." It would take a very long time to carry out the programme, but if the members of the Progres- sive Labour League would support them they would do what they could to further it. (Applause). When that was carried out we should have reached not, perhaps, an ideal style of civilization, but, at any rate, a higher state of civilization in England than we had to-day. Before they set out on the forward path of progress they must take good care that no trickery, no wire-pulling none of the artifices of the American " boss," in which the great political plunger of Birmingham excelled— that none of these things led them to take a serious and

div.head: MEETING AT BRICK-STREET.
div.p: MEETING AT BRICK-STREET.
MR. CROSFIELD AND TRADE UNIONISM.

A WORD TO MR. RYLANDS. Another successful meeting was held in Brick-street Mission on Tuesday evening, and was largely attended. Mr. A. H. Crosfield again presided, and was supported on the platform by Councillors Maginn and P. Peacoek, Messrs. F. Maddison, Joseph Howes. William Furness, S. Wright, Wilkinson Haigh, and J. Morton. MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.

The CHAIRMAN said it was most encouraging to see such an admirable audience on that pleasant May even- ing. It was an indication of the revival of Liberalism 'in Warrington that so many stalwart supporters of the Progressive party attended their meetings. He had had the honour of taking the chair at meetings for Mr. Vivian and Mr. Maddison, and after listening to the address they had had from those splendid and prominent labour leaders on the burning topic of the day, he thought any chairman would need a great deal of pluck who ventured to forestall them with any lengthy address on the gr3at question of Free Trade. He had ventured to the best of his poor abilities to argue out in some detail in the Warrington Press what seemed to him to be the vital issues on the question. Perhaps some of them did him the honour to read the lengthy correspond- ence he had with MR. W. PETER ItYLANDS. He was going to say .a word in disparagement of that gentleman's abilities as a controversialist. On the con- trary he recognized in him a man of. very great energy and ability, and it was not at all owing to a lack of capacity that he had utterly and entirely failed to make out any case for Protection. It simply came to this— that Mr. Rylands had got the wrong end of the stick— (applause)—and he had yet to learn that while the verdict of England would be given in no uncertain manner in the near future, in Lancashire, of all places, we were less inclined to deal a staggering blow at the great industry on which the county palatine mainly depended, at the vast shipping industry which was one of the most valuable assets of our country, and at every other industry which, directly and indirectly, would suffer by the loss which these trades, and many other trades would suffer if this new fangled or old fangled and obsolete and played out policy of Protection was introduced. (Applause.) On Monday evening Mr.aladdison dealt with the Trade Disputes Bill, and they had also a speech by Mr.Elwell, who was a very fine representative of trade unionism in Warrington. lie (Hr. Crosfleld) would like with all respect to associate himself thoroughly and sincerely with every syllable that Mr. Elwell had to say on the matter. (Applause.) lie XV3S glad to hear in Mr. Maddison's speech the tribute paid to Mr. Whittaker, who introduced the Bill into the House of Commons the other day. A more well-balanced, well-reasoned or conclusive speech than Mr. Whittaker delivered on that occasion he (the chairman)had seldom read. One heard a great deal of talk about

TRA.DE UNIONISM and there were plenty of Toryemployers of labour who ha ted trade unionism, and they charged people like himself (Mr.. Crosileld), who were strong supporters of trade unionism, with the disposition to set labour against capital and class against class. He ventured to say in reply to that in one brief sentence that it was a gross libel. (Applause.) He dare sty it was said in good faith, but it must be said in most hopeless ignor- ance because it was an absolute fact that before trade unionism had developed in this country, the amount of friction between labour and capital and the number of strikes and rows were far more thin they had been since that organization of labour had developed a sense of responsibility and a disposition to settle differences between capital and labour by fair- ness and arbitration.He had had the privilege of discuss- ing the question with some of the L L.) )ur members of Parliament, and had had many an hour's talk with some of their able trade union leaders in the town, and he had not found one who did not scout the notion of violence and coercion. (Applause.) When by a miser- able manceuvre by an attempt at a meeting of the Grand Committee they sought to prevent people who were picketing outsidejvvorks not merely from stating the facts but using all the persuasion they could, he said the people who did that no longer wished to see that em- ployees as well as employers were eq.ial before the law. (Hear, hear.) Talk about social pressure, they need not go a hundred miles from Warrington to find a good deal of it employed by the very people who were com- plaining of it when it was used on behalf of the trade unionists. He knew of lots of people in Warrington who would like to put their backs into the work on behalf of the Progressive Party and cause, but they dared not do it openly for fear of the effect on their position in life and their means of earning a livelihood. That was social pressure, if they liked so to call it, but he celled it going a great deal too far. (Applause.) He dare say there might be instances where the sup- porters of trade unions were anxious to go too far—he had not a doubt of it. But they would not find the responsible leaders of the trade unions approving of that. He thought it was a shame that the resources and the funds of the great institutions which had helped to raise the standard of labour throughout the Kingdom should be risked, simply because some careless, thought- less, or reckless member of any society did that which the vast majority of his fellow-members utterly dis- approved of. (Applause.) He also subscribed to every- thing their honoured president, Mr. Charles E. Parker,

div.head: FATAL STEP BACKWARD.
div.p: FATAL STEP BACKWARD.

That was what they had first to do. They must secure the position they had got now,. and he submitted to them in all seriousness that thal issue ought to be decid- ed so decisively at the next election that it should not be left as it were blocking the way,and that they should not be delayed by this protectionist agitation any more than by foolish and reckless foreign wars, in going for- ward in the path of progress of which he had spoken, leading the people to a higher standard of civilization where men could be happy and happier in better ways, where the condition of England would be more glorious even than it was to-day for the benefit of our own people, and as an example by way of leadership to other countries in the world, (Applause). MR. MADDISON AND THE IRISH QUESTION.

Mr. MaDnisoN devoted the main nortion of his address to a consideration of Irish affairs. Mr. Glad- stone, be said, tackled the question and declared that unless they fairly met Irish national aspirations they would fail. Unfortunately he was not sufficiently well supported, and to-day in spite of Land Bills and the Irish Self-Government Act, we were confronted in its most palpable form with that same Irish national spirit which through the drear and dark night had always asserted itself. Mr. Gladstone had again been vindicated in the House of Commons, and the Minister who was lately Irish Secretary was doing penance before Orange fanatics. He hoped Sir Antony McDonnell would stick to his post until the Liberal Government came into power, and it would. be able, instead of curtailing and restricting his powers, to give him free scope, within all that was fair and reason- able, to carry out what he believed to be best for the country. (Applause.) Why did not Mr. Balfour resign? If Mr. Wyndham could not honourably keep his position neither could Mr. Balfour, because Mr. Wyndham acted with the full knowledge and con- sent of Mr. Balfour. Ireland was the only part of the Kingdom which had not shared in the mar- vellous prosperty of the last fifty years. As an English Radical he was there to say that until we had applied the principles of liberty to every part of the kingdom we were that much short of our principles. He was glad Mr. Crosileld was an Englishman who favoured Home Rule. That Ireland should be governed in all her domestic affairs by Irishmen who lived in the country was simply a piece of Liberalism, and he (the speaker) was prepared to endorse it and put it into-law. (Applause) Mr. Maddison dealt with the Agricultural Rating Act and pointed out how adversely it a ffected the towns. Continuing he said he believed Mr. Crosfleld was a politician because he had certain principles and ideals, and because he was moved to his candidature by a solemn sense of duty. (Applause.) Whether a man was a Capitalist or Labour man, if his principles were just and equitable and made for progress, he (Mr. Maddison) was on his platform. Despite the fact that it now appeared to be Mr. Chamberlain's awful fate to be left, the Tory party was

ALL THE MORE DANGEROUS ' because there was latent Protection in every fibre and sinew of the party. With regard to our trade, the whole trend of exports and imports for the first three months of this year was to show that there was an enormous excess of exports as compared with imports. It was worthy of note that while 51- millions of those exports went to foreign countries, only half a million went to British possessions. During the last five years of Protection, the price of wheat averaged 555. per quarter. In the last five years of Free Trade it averaged 275. An agricultural labourer in the Corn Law days earned 10s. a week, so that he had to work floe weeks and a half to buy a quarter of wheat. Under Free Trade he earned 155., and the price of wheat was only 275., so that he had to work less than two weeks to buy the same quantity of wheat that cost five and a half weeks work under Protection. Behind all Protection was an aggressive imperialism. The Government had been annexing swamps and neglecting home trade, Protec- tionists said they wanted to unite the empire with the golden bonds of commerce. The colonies would just act in their own interests if we did that. Liberals said 'Unite the empire with the golden bonds of a common tradition, and it is that bond which in the end alone will hold." (Applause.) They believed that in the principles of Free exchange of commodities they had the very best security for a prosperous people. All the great causes, concluded Mr. Illaddison, had been attacked. Freedom of combination !aye derelict at the present time ; edu- cation had been made an offence to large masses of our fellow-countrymen ; freedom had been prostituted in the ignominious fiame of capital on the Rand ; temper- ance reform had been struck the dagger blow of the men who lived on a bloated monopoly. Wherever they turned, THE TORY MARAUDERS . _ _

had been striking- at the citadel of freedom. At the next election the question would be that of citizenship against interest. Tn Warrington privilege, monopoly, and reaction were represented by Mr. Pierpoint— Liberalism—the rising hopes of the democracy—was embodied in Mr. Crosfleld. (Applause.) With the traditions of the past and the hopes of the future, he asked them to return Mr. Crosfleld as the representa- tive of liberty and justice. (Applause.) COUNCILLOR MAGINN AND IRELAND'S GRIEVANCES.

Councillor MAGINN, in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Maddison, delivered 'a vigorous criticism of the misdemeanours of the Government which, he remarked, were as numerous as the quills on a porcupine. They had increased the national debt by 109 millions, and the cost of the upkeep of the country by 70 millions, and had reduced consols from 114 to 85. In return they had given us the new Imperialism. (Laughter.) Had that made England a single bit stronger ? No. Had it made England greater in the eyes of the nations? Quite the reverse. The Aliens Bill, continued the speaker, was a juggling election Bill. He proceeded to deal with Irish affairs, and said he advocated Home Rule from the point ' of view of the Englishman. We had a great surplus of labour in this country, and Ireland would provide a field , for it, if there were proper land laws. Ireland only asked

to govern her own affairs, just as the people of Warring- ton insisted on governing their affairs within their own town, (Applause). There must have been mismanage- ment, or Ireland could not have been depopulated to such an extent. In fighting for Home Rule they would be as much for the working classes of this country as for Ireland. (Applause). The vote was heartily accorded. A WORD TO WORKINGMEN.

Mr. WILKINSON HAIGH moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman and predicted on behalf of Fairfield Ward that it would not be behind any other ward in doing its duty, under the able chairmanship of Mr. George Walker. If they would only put their shoulders to the wheel, Mr. Crosfleld would be the member for Warring- ton. (Applause.) He would remind the audience that Mr. Pierpoint voted against the Children's Messenger Bill, and on every occasion he had voted against the principles of Trade Unionism. Mr. Pierpoint had declared himself a " whole-hogger" and Mr. Bonar Law, who came clown to support him, distinctly stated that the new policy would raise the price of bread but it might lower the price of tea. He (the speaker) asked his hearers to vote for the man who would support the cheap loaf—(applause)—and who would go with such men as Mr. Maddison and Mr. Shackleton into tho right lobby. (Applause.) Mr. How Es seconded and said the League was determined to continue the fighting right up to the day of the poll. (Applause.) The vote was enthusiastically carried. A HOPEFUL OUTLOOK.

In acknowledging the compliment Mr. CROSFIELD said they had an enoimous amount of work to do and they had very great forces against them, especially in a town like Warrington. Tf they did him the great honour of allowing him to be the standard-bearer, and in that way to tight for the cause which, as John Morley said, gave them the best hope in the world for the steady progress of humanity—and that was the Liberal cause—he would go into the fight with a very big heart. (Applause.) Even if he were defeated he would not in the slightest degree feel disgraced, because they were fighting that battle with absolutely clean hands and for great causes. (Applause.) Although on the last occasion, knowing the conditions under which they fought, he did not pretend to talk about being cock-sure of winning, because the odds were very much against them, still, without indulging in any silly or extravagant optimism, or without being too cock-sure, it was his belief that they were going to win this time. (Applause.) He was sure that after the long reign of Toryism in Warrington, and after the rather drear job some of those who had been responsible for keeping the Liberal end up all this time had bad, they might fairly appeal to their fellow townsmen to give them not merely a passive, but a very active backing. (Applause.)

div.head: PHYLLIS THE ELUSIVE.
div.p: PHYLLIS THE ELUSIVE.
Mars and Cupid. [By Godfrey Dean.]
I was speaking in a low tone, though we were quite alone ; for what I was saying was not to be expressed in a conversational voice.

Phyllis leaned towards me. Her eyes, wide and innocent in expression, exercised more and more, as I proceeded, a disturbing influence on me. Suddenly as I paused, and darting a glance of doubt at me, ' really," she said. "You asked me to tell you something nice," • I replied, as if repenting of it, " and that was the nicest thing I could say. I might, certainly, have told you of the latest book, or play, but--" I stopped. Phyllis, with that wonderful dignity she so ensily commands, which always arouses my admiration and awe, stood up and turned her face coldly aside. Instead of being only three feet, I was three hundred miles away. After all, temperature is not a question solely of climate. "Think, Phyllis," I said, in excuse of my indiscre- tion, "I have not seen you for an age—forety-eight hours, isn't it?—.and when I told you that endless story—and my future—in three words, and you remarked ` really ' "--I couldn't finish in words." Her figure was motionless, and still only her profile was to be seen. I approached close to her. The subtle fragrance diffused from her hair invaded my nostrils and took hold of my senses. "I didn't wish to tell you anything. else," whispered. 'Really," she repeated, half mockingly. Not being quite sure of her I sought consolation in assertion.

"Woman," I said "remains a profound mystery after the centuries of study man has devoted to the subject—though I must say (this was an afterthought) every man has to study the subject on i7dependent lines, and in his own personal way." I have a suspicion Phyllis is pleased when she has tempted me into this sort of thing. " That," she said, quickly, and sitting down again, "is the man's point of view. The woman's is just the reverse, and if you can justify him—well, I'll forgive you." " Well ?"

"You've heard of Mahomet and the mountain, and —but I was going to tell you," she said, checking my intention, "that in a woman's eyes man is a mystery.' " Of course," I said. " If you Know all about it---" correcting myself, " I don't." To learn anything, don't know. Man," sho said, "- ought to be ashamed of him- self." •

" And he always is, except at particular times; whed his probably engaged in something, which he will be ashamed of eventually." "I am glad you see things as they are," she said, " but the particular thing I meant to point out was war." - "War ! What about it?
" Why should there ever be war ?" "Well," I said, " there are often marked differences of opinion. I might add, on matters, which, being questions of fact, are; apparently, all the more debateable."

"I don't know anything at all about that," she said " but why should nations wish to destroy each other ?" "Now you ask me," f said, "I don't see why they should. Man is a curious compound of the reasoning being, lapsing at times into the animal, which must rend and destroy, once its fangs are bared." "You can't explain it," Phyllis said. "The only explanation I can offer is this, individu- ally, man reasons! collectively, he doesn't, or can't. I admit, considered from the point of view of pure reason, two countries are not justified in going to war. Ordinarily two men would rather dine together, say, than fight. In the one case they run a grave risk." Phyllis looked suspiciously at me. " And dining together would tend to a better appre- ciation of each others good qualities. The more one thinks of it the more extraordinary it, seems. Taking him all round, man is a peaceful person. An apology is usually sufficient for a slight trespass or bit of hastiness on the part of his neighbour ; or else, the Law Courts, which punish offender and offended alike —at least he dosen't rush for the (nearest weapon with which to exterminate the other. But two Govern- ments having had words, with a stroke of the pen, so many men, forsooth, are transformed into savages. Why not settle a dispute by a game (or series of games) of chess, the loser to be mulcted in the pro- portion to the extent of his defeat ?" "You haven't justified it, or explained "I know. There are other things, even, that I can't explain." "Really "—again. "I can't explain why a man, knowing that he never will understand a woman—though he has all the essays of the ages to guide him in his researches— continues his studies. Take a woman's no,' for instance. Some men say it means 'yes.' But I never like generalising from particular cases; its risky. What does it mean?"

• "It might mean yes," she' said, "if the man desired it ; if he didn't then it would, of course, mean " Good hedging. But what must the poor man do with the awful possibility that it may mean no ' all the time." _

"Risk it, if In has any sp'rit.", "Take the case of a man and woman whose rela- tions towards each other are established, and the min tells the woman what he has told her often before." " Suppose such a case," added I, in deference to her look, " And the woman listens to it all, remarks really ' in a tone. that might mean anything, and afterwards make him feel by her manner that he has committed a crime. What is the man to do ?" "He need not assume superiority, meanwhile, by standing, up," she suggested. " But didn't he offend in any way; say something that he ought not to have said, or misconstrue? "Did he?"
" --ought to know. It is for you to know." "Then he can begin where he left off ?" Phyllis regarded me with surprise. "He must begin all over again, missing nothing out."
(These article!: orioinciily appeared in the "London Echo.") (To be concluded.)

div.head: GEORGE HOTEL LICENCE
div.p: THE GEORGE HOTEL LICENCE
MAGISTRATES DECLINE TO GRANT A RENEWAL.
Corporation Ask £3,000 Compensation.

The fate of the George Hotel licence was finally settled on 'Thursday, when the licensing compensation authority decided to allow it to lapse. It now only remains for the assessment of the amount of com- pensation which is to be paid and this question will De decided by the magistrates after expiration of the period of 21 days required by the Licensing act. The meeting of the compensation authority was held at the Police Court on Thursday, under the chairmanship of Mr. John Fairclough. The other magistrates pre- sent were Aldermen Fairclough, Smethurst, Hutchin- son, Francombe, Dr. Fox, Messrs. H. Roberts, J. Geddis. S. Wright, E. J. Guest; R. T. Fairclough, C. Jackson Holmes, W. Roberts, H. Thornton A. J. Jolley, G. Pilling and L. W. Reynolds. The Chairman at the outset said the question had been raised as to whether magistrates who were members Of the Corporation had power to vote upon I that question. The Magistrates' Clerk did not see any I objection but was not going to advise that course, and it was a matter for each individual member to use his own judgment as to whether he should vote or not. He did not know whether they cared to discuss the ques- tion then and have it settled or whether they would take their own course afterwards.

The Town Clerk : I think the members of the Town Council ought not to vote, not that it is a disqualifica- tion, but I think it is not advisable that they should vote. Alderman Smethurst : I think it was decided that the members of the Corporation have a right to vote and to be present. If we had a right to vote at a previous meeting we have a right to vote now. Mr. G. F. F. White (magistrates' clerk) : You are not legally disqualified. Mr. Wm. Roberts: Morally Mr. H. Roberts : The Town Clerk's suggestion is not a question of right but of policy. The Chairman : Each individual magistrate must use his own judgment. Alderman Fairclough : I am not here to grind my own axe. (Laughter.) Alderman Smethurst : Neither am 1. The Magistrates' Clerk : The question before you is whether or not you will renew the George Flotel licence. Mr. Browne asked the indulgence of the Court, as their worships would remember at the adjourned licensing sessions Mr. Benjamin Kenyon of the Green Man, suggested that instead of compensation being paid he would give £l,OOO for the transferring of the licence to the Green Man. He understood that some gentle- men of influence in the town thought that the wiser course as it would reduce the number of licences by one, and the £l,OOO to be paid would not come out of the othEr licencees of the town. Mr. Kenyon was still prepared to carry that offer out, if their worships thought it the better course. The Chairman : If we take that course I think we shall be out of Court. That is my feeling. Alderman Hutchinson: I don't think so. Mr. G. F. F. White : It is only in case the magtrates renew the licence that the offer is still open. The Town Clerk : The suggestion is that the Cor- poration should be content with £l,OOO in face of an offer of £2,500 from someone else. It is absurd. Mr. Browne : That is if you got it. Mr. Thornton: I thought that at our last meeting it was settled that we :hould give compensation. Mr. H. Roberts: We have to proceed by steps. All along we have been under the impression those steps were leading us to the extinction of the licence. It seems to me that if we entertain another question as the last moment it is only stultifying our previous action
I

The Chairman then asked for a vote as to whether the magistrates were in favour of the lapsing of the license, the response being in the affirmative by 17 votes to 1. Mr. A. J. Jolley was the dissentient. The Town Clerk : As you have decided that the license shall not be renewed, I put in a claim for com- pensation on behalf of the Corporation. Your Clerk will advise you that it is necessary for you to give 21 days' notice, during which claims can be entered by anY Persons having an interest in the license or the premises. I do not propose to enter into the question of compensa- tion this morning, but with all due respect to the magis- trates I suggest that the value of the license is £3,900. I can give figures to substantiate that. The valuation of a prominent architect in the town, of a license in Bridge-street was £l,OOO. The magistrates consented to the transfer of that licence to Lovely-lane to premises which cost £l,OOO. I submit that the difference between the two figures is the value of the licence and put the figures before you in order that you may consider them. I propose to submit a claim in due course. Mr. H. Roberts: I take it our position is simply to wait until a claim is made. Mr. G. F. F. White: You are bound to wait 21 days when a supplimental meeting will be called. If you approve of the amount suggested by the owners that amount will stand. If you do no approve the com- missioners will have to settle the amount. Alderman Hutchinson: Where will the money come from? Mr. G. F. F. White: Out of the compensation fund, contributed by the remaining licences. Alderman Hutchinson: Have you any fund before you ? Mr. White : No we have no fund at all as yet. Alderman Hutchinson : Then it simply means levy- ing upon the various publicans in the town? Mr. White : Yes that is what the compensation fund is. The Town Clerk : lam prepared to wait until you have money in hand and not to mortgage the fund. Mr. H. Roberts : Some weeks ago the magistratr9 decided to levy tho maximum amount upon licencee's• which will realize a certain 'sum. At the end of the year we anticipate that sum will be at our disposal. Alderman Hutchinson : What is the vote of the levy. Mr. White: It is the maximum vote under the Act, according to the levying value. Mr. Browne: It is an unknown quantity. The Town Clerk: As you have refused to renew the licence you are bound to give compensation. I propose to pull clown the premises as soon as possible as the building prevents the improvements in Bridge-street being proceeded with. Mr. White : The Corporation are entitled to keep the building up until compensation is paid. Mr. T. Halton: It is ray intention to apply for com- pensation as licensee of the premises, and I hope 9°ll will take my case into consideration. I have been ill the town for 21 years and am, really speaking, being kicked out of the premises for street improvement pr.. poses. Mr. White explained that the magistrates would have to award one sum for compensation, but could apportion that sum.

Mr. H. Roberts : We must wait until we have per" ticuinrs of the tenant's claim as to the business and profits of the house. Mr. White : Mr. Halton will be prepared with evidence as to his loss. This concluded the proceedings.

div.head: THREE ACRES AND A COW.
div.p: THREE ACRES AND A COW.
Mr. Marshall Hall Will Not Give Them AwaY•

Correspondence has taken place between Mr. Marshall Hall,-K.C., M. 13, and Mr. H. Turney, a gardener, residing at Redhill, in connection with the recent Con- servative meeting at Reigate in support of Captain Rawson, Conservative candidate. Writing on May Bth, Mr. Turney accepted the challenge, which, he says, Mr. Marshall Hall threw out that the latter would give three acres of land and a cow' if Mr. Turney would cultivate the land and milk the con'. Mr. Marshall Hall, in reply, says the ill-mannered interruption to Captain Rawson seemed to come from o' group of young fellows in the body of the hall, and it was to one of these that he addressed remarks that were intended as a rebuke. Mr. Marshall Hall concludes:—

"I am afraid that I do not feel myself under the smallest obligation to you, more especially as if s'o were present at the meeting you must know that Ile, such offer was ever made,and no such offer was accepted•A' Mr. Turney, in rejoinder, says he can bring forwar`f witnesses to prove his presence at the meeting, and that he made the interruption in question, and calls upon Mr. Hall to fulfil the offer, which was unmistakable.

WHAT MR. HALL SAID. The " Surrey Mirror's" verbatim note of what Mr' Marshall Hall said is as follows :—"I noticed that whel3 Captain Rawson was speaking one of those many young fellows at the back of the hall—(laughter)—whom I Oa so very pleased to see here, asked hitn, "How about the three acres and a cow"? "I, personally, should be ve?; pleased to give him the three acres, if I thought ha would ever take the trouble to cultivate them, aa possibly also the cow, if he knew how to milk her.

The impossibility of a right-angle screw by means of a half-ball contact when the cue ball is a long distance from the .object ball, and the simplicity of this stroke when the cue ball is quite near to the object ball.—Red ball on the spot, cue ball at A, five inches from the side cushion and on the baulk line—at R nine inches from the red.

• the cue ball be placed on the baulk line as shown on the diagram, the three balls will form a right angle, yet no one in the world could make- a ball-to-ball cannon from the D without taking the red fuller than half-ball. No matter Low hard the cue ball- were struck and how low it were hit it would, after catching the red half-ball, always pass between the red and the white, for the friction of the cloth so wears away the reverse rotation which has been imparted to the cue ball, that by the time the red ball is struck, the amount that is left is not nearly sufficient to cause the cue ball to be deflected at a- right angle. Place the cue ball high up the table, as also shown on the diagram; the balls still form exactly the same angle, but the half-ball screw is now comparatively easy. DIAGRAM 101. • s •
. . The contact between a right-angle screw and the angle of the ordinary screw In-off from the red on the spot.

Many ordinary players consider they do a big screw when they screw the in-off from the red on the spot playing from the D, but Such a stroke is not nearly a right angle screw. With the red on the spot, the cue ball cannot form a right angle with . it and the pocket from any- where on the D line, nor as a matter of fact even from anywhere on the baulk line. A line drawn at right angles to the red and the pocket would meet the side cushion several inches outside baulk, and from anywhere near the termination of this line the screw in-off would be a very big shot, though by no means impossible. It would, however, be quite impossible were the object ball hit vgi fuller than half-ball. I DIAGRAM 102 1 ... k.‘ i % '1 /. !RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. Motorists "Abominable and Disgraceful Conduct." The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present Messrs. S. Woodward (presiding), G. Pilling, C. Roylance, J. Bolshaw,H. Eyes, G. Egerton- Warburton, A. Broom, 11, H. Davies, C. E. Linaker, C. E. Linaker, jun., J. fl. Davies, J. Smith, T. Wright, H. Mawdsley,J. L. Jones, E. Bretherton' C Houghton, R. A. Chrimes, J. Fryer, J. Spruce, J. Hallows, J. Whitley R. Billington, W. Turner, J. B. Chadwick, T. Antwis, Admiral Jones-Parry, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), J. Swinton, W. Diggle (surveyors), J. Farrington (inspector of nnisances) and Dr. Adams (medical officer). D tNGER 0 US ROADWAY AT WALTON. Mr. Hunter, engineer to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, wrote in reply to a letter from the Council with regard to the dangerous state of the roadway at Walton Arches. He enclosed a plan which he said showed that it was impossible that the dredging of the river could have affected the banks, especially when it was remembered that the river had only been dredged twice in two years in that neighbourhood. Mr. Whilley said that the high tides had wasted away the park to such an extent that the roadway had become I dangerous. ! Mr. Swinton said that the subsidence of the banlr had been going on ever since he came into the district. The , Camel' attempted to stop it by planting willows and ' he believed they would have been successful had it not been for the dredging. Mr. Roylance thought the diverting of the river had had some effect on the bank. The matter was allowed to drop. A COMPLAINT FROM MOORE. Dr. Adams reported that he had received a letter from Dr. 'smith, who wrote writhe medical attendant of Mr. Bleckley, calling attention to the drain which crossed the railway at Moore. Theattention of the authorities should be directed to the insanitary state of the sewer and it was necessary something should be done before the present summer advanced. • Dr. Adams said he had visited the premises and had found not the slightest trace of an objectionable smell. He had left word for Mr. Bleckley to state specifically what he complained of. Mr. Ashton pointed out that the Council and the Railway Company were, and had been for sometime, in communication with regard to the sewer. THE REGULATION OF MOTOR TRAFFIC., STRONG REMARKS BY MR. ANTWIS. Mr. Antwis moved that the Clerk be instructed to write to the District Councils in Cheshire with respect to the revising of the speed of motor bicycles and motor cars of the two he thought the motor " byke was the worst. Mr. Antwis went on to speak of the dust caused by motorists and remarked that at Hartford young ladies could not go to Sunday evening service for fear of having their clothing spoiled by the dust. He had been waiting for the County Council to take , action. He thought the speed limit should be 18 miles an hour at the outside. He did not care so much about motor cars as about motor bicyclists who conducted themselves in an abominable and disgraceful way. He had as good a pony as anyone for passing motors and recently he drove to Northwich. While there two motor bykes "came along and as they passed the drivers caused the machine to make a noise like guns being fired with the result that he had difficulty in keeping his pony off the footpath. If a man discharged a gun within 50 yards of the roadway he was fined for it. The conduct of motor bicyclists was disgraceful. They deliberately tried to terrify women and when they , succeeded they turned round and jeered. Now-a-days it was impossible for old couples to drive along the roads which they had made on account of those abom- inable trespassers. Mr. Linaker seconded. Mr. Antwis said motor bicyclists should be given three months in which to put their machines in order and if in that time they could not prevent them being explosive nuisances they should be shut off the roadway altogether. The Chairman said they were all agreed that the speed , of motors should be reduced. They, however, had nothing to do with the mechanism of a motet. On the 'suggestion of the Chairman, Mr. Antwis gave notice that he would move in the matter at the next meeting of the Council. „ Mr. Linaker said he was surprised at the remarks made by Mr. Antwis with regard to the young ladies in Hartford. If Mr. Antwis had said the young ladies i tempers were ruffled and that they were not n a fit Christian spirit to go to Church he would have under- stood it. (Laughter.) Mr. Whitley said that motors in Stockton Heath had become a nuisance and a danger. He thought tie fining of motorists was not enough. He thought the cars should be confiscated. On the motion of Mr. Spruce, Messrs. Woodward, Pilling, Antwis, Whitley and Linaker were appointed a sub-committee to go into the question before the next meeting of the Council. 41111 k RUNCORN AND WIDNES. __— THE TRANSPORTER BRIDGE. The Widnes aed Runcorn Bridge Company, of which Sir John Brunner, M.P., is chatrman, will! open the transporter bridge across the Mersey an Monday, 29th inst. There will be a recepti on at the Widnes own Hall at half-past twelve, and a luncheon at the Drill Hall, Runcorn, at two o'clock. Tom RUNCORN TRAGEDY. On Wednesday, the boy Frederick Walker was again brought before Mr Inman, at Runcorn, charged with the attempted murder of Ethel Gatley.—Superintendent Ennion applied for a further remand for a week. The girl, he said, had a relapse on Saturday., but she was now going on well.—The prisoner was again remanded. WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD SHOW. The Council of the Wirral and Birkenhead Agricul- tural Society has now Issued the prize schedule for the forthcoming show, to be held in the magnificent show- yard at Bebington on the 22nd, 23rd and 24th June next under the presidency of Sir Elliott Lees, Bart., D. 5.0., M.P. There are several alterations and improvements inlthe prize list for this year. The machinery-in-motion also motor cars, lurries, Boa., are specially catered for— several of the society's gold medals being offered for competition in each section. Some additional challenge cups are offered for competition, including a 25-guinea cup for Shropshire sheep open competition. Handsome prizes are also being oiled for the leaping competitions each day. The total amount of prizes offered for com- petition this year amounts to some £3,000. Prize schedules have already been posted to the leading exhibitors throughout the kingdom,and should a further copy be required, or any other information, same can be obtained on application to the secretary' Mr. Arthur H. Edwardson, 6, Hamilton-square, Birkenhead. RADIUM AT £600,000 AN OUNCE. The price of radium has increased so much recently, wing to the difficulty of obtaining further supplies, , that research work is almost at a standstill. Sir William Ramsay told an" Evening Standard" representative on Wednesday that as much as £2O a milligramme,or at the rate of £600,000 an ounce, was being demanded, and the quantity available, even at that price, is very small I indeed. The largest electric generator in the world has been completed at Niagara Falls by the Canada Electric Com- pany. It is to be used in the power works erected at the Falls, and is of 12,000 horse-power.
